senses.d: A shortened form of Papa.
A kind of moccasin, having the edges of the sole turned up and sewed to the upper.
A single movement from one foot to the other in walking; a step.
The length of a step in walking or marching, reckoned from the heel of one foot to the heel of the other; — used as a unit in measuring distances; as, he advanced fifty paces.
Manner of stepping or moving; gait; walk; as, the walk, trot, canter, gallop, and amble are paces of the horse; a swaggering pace; a quick pace.
q: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, Creeps in this petty pace from day to day.
In the military schools of riding a variety of paces are taught.

senses.d: A slow gait; a footpace.
Specifically, a kind of fast amble; a rack.
Any single movement, step, or procedure.
q: The first pace necessary for his majesty to make is to fall into confidence with Spain.

senses.d: A broad step or platform; any part of a floor slightly raised above the rest, as around an altar, or at the upper end of a hall.
A device in a loom, to maintain tension on the warp in pacing the web.

Pace.etym: [OE. pas, F. pas, from L. passus a step, pace, orig., a stretching out of the feet in walking; cf. pandere, passum, to spread, stretch; perh. akin to E. patent. Cf. Pas, Pass.]

senses.d: To go; to walk; specifically, to move with regular or measured steps.
To proceed; to pass on.
q: Or that I further in this tale pace.

senses.d: To move quickly by lifting the legs on the same side together, as a horse; to amble with rapidity; to rack.
To pass away; to die.
To walk over with measured tread; to move slowly over or upon; as, the guard paces his round.
To measure by steps or paces; as, to pace a piece of ground.
To develop, guide, or control the pace or paces of; to teach the pace; to break in.
q: If you can, pace your wisdom In that good path that I would wish it go.

senses.d: To make to be at peace; to appease; to calm; to still; to quiet; to allay the agitation, excitement, or resentment of; to tranquillize; as, to pacify a man when angry; to pacify pride, appetite, or importunity.
q: To pacify and settle those countries.

Pacify.etym: [F. pacifier, L. pacificare; pax, pacis, peace + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Peace, and -fy.]

senses.d: To use the hands or fingers in toying; to make caressing strokes.
To dabble in water with hands or feet; to use a paddle, or something which serves as a paddle, in swimming, in paddling a boat, etc.
q: As the men were paddling for their lives.
While paddling ducks the standing lake desire.

Paddle.etym: [Prob. for pattle, and a dim. of pat, v.; cf. also E. pad to tread, Prov. G. paddeln, padden, to walk with short steps, to paddle, G. patschen to splash, dash, dabble, F. patouiller to dabble, splash, fr. patte a paw. √21.]

senses.d: To pat or stroke amorously, or gently.
q: To be paddling palms and pinching fingers.

senses.d: To propel with, or as with, a paddle or paddles.
To pad; to tread upon; to trample.
An implement with a broad blade, which is used without a fixed fulcrum in propelling and steering canoes and boats.
The broad part of a paddle, with which the stroke is made; hence, any short, broad blade, resembling that of a paddle.
q: Thou shalt have a paddle upon thy weapon.

senses.d: One of the broad boards, or floats, at the circumference of a water wheel, or paddle wheel.
A small gate in sluices or lock gates to admit or let off water; — also called clough.
A paddle-shaped foot, as of the sea turtle.
A paddle-shaped implement for stirring or mixing.
Receiving pay; compensated; hired; as, a paid attorney.
Satisfied; contented.
Punishment suffered or denounced; suffering or evil inflicted as a punishment for crime, or connected with the commission of a crime; penalty.
q: We will, by way of mulct or pain, lay it upon him.
Interpose, on pain of my displeasure.
None shall presume to fly, under pain of death.

senses.d: Any uneasy sensation in animal bodies, from slight uneasiness to extreme distress or torture, proceeding from a derangement of functions, disease, or injury by violence; bodily distress; bodily suffering; an ache; a smart.
Specifically, the throes or travail of childbirth.
q: She bowed herself and travailed, for her pains came upon her.

senses.d: Uneasiness of mind; mental distress; disquietude; anxiety; grief; solicitude; anguish.
q: In rapture as in pain.

Pain.etym: [OE. peine, F. peine, fr. L. poena, penalty, punishment, torment, pain; akin to Gr. ποινή penalty. Cf. Penal, Pine to languish, Punish.]

senses.d: To inflict suffering upon as a penalty; to punish.
To put to bodily uneasiness or anguish; to afflict with uneasy sensations of any degree of intensity; to torment; to torture; as, his dinner or his wound pained him; his stomach pained him.
q: Excess of cold, as well as heat, pains us.

senses.d: To render uneasy in mind; to disquiet; to distress; to grieve; as, a child's faults pain his parents.
q: I am pained at my very heart.

Pain.syn: To disquiet; trouble; afflict; grieve; aggrieve; distress; agonize; torment; torture.
Pain.etym: [OE. peinen, OF. pener, F. peiner to fatigue. See Pain, n.]

senses.d: Full of pain; causing uneasiness or distress, either physical or mental; afflictive; disquieting; distressing.
Requiring labor or toil; difficult; executed with laborious effort; as a painful service; a painful march.
Painstaking; careful; industrious.
q: A very painful person, and a great clerk.
Nor must the painful husbandman be tired.

Painful.syn: Disquieting; troublesome; afflictive; distressing; grievous; laborious; toilsome; difficult; arduous.

senses.d: Labor; toilsome effort; care or trouble taken; — plural in form, but used with a singular or plural verb, commonly the former.
q: And all my pains is sorted to no proof.
The pains they had taken was very great.
The labored earth your pains have sowed and tilled.

senses.d: To cover with coloring matter; to apply paint to; as, to paint a house, a signboard, etc.
q: Jezebel painted her face and tired her head.

senses.d: Fig.: To color, stain, or tinge; to adorn or beautify with colors; to diversify with colors.
q: Not painted with the crimson spots of blood.
Cuckoo buds of yellow hue Do paint the meadows with delight.

senses.d: To form in colors a figure or likeness of on a flat surface, as upon canvas; to represent by means of colors or hues; to exhibit in a tinted image; to portray with paints; as, to paint a portrait or a landscape.
Fig.: To represent or exhibit to the mind; to describe vividly; to delineate; to image; to depict.
q: Disloyal? The word is too good to paint out her wickedness.
If folly grow romantic, I must paint it.

Paint.syn: To color; picture; depict; portray; delineate; sketch; draw; describe.
Paint.etym: [OE. peinten, fr. F. peint, p. p. of peindre to paint, fr. L. pingere, pictum; cf. Gr. ποικίλοσ many-colored, Skr. piç to adorn. Cf. Depict, Picture, Pigment, Pint.]

senses.d: To practice the art of painting; as, the artist paints well.
To color one's face by way of beautifying it.
q: Let her paint an inch thick.

senses.d: A pigment or coloring substance.
A cosmetic; rouge.
Covered or adorned with paint; portrayed in colors.
q: As idle as a painted ship Upon a painted ocean.

senses.d: Marked with bright colors; as, the painted turtle; painted bunting.
The act or employment of laying on, or adorning with, paints or colors.
The work of the painter; also, any work of art in which objects are represented in color on a flat surface; a colored representation of any object or scene; a picture.
Color laid on; paint.
A depicting by words; vivid representation in words.
A number of things resembling one another, or belonging together; a set; as, a pair or flight of stairs. “A pair of beads.” Chaucer. Beau. & Fl. “Four pair of stairs.” Macaulay.
q: Two crowns in my pocket, two pair of cards.

senses.d: Two things of a kind, similar in form, suited to each other, and intended to be used together; as, a pair of gloves or stockings; a pair of shoes.
Two of a sort; a span; a yoke; a couple; a brace; as, a pair of horses; a pair of oxen.
A married couple; a man and wife.
A single thing, composed of two pieces fitted to each other and used together; as, a pair of scissors; a pair of tongs; a pair of bellows.

Two members of opposite parties or opinion, as in a parliamentary body, who mutually agree not to vote on a given question, or on issues of a party nature during a specified time; as, there were two pairs on the final vote.
In a mechanism, two elements, or bodies, which are so applied to each other as to mutually constrain relative motion.

Pair.etym: [F. paire, LL. paria, L. paria, pl. of par pair, fr. par, adj., equal. Cf. Apparel, Par equality, Peer an equal.]

senses.d: To be joined in pairs; to couple; to mate, as for breeding.
To suit; to fit, as a counterpart.
q: My heart was made to fit and pair with thine.

senses.d: Same as To pair off. See phrase below.
To unite in couples; to form a pair of; to bring together, as things which belong together, or which complement, or are adapted to one another.
q: Glossy jet is paired with shining white.

senses.d: To engage (one's self) with another of opposite opinions not to vote on a particular question or class of questions.
To impair.
The residence of a sovereign, including the lodgings of high officers of state, and rooms for business, as well as halls for ceremony and reception.
The official residence of a bishop or other distinguished personage.
Loosely, any unusually magnificent or stately house.

Palace.etym: [OE. palais, F. palais, fr. L. palatium, fr. Palatium, one of the seven hills of Rome, on which Augustus had his residence. Cf. Paladin.]

senses.d: Wanting in color; not ruddy; dusky white; pallid; wan; as, a pale face; a pale red; a pale blue.
q: Speechless he stood and pale.
They are not of complexion red or pale.

senses.d: Not bright or brilliant; of a faint luster or hue; dim; as, the pale light of the moon.
q: The night, methinks, is but the daylight sick; It looks a little paler.

Pale.etym: [F. pâle, fr. pâlir to turn pale, L. pallere to be or look pale. Cf. Appall, Fallow, Pall, v. i., Pallid.]

senses.d: Paleness; pallor.
To turn pale; to lose color or luster.
q: Apt to pale at a trodden worm.

senses.d: To make pale; to diminish the brightness of.
q: The glowworm shows the matin to be near, And 'gins to pale his uneffectual fire.

senses.d: A pointed stake or slat, either driven into the ground, or fastened to a rail at the top and bottom, for fencing or inclosing; a picket.
q: Deer creep through when a pale tumbles down.

senses.d: That which incloses or fences in; a boundary; a limit; a fence; a palisade.
A space or field having bounds or limits; a limited region or place; an inclosure; — often used figuratively.
A stripe or band, as on a garment.
One of the greater ordinaries, being a broad perpendicular stripe in an escutcheon, equally distant from the two edges, and occupying one third of it.
A cheese scoop.
A shore for bracing a timber before it is fastened.

Pale.etym: [F. pal, fr. L. palus: cf. D. paal. See Pole a stake, and 1st Pallet.]

senses.d: To inclose with pales, or as with pales; to encircle; to encompass; to fence off.
q: ribbed and paled in With rocks unscalable and roaring waters.

senses.d: The quality or condition of being pale; want of freshness or ruddiness; a sickly whiteness; lack of color or luster; wanness.
q: The blood the virgin's cheek forsook; A livid paleness spreads o'er all her look.

senses.d: Same as Palea.
The inner and somewhat concave part of the hand between the bases of the fingers and the wrist.
q: Clench'd her fingers till they bit the palm.

senses.d: A lineal measure equal either to the breadth of the hand or to its length from the wrist to the ends of the fingers; a hand; — used in measuring a horse's height.
A metallic disk, attached to a strap, and worn on the palm of the hand, — used to push the needle through the canvas, in sewing sails, etc.
The broad flattened part of an antler, as of a full-grown fallow deer; — so called as resembling the palm of the hand with its protruding fingers.
The flat inner face of an anchor fluke.

Palm.etym: [OE. paume, F. paume, L. palma, Gr. παλάμη, akin to Skr. pāṇi hand, and E. fumble. See Fumble, Feel, and cf. 2d Palm.]

senses.d: Any endogenous tree of the order Palmæ or Palmaceæ; a palm tree.
A branch or leaf of the palm, anciently borne or worn as a symbol of victory or rejoicing.
q: A great multitude . . . stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palme in their hands.

senses.d: Any symbol or token of superiority, success, or triumph; also, victory; triumph; supremacy.
q: So get the start of the majestic world And bear the palm alone.

Palm.etym: [AS. palm, L. palma; — so named fr. the leaf resembling a hand. See 1st Palm, and cf. Pam.]

senses.d: To handle.
To manipulate with, or conceal in, the palm of the hand; to juggle.
q: They palmed the trick that lost the game.

senses.d: To impose by fraud, as by sleight of hand; to put by unfair means; — usually with off.
q: For you may palm upon us new for old.

senses.d: To “grease the palm” of; to bribe or tip.
Any hairy caterpillar which appears in great numbers, devouring herbage, and wandering about like a palmer. The name is applied also to other voracious insects.
In America, the larva of any one of several moths, which destroys the foliage of fruit and forest trees, esp. the larva of Ypsolophus pometellus, which sometimes appears in vast numbers.
Paralysis, complete or partial. See Paralysis.

Palsy.etym: [OE. palesie, parlesy, OF. paralesie, F. paralysie, L. paralysis. See Paralysis.]

senses.d: To affect with palsy, or as with palsy; to deprive of action or energy; to paralyze.
A part; a portion.
The distance comprised between the angle of the epaule and the flanked angle.
A leaf of gold or silver.
To join or fit together; to unite.

Pan.etym: [Cf. F. pan skirt, lappet, L. pannus a cloth, rag, W. panu to fur, to full.]

senses.d: The betel leaf; also, the masticatory made of the betel leaf, etc. See Betel.

The god of shepherds, guardian of bees, and patron of fishing and hunting. He is usually represented as having the head and trunk of a man, with the legs, horns, and tail of a goat, and as playing on the shepherd's pipe, which he is said to have invented.
A shallow, open dish or vessel, usually of metal, employed for many domestic uses, as for setting milk for cream, for frying or baking food, etc.; also employed for various uses in manufacturing.
A closed vessel for boiling or evaporating. See Vacuum pan, under Vacuum.
The part of a flintlock which holds the priming.
The skull, considered as a vessel containing the brain; the upper part of the head; the brainpan; the cranium.
A recess, or bed, for the leaf of a hinge.
The hard stratum of earth that lies below the soil. See Hard pan, under Hard.
A natural basin, containing salt or fresh water, or mud.

Pan.etym: [OE. panne, AS. panne; cf. D. pan, G. pfanne, OHG. pfanna, Icel., Sw., LL., & Ir. panna, of uncertain origin; cf. L. patina, E. paten.]

senses.d: To separate, as gold, from dirt or sand, by washing in a kind of pan.
q: We . . . witnessed the process of cleaning up and panning out, which is the last process of separating the pure gold from the fine dirt and black sand.

senses.d: To yield gold in, or as in, the process of panning; — usually with out; as, the gravel panned out richly.
To turn out (profitably or unprofitably); to result; to develop; as, the investigation, or the speculation, panned out poorly.
A paroxysm of extreme pain or anguish; a sudden and transitory agony; a throe; as, the pangs of death.
To torture; to cause to have great pain or suffering; to torment.
To breathe quickly or in a labored manner, as after exertion or from eagerness or excitement; to respire with heaving of the breast; to gasp.
q: Pluto plants for breath from out his cell.

senses.d: Hence: To long eagerly; to desire earnestly.
q: As the hart panteth after the water brooks.
Who pants for glory finds but short repose.

senses.d: To beat with unnatural violence or rapidity; to palpitate, or throb; — said of the heart.
To sigh; to flutter; to languish.
q: The whispering breeze Pants on the leaves, and dies upon the trees.

Pant.etym: [Cf. F. panteler to gasp for breath, OF. panteisier to be breathless, F. pantois out of breath; perh. akin to E. phantom, the verb prob. orig. meaning, to have the nightmare.]

senses.d: To breathe forth quickly or in a labored manner; to gasp out.
q: There is a cavern where my spirit Was panted forth in anguish.

senses.d: To long for; to be eager after.
q: Then shall our hearts pant thee.

senses.d: A quick breathing; a catching of the breath; a gasp.
A violent palpitation of the heart.
A nipple; a mammilla; a teat.
q: The paps which thou hast sucked.

senses.d: A rounded, nipplelike hill or peak; anything resembling a nipple in shape; a mamelon.

Pap.etym: [Cf. OSw. papp. Cf. Pap soft food.]

senses.d: A soft food for infants, made of bread boiled or softened in milk or water.
Nourishment or support from official patronage; as, treasury pap.
The pulp of fruit.

Pap.etym: [Cf. D. pap, G. pappe, both perh. fr. L. papa, pappa, the word with which infants call for food: cf. It. pappa.]

senses.d: To feed with pap.
A spiritual father; specifically, the pope.

Pape.etym: [Cf. F. pape, fr. L. papa. See Pope.]

senses.d: A substance in the form of thin sheets or leaves intended to be written or printed on, or to be used in wrapping. It is made of rags, straw, bark, wood, or other fibrous material, which is first reduced to pulp, then molded, pressed, and dried.
A sheet, leaf, or piece of such substance.
A printed or written instrument; a document, essay, or the like; a writing; as, a paper read before a scientific society.
q: They brought a paper to me to be signed.

senses.d: A printed sheet appearing periodically; a newspaper; a journal; as, a daily paper.
Negotiable evidences of indebtedness; notes; bills of exchange, and the like; as, the bank holds a large amount of his paper.
Decorated hangings or coverings for walls, made of paper. See Paper hangings, below.
A paper containing (usually) a definite quantity; as, a paper of pins, tacks, opium, etc.
A medicinal preparation spread upon paper, intended for external application; as, cantharides paper.

Paper.etym: [F. papier, fr. L. papyrus papyrus, from which the Egyptians made a kind of paper, Gr. πάπυροσ. Cf. Papyrus.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to paper; made of paper; resembling paper; existing only on paper; unsubstantial; as, a paper box; a paper army.
To cover with paper; to furnish with paper hangings; as, to paper a room or a house.
To fold or inclose in paper.
To put on paper; to make a memorandum of.
Procurable.
A comparison; a similitude; specifically, a short fictitious narrative of something which might really occur in life or nature, by means of which a moral is drawn; as, the parables of Christ.
q: Declare unto us the parable of the tares.

Parable.syn: See Allegory, and Note under Apologue.
Parable.etym: [F. parabole, L. parabola, fr. Gr. � a placing beside or together, a comparing, comparison, a parable, fr. � to throw beside, compare; παρά beside + � to throw; cf. Skr. gal to drop. Cf. Emblem, Gland, Palaver, Parabola, Parley, Parabole, Symbol.]

senses.d: To represent by parable.
q: Which by the ancient sages was thus parabled.

senses.d: The garden of Eden, in which Adam and Eve were placed after their creation.
The abode of sanctified souls after death.
q: To-day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
It sounds to him like her mother's voice, Singing in Paradise.

senses.d: A place of bliss; a region of supreme felicity or delight; hence, a state of happiness.
q: The earth Shall be all paradise.
Wrapt in the very paradise of some creative vision.

senses.d: An open space within a monastery or adjoining a church, as the space within a cloister, the open court before a basilica, etc.
A churchyard or cemetery.

Paradise.etym: [OE. & F. paradis, L. paradisus, fr. Gr. παράδεισοσ park, paradise, fr. Zend pairidaēza an inclosure; pairi around (akin to Gr. περί) + diz to throw up, pile up; cf. Skr. dih to smear, and E. dough. Cf. Parvis.]

senses.d: To affect or exalt with visions of felicity; to entrance; to bewitch.

A lover, of either sex; a wooer or a mistress (formerly in a good sense, now only in a bad one); one who takes the place, without possessing the rights, of a husband or wife; — used of a man or a woman.
q: The seducer appeared with dauntless front, accompanied by his paramour

senses.d: Love; gallantry.

Paramour.etym: [F. par amour, lit., by or with love. See 2d Par, and Amour.]

senses.d: By or with love, esp. the love of the sexes; — sometimes written as two words.
q: For par amour, I loved her first ere thou.

senses.d: A portion of anything taken separately; a fragment of a whole; a part.
q: Two parcels of the white of an egg.
The parcels of the nation adopted different forms of self-government.

senses.d: A part; a portion; a piece; as, a certain piece of land is part and parcel of another piece.
An indiscriminate or indefinite number, measure, or quantity; a collection; a group.
q: This youthful parcel Of noble bachelors stand at my disposing.

senses.d: A number or quantity of things put up together; a bundle; a package; a packet.
q: 'Tis like a parcel sent you by the stage.

Parcel.etym: [F. parcelle a small part, fr. (assumed) LL. particella, dim. of L. pars. See Part, n., and cf. Particle.]

senses.d: To divide and distribute by parts or portions; — often with out or into.
q: These ghostly kings would parcel out my power.
The broad woodland parceled into farms.

senses.d: To add a parcel or item to; to itemize.
q: That mine own servant should Parcel the sum of my disgraces by Addition of his envy.

senses.d: To make up into a parcel; as, to parcel a customer's purchases; the machine parcels yarn, wool, etc.
Part or half; in part; partially. Shak.
q: The worthy dame was parcel-blind.
One that . . . was parcel-bearded .

senses.d: To burn the surface of; to scorch; to roast over the fire, as dry grain; as, to parch the skin; to parch corn.
q: Ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn.

senses.d: To dry to extremity; to shrivel with heat; as, the mouth is parched from fever.
q: The ground below is parched.

Parch.etym: [OE. perchen to pierce, hence used of a piercing heat or cold, OF. perchier, another form of percier, F. percer. See Pierce.]

senses.d: To become scorched or superficially burnt; to be very dry.
The skin of a lamb, sheep, goat, young calf, or other animal, prepared for writing on. See Vellum.
q: But here's a parchment with the seal of Cæsar.

senses.d: The envelope of the coffee grains, inside the pulp.

Parchment.etym: [OE. parchemin, perchemin, F. parchemin, LL. pergamenum, L. pergamena, pergamina, fr. L. Pergamenus of or belonging to Pergamus an ancient city of Mysia in Asia Minor, where parchment was first used.]

senses.d: The act of pardoning; forgiveness, as of an offender, or of an offense; release from penalty; remission of punishment; absolution.
q: Pardon, my lord, for me and for my tidings.
But infinite in pardon was my judge.

senses.d: An official warrant of remission of penalty.
q: Sign me a present pardon for my brother.

senses.d: The state of being forgiven.

A release, by a sovereign, or officer having jurisdiction, from the penalties of an offense, being distinguished from amnesty, which is a general obliteration and canceling of a particular line of past offenses.

Pardon.etym: [F., fr. pardonner to pardon. See Pardon, v. t.]

senses.d: To absolve from the consequences of a fault or the punishment of crime; to free from penalty; — applied to the offender.
q: In this thing the Lord pardon thy servant.
I pray you, pardon me; pray heartily, pardon me.

senses.d: To remit the penalty of; to suffer to pass without punishment; to forgive; — applied to offenses.
q: I pray thee, pardon my sin.
Apollo, pardon My great profaneness 'gainst thine oracle!

senses.d: To refrain from exacting as a penalty.
q: I pardon thee thy life before thou ask it.

senses.d: To give leave (of departure) to.
q: Even now about it! I will pardon you.

Pardon.syn: To forgive; absolve; excuse; overlook; remit; acquit. See Excuse.
Pardon.etym: [Either fr. pardon, n., or from F. pardonner, LL. perdonare; L. per through, thoroughly, perfectly + donare to give, to present. See Par-, and Donation.]

senses.d: To cut off, or shave off, the superficial substance or extremities of; as, to pare an apple; to pare a horse's hoof.
To remove; to separate; to cut or shave, as the skin, rind, or outside part, from anything; — followed by off or away; as, to pare off the rind of fruit; to pare away redundancies.
Fig.: To diminish the bulk of; to reduce; to lessen.
q: The king began to pare a little the privilege of clergy.

Pare.etym: [F. parer to pare, as a horse's hoofs, to dress or curry, as, leather, to clear, as anchors or cables, to parry, ward off, fr. L. parare to prepare. Cf. Empire, Parade, Pardon, Parry, Prepare.]

senses.d: One who begets, or brings forth, offspring; a father or a mother.
q: Children, obey your parents in the Lord.

senses.d: That which produces; cause; source; author; begetter; as, idleness is the parent of vice.
q: Regular industry is the parent of sobriety.

Parent.etym: [L. parens, -entis; akin to parere to bring forth; cf. Gr. πορει̑ν to give, beget: cf. F. parent. Cf. Part.]

senses.d: One of the portions, equal or unequal, into which anything is divided, or regarded as divided; something less than a whole; a number, quantity, mass, or the like, regarded as going to make up, with others, a larger number, quantity, mass, etc., whether actually separate or not; a piece; a fragment; a fraction; a division; a member; a constituent.
q: And kept back part of the price, . . . and brought a certain part and laid it at the apostles'feet.
Our ideas of extension and number — do they not contain a secret relation of the parts ?
I am a part of all that I have met.

senses.d: An equal constituent portion; one of several or many like quantities, numbers, etc., into which anything is divided, or of which it is composed; proportional division or ingredient.
q: An homer is the tenth part of an ephah.
A thought which, quartered, hath but one part wisdom, And ever three parts coward.

senses.d: A constituent portion of a living or spiritual whole; a member; an organ; an essential element.
q: All the parts were formed . . . into one harmonious body.
The pulse, the glow of every part.

senses.d: A constituent of character or capacity; quality; faculty; talent; — usually in the plural with a collective sense.
q: Which maintained so politic a state of evil, that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them.

senses.d: Quarter; region; district; — usually in the plural.
q: All parts resound with tumults, plaints, and fears.

senses.d: Such portion of any quantity, as when taken a certain number of times, will exactly make that quantity; as, 3 is a part of 12; — the opposite of multiple. Also, a line or other element of a geometrical figure.
That which belongs to one, or which is assumed by one, or which falls to one, in a division or apportionment; share; portion; lot; interest; concern; duty; office.
q: We have no part in David.
Accuse not Nature! she hath done her part; Do thou but thine.
Let me bear My part of danger with an equal share.

senses.d: One of the opposing parties or sides in a conflict or a controversy; a faction.
q: For he that is not against us is on our part.
Make whole kingdoms take her brother's part.

senses.d: A particular character in a drama or a play; an assumed personification; also, the language, actions, and influence of a character or an actor in a play; or, figuratively, in real life. See To act a part, under Act.
q: That part Was aptly fitted and naturally performed.
It was a brute part of him to kill so capital a calf.
Honor and shame from no condition rise; Act well your part, there all the honor lies.

senses.d: One of the different melodies of a concerted composition, which heard in union compose its harmony; also, the music for each voice or instrument; as, the treble, tenor, or bass part; the violin part, etc.

Part.syn: Portion; section; division; fraction; fragment; piece; share; constituent. See Portion, and Section.
Part.etym: [F. part, L. pars, gen. partis; cf. parere to bring forth, produce. Cf. Parent, Depart, Parcel, Partner, Party, Portion.]

senses.d: To divide; to separate into distinct parts; to break into two or more parts or pieces; to sever.
q: There, parted into rainbow hues.

senses.d: To divide into shares; to divide and distribute; to allot; to apportion; to share.
q: To part his throne, and share his heaven with thee.
They parted my raiment among them.

senses.d: To separate or disunite; to cause to go apart; to remove from contact or contiguity; to sunder.
q: The Lord do so to me, and more also, if aught but death part thee and me.
While he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven.
The narrow seas that part The French and English.

senses.d: To hold apart; to stand between; to intervene betwixt, as combatants.
q: The stumbling night did part our weary powers.

senses.d: To separate by a process of extraction, elimination, or secretion; as, to part gold from silver.
q: The liver minds his own affair, . . . And parts and strains the vital juices.

senses.d: To leave; to quit.
q: Since presently your souls must part your bodies.

Part.etym: [F. partir, L. partire, partiri, p. p. partitus, fr. pars, gen. partis, a part. See Part, n.]

senses.d: To be broken or divided into parts or pieces; to break; to become separated; to go asunder; as, rope parts; his hair parts in the middle.
To go away; to depart; to take leave; to quit each other; hence, to die; — often with from.
q: He wrung Bassanio's hand, and so they parted.
He owned that he had parted from the duke only a few hours before.
His precious bag, which he would by no means part from.

senses.d: To perform an act of parting; to relinquish a connection of any kind; — followed by with or from.
q: Celia, for thy sake, I part With all that grew so near my heart.
Powerful hands . . . will not part Easily from possession won with arms.
It was strange to him that a father should feel no tenderness at parting with an only son.

senses.d: To have a part or share; to partake.
Partly; in a measure.
To take a part, portion, lot, or share, in common with others; to have a share or part; to participate; to share; as, to partake of a feast with others.
q: When I against myself with thee partake.

senses.d: To have something of the properties, character, or office; — usually followed by of.
q: The attorney of the Duchy of Lancaster partakes partly of a judge, and partly of an attorney-general.

senses.d: To partake of; to have a part or share in; to share.
q: Let every one partake the general joy.

senses.d: To admit to a share; to cause to participate; to give a part to.
To distribute; to communicate.
One who partakes; a sharer; a participator.
q: Partakers of their spiritual things.
Wish me partaker in my happiness.

senses.d: An accomplice; an associate; a partner.
q: Partakers wish them in the blood of the prophets.

senses.d: Separated; divided.
Endowed with parts or abilities.
Cleft so that the divisions reach nearly, but not quite, to the midrib, or the base of the blade; — said of a leaf, and used chiefly in composition; as, three-parted, five-parted, etc.
Of or pertaining to ancient Parthia, in Asia.
A native of Parthia.
Of, pertaining to, or affecting, a part only; not general or universal; not total or entire; as, a partial eclipse of the moon.
Inclined to favor one party in a cause, or one side of a question, more then the other; biased; not indifferent; as, a judge should not be partial.
q: Ye have been partial in the law.

senses.d: Having a predilection for; inclined to favor unreasonably; foolishly fond.
q: Not partial to an ostentatious display.

senses.d: Pertaining to a subordinate portion; as, a compound umbel is made up of a several partial umbels; a leaflet is often supported by a partial petiole.

Partial.etym: [F., fr. LL. partials, fr. L. pars, gen. partis, a part; cf. (for sense 1) F. partiel. See Part, n.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being partial; inclination to favor one party, or one side of a question, more than the other; undue bias of mind.
A predilection or inclination to one thing rather than to others; special taste or liking; as, a partiality for poetry or painting.

Relating to a part or portion of anything; concerning a part separated from the whole or from others of the class; separate; sole; single; individual; specific; as, the particular stars of a constellation.
q: each particular hair to stand an end, Like quills upon the fretful porpentine.
Seken in every halk and every herne Particular sciences for to lerne.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a single person, class, or thing; belonging to one only; not general; not common; hence, personal; peculiar; singular.
q: Wheresoever one plant draweth such a particular juice out of the earth.

senses.d: Separate or distinct by reason of superiority; distinguished; important; noteworthy; unusual; special; as, he brought no particular news; she was the particular belle of the party.
Concerned with, or attentive to, details; minute; circumstantial; precise; as, a full and particular account of an accident; hence, nice; fastidious; as, a man particular in his dress.
Containing a part only; limited; as, a particular estate, or one precedent to an estate in remainder.

Forming a part of a genus; relatively limited in extension; affirmed or denied of a part of a subject; as, a particular proposition; — opposed to universal: e. g. (particular affirmative) Some men are wise; (particular negative) Some men are not wise.

Particular.syn: Minute; individual; respective; appropriate; peculiar; especial; exact; specific; precise; critical; circumstantial. See Minute.
Particular.etym: [OE. particuler, F. particulier, L. particularis. See Particle.]

senses.d: A separate or distinct member of a class, or part of a whole; an individual fact, point, circumstance, detail, or item, which may be considered separately; as, the particulars of a story.
q: Particulars which it is not lawful for me to reveal.
It is the greatest interest of particulars to advance the good of the community.

senses.d: Special or personal peculiarity, trait, or character; individuality; interest, etc.
q: For his particular I'll receive him gladly.
If the particulars of each person be considered.
Temporal blessings, whether such as concern the public . . . or such as concern our particular.

senses.d: One of the details or items of grounds of claim; — usually in the pl.; also, a bill of particulars; a minute account; as, a particular of premises.
q: The reader has a particular of the books wherein this law was written.

senses.d: In a particular manner; expressly; with a specific reference or interest; in particular; distinctly.
In an especial manner; in a high degree; as, a particularly fortunate man; a particularly bad failure.
q: The exact propriety of Virgil I particularly regarded as a great part of his character.

senses.d: Serving to part; dividing; separating.
Given when departing; as, a parting shot; a parting salute.
Departing.
Admitting of being parted; partible.
The act of parting or dividing; the state of being parted; division; separation.
A separation; a leave-taking.
q: And there were sudden partings, such as press The life from out young hearts.

senses.d: A surface or line of separation where a division occurs.
The surface of the sand of one section of a mold where it meets that of another section.
The separation and determination of alloys; esp., the separation, as by acids, of gold from silver in the assay button.
A joint or fissure, as in a coal seam.
The breaking, as of a cable, by violence.
Lamellar separation in a crystallized mineral, due to some other cause than cleavage, as to the presence of twinning lamellæ.
The act of parting or dividing; the state of being parted; separation; division; distribution; as, the partition of a kingdom.
q: And good from bad find no partition.

senses.d: That which divides or separates; that by which different things, or distinct parts of the same thing, are separated; separating boundary; dividing line or space; specifically, an interior wall dividing one part or apartment of a house, an inclosure, or the like, from another; as, a brick partition; lath and plaster partitions.
q: No sight could pass Betwixt the nice partitions of the grass.

senses.d: A part divided off by walls; an apartment; a compartment.
The severance of common or undivided interests, particularly in real estate. It may be effected by consent of parties, or by compulsion of law.
A score.

Partition.etym: [F. partition, L. partitio. See Part, v.]

senses.d: To divide into parts or shares; to divide and distribute; as, to partition an estate among various heirs.
To divide into distinct parts by lines, walls, etc.; as, to partition a house.
q: Uniform without, though severally partitioned within.

senses.d: In part; in some measure of degree; not wholly.
One who has a part in anything with an other; a partaker; an associate; a sharer.
q: My other self, the partner of my life.

senses.d: An associate in any business or occupation; a member of a partnership. See Partnership.
A framework of heavy timber surrounding an opening in a deck, to strengthen it for the support of a mast, pump, capstan, or the like.

Partner.syn: Associate; colleague; coadjutor; confederate; partaker; participator; companion; comrade; mate.

senses.d: To associate, to join.
Any one of numerous species of small gallinaceous birds of the genus Perdix and several related genera of the family Perdicidæ, of the Old World. The partridge is noted as a game bird.
q: Full many a fat partrich had he in mew.

senses.d: Any one of several species of quail-like birds belonging to Colinus, and allied genera.
The ruffed grouse (Bonasa umbellus).

Partridge.etym: [OE. partriche, pertriche, OF. pertris, perdriz, F. perdrix, L. perdix, -icis, fr. Gr. πέρδιξ.]

senses.d: A part or portion.

A number of persons united in opinion or action, as distinguished from, or opposed to, the rest of a community or association; esp., one of the parts into which a people is divided on questions of public policy.
q: Win the noble Brutus to our party.
The peace both parties want is like to last.

senses.d: A part of a larger body of company; a detachment; especially (Mil.), a small body of troops dispatched on special service.
A number of persons invited to a social entertainment; a select company; as, a dinner party; also, the entertainment itself; as, to give a party.
One concerned or interested in an affair; one who takes part with others; a participator; as, he was a party to the plot; a party to the contract.
The plaintiff or the defendant in a lawsuit, whether an individual, a firm, or corporation; a litigant.
q: The cause of both parties shall come before the judges.

senses.d: Hence, any certain person who is regarded as being opposed or antagonistic to another.
q: If the jury found that the party slain was of English race, it had been adjudged felony.

senses.d: Cause; side; interest.
q: Have you nothing said Upon this Party 'gainst the Duke of Albany?

senses.d: A person; as, he is a queer party.

Party.etym: [F. parti and partie, fr. F. partir to part, divide, L. partire, partiri. See Part, v.]

senses.d: Parted or divided, as in the direction or form of one of the ordinaries; as, an escutcheon party per pale.
Partial; favoring one party.
q: I will be true judge, and not party.

Party.etym: [F. parti divided, fr. partir to divide. See Part, v., and cf. Partite.]

senses.d: Partly.
A pace; a step, as in a dance.
Right of going foremost; precedence.

To go; to move; to proceed; to be moved or transferred from one point to another; to make a transit; — usually with a following adverb or adverbal phrase defining the kind or manner of motion; as, to pass on, by, out, in, etc.; to pass swiftly, directly, smoothly, etc.; to pass to the rear, under the yoke, over the bridge, across the field, beyond the border, etc.
q: On high behests his angels to and fro Passed frequent.
Sweet sounds rose slowly through their mouths, And from their bodies passed.

senses.d: To move or be transferred from one state or condition to another; to change possession, condition, or circumstances; to undergo transition; as, the business has passed into other hands.
q: Others, dissatisfied with what they have, . . . pass from just to unjust.

senses.d: To move beyond the range of the senses or of knowledge; to pass away; hence, to disappear; to vanish; to depart; specifically, to depart from life; to die.
q: Disturb him not, let him pass paceably.
Beauty is a charm, but soon the charm will pass.
The passing of the sweetest soul That ever looked with human eyes.

senses.d: To move or to come into being or under notice; to come and go in consciousness; hence, to take place; to occur; to happen; to come; to occur progressively or in succession; to be present transitorily.
q: So death passed upon all men.
Our own consciousness of what passes within our own mind.

senses.d: To go by or glide by, as time; to elapse; to be spent; as, their vacation passed pleasantly.
q: Now the time is far passed.

senses.d: To go from one person to another; hence, to be given and taken freely; as, clipped coin will not pass; to obtain general acceptance; to be held or regarded; to circulate; to be current; — followed by for before a word denoting value or estimation.
q: False eloquence passeth only where true is not understood.
This will not pass for a fault in him.

senses.d: To advance through all the steps or stages necessary to validity or effectiveness; to be carried through a body that has power to sanction or reject; to receive legislative sanction; to be enacted; as, the resolution passed; the bill passed both houses of Congress.
To go through any inspection or test successfully; to be approved or accepted; as, he attempted the examination, but did not expect to pass.
To be suffered to go on; to be tolerated; hence, to continue; to live along.
To go unheeded or neglected; to proceed without hindrance or opposition; as, we let this act pass.
To go beyond bounds; to surpass; to be in excess.
To take heed; to care.
q: As for these silken-coated slaves, I pass not.

Pass.etym: [F. passer, LL. passare, fr. L. passus step, or from pandere, passum, to spread out, lay open. See Pace.]

senses.d: To go by, beyond, over, through, or the like; to proceed from one side to the other of; as, to pass a house, a stream, a boundary, etc.
q: She loved me for the dangers I had passed.

senses.d: To go by without noticing; to omit attention to; to take no note of; to disregard.
q: Please you that I may pass This doing.
I pass their warlike pomp, their proud array.

senses.d: To transcend; to surpass; to excel; to exceed.
q: And strive to pass . . . Their native music by her skillful art.
Whose tender power Passes the strength of storms in their most desolate hour.

senses.d: To go successfully through, as an examination, trail, test, etc.; to obtain the formal sanction of, as a legislative body; as, he passed his examination; the bill passed the senate.

To cause to move or go; to send; to transfer from one person, place, or condition to another; to transmit; to deliver; to hand; to make over; as, the waiter passed bisquit and cheese; the torch was passed from hand to hand.
q: I had only time to pass my eye over the medals.
Waller passed over five thousand horse and foot by Newbridge.

senses.d: To cause to pass the lips; to utter; to pronounce; hence, to promise; to pledge; as, to pass sentence.
q: Father, thy word is passed.

senses.d: To cause to advance by stages of progress; to carry on with success through an ordeal, examination, or action; specifically, to give legal or official sanction to; to ratify; to enact; to approve as valid and just; as, he passed the bill through the committee; the senate passed the law.
To put in circulation; to give currency to; as, to pass counterfeit money.
To cause to obtain entrance, admission, or conveyance; as, to pass a person into a theater, or over a railroad.
To emit from the bowels; to evacuate.
To take a turn with (a line, gasket, etc.), as around a sail in furling, and make secure.
To make, as a thrust, punto, etc.
An opening, road, or track, available for passing; especially, one through or over some dangerous or otherwise impracticable barrier; a passageway; a defile; a ford; as, a mountain pass.
q: “Try not the pass!” the old man said.

senses.d: A thrust or push; an attempt to stab or strike an adversary.
A movement of the hand over or along anything; the manipulation of a mesmerist.
A single passage of a bar, rail, sheet, etc., between the rolls.
State of things; condition; predicament.
q: Have his daughters brought him to this pass.
Matters have been brought to this pass.

senses.d: Permission or license to pass, or to go and come; a psssport; a ticket permitting free transit or admission; as, a railroad or theater pass; a military pass.
q: A ship sailing under the flag and pass of an enemy.

senses.d: Fig.: a thrust; a sally of wit.
Estimation; character.
q: Common speech gives him a worthy pass.

senses.d: A part; a division.

Pass.etym: [Cf. F. pas (for sense 1), and passe, fr. passer to pass. See Pass, v. i.]

senses.d: In football, hockey, etc., a transfer of the ball, etc., to another player of one's side, usually at some distance.
In football, hockey, etc., to make pass; to transfer the ball, etc., to another player of one's own side.

The act of passing; transit from one place to another; movement from point to point; a going by, over, across, or through; as, the passage of a man or a carriage; the passage of a ship or a bird; the passage of light; the passage of fluids through the pores or channels of the body.
q: What! are my doors opposed against my passage!

senses.d: Transit by means of conveyance; journey, as by water, carriage, car, or the like; travel; right, liberty, or means, of passing; conveyance.
q: The ship in which he had taken passage.

senses.d: Price paid for the liberty to pass; fare; as, to pay one's passage.
Removal from life; decease; departure; death.
q: When he is fit and season'd for his passage.

senses.d: Way; road; path; channel or course through or by which one passes; way of exit or entrance; way of access or transit. Hence, a common avenue to various apartments in a building; a hall; a corridor.
q: And with his pointed dart Explores the nearest passage to his heart.
The Persian army had advanced into the . . . passages of Cilicia.

senses.d: A continuous course, process, or progress; a connected or continuous series; as, the passage of time.
q: The conduct and passage of affairs.
The passage and whole carriage of this action.

senses.d: A separate part of a course, process, or series; an occurrence; an incident; an act or deed.
q: The . . . almost incredible passage of their unbelief.

senses.d: A particular portion constituting a part of something continuous; esp., a portion of a book, speech, or musical composition; a paragraph; a clause.
q: How commentators each dark passage shun.

senses.d: Reception; currency.
A pass or en encounter; as, a passage at arms.
q: No passages of love Betwixt us twain henceforward evermore.

senses.d: A movement or an evacuation of the bowels.

In parliamentary proceedings: (a) The course of a proposition (bill, resolution, etc.) through the several stages of consideration and action; as, during its passage through Congress the bill was amended in both Houses. (b) The advancement of a bill or other proposition from one stage to another by an affirmative vote; esp., the final affirmative action of the body upon a proposition; hence, adoption; enactment; as, the passage of the bill to its third reading was delayed.
q: The final question was then put upon its passage.

senses.d: A passer or passer-by; a wayfarer.
A traveler by some established conveyance, as a coach, steamboat, railroad train, etc.

Passenger.etym: [OE. & F. passager. See Passage, and cf. Messenger.]

senses.d: The act of one who, or that which, passes; the act of going by or away.
Relating to the act of passing or going; going by, beyond, through, or away; departing.
Exceeding; surpassing, eminent.
Exceedingly; excessively; surpassingly; as, passing fair; passing strange.

A suffering or enduring of imposed or inflicted pain; any suffering or distress (as, a cardiac passion); specifically, the suffering of Christ between the time of the last supper and his death, esp. in the garden upon the cross.
q: To whom also he showed himself alive after his passion, by many infallible proofs.

senses.d: The state of being acted upon; subjection to an external agent or influence; a passive condition; — opposed to action.
q: A body at rest affords us no idea of any active power to move, and, when set in motion, it is rather a passion than an action in it.

senses.d: Capacity of being affected by external agents; susceptibility of impressions from external agents.
q: Moldable and not moldable, scissible and not scissible, and many other passions of matter.

senses.d: The state of the mind when it is powerfully acted upon and influenced by something external to itself; the state of any particular faculty which, under such conditions, becomes extremely sensitive or uncontrollably excited; any emotion or sentiment (specifically, love or anger) in a state of abnormal or controlling activity; an extreme or inordinate desire; also, the capacity or susceptibility of being so affected; as, to be in a passion; the passions of love, hate, jealously, wrath, ambition, avarice, fear, etc.; a passion for war, or for drink; an orator should have passion as well as rhetorical skill.
q: We also are men of like passions with you.

The nature of the human mind can not be sufficiently understood, without considering the affections and passions, or those modifications or actions of the mind consequent upon the apprehension of certain objects or events in which the mind generally conceives good or evil.
The term passion, and its adverb passionately, often express a very strong predilection for any pursuit, or object of taste — a kind of enthusiastic fondness for anything.
The bravery of his grief did put me Into a towering passion.
The ruling passion, be it what it will, The ruling passion conquers reason still.
Who walked in every path of human life, Felt every passion.
When statesmen are ruled by faction and interest, they can have no passion for the glory of their country.

senses.d: Disorder of the mind; madness.
Passion week. See Passion week, below.

Passion.etym: [F., fr. L. passio, fr. pati, passus, to suffer. See Patient.]

senses.d: To give a passionate character to.
To suffer pain or sorrow; to experience a passion; to be extremely agitated.

A feast of the Jews, instituted to commemorate the sparing of the Hebrews in Egypt, when God, smiting the firstborn of the Egyptians, passed over the houses of the Israelites which were marked with the blood of a lamb.
The sacrifice offered at the feast of the passover; the paschal lamb.
Of or pertaining to a former time or state; neither present nor future; gone by; elapsed; ended; spent; as, past troubles; past offences.
A former time or state; a state of things gone by.
q: The present is only intelligible in the light of the past, often a very remote past indeed.

senses.d: Beyond, in position, or degree; further than; beyond the reach or influence of.
q: Until we be past thy borders.
Love, when once past government, is consequently past shame.

senses.d: Beyond, in time; after; as, past the hour.
q: Is it not past two o'clock?

senses.d: Above; exceeding; more than.
q: Not past three quarters of a mile.
Bows not past three quarters of a yard long.

senses.d: By; beyond; as, he ran past.
q: The alarum of drums swept past.

senses.d: A shepherd; one who has the care of flocks and herds.
A guardian; a keeper; specifically (Eccl.), a minister having the charge of a church and parish.
A species of starling (Pastor roseus), native of the plains of Western Asia and Eastern Europe. Its head is crested and glossy greenish black, and its back is rosy. It feeds largely upon locusts.

Pastor.etym: [L., fr. pascere, pastum, to pasture, to feed. Cf. Pabulum, Pasture, Food.]

senses.d: Food; nourishment.
q: Toads and frogs his pasture poisonous.

senses.d: Specifically: Grass growing for the food of cattle; the food of cattle taken by grazing.
Grass land for cattle, horses, etc.; pasturage.
q: He maketh me to lie down in green pastures.
So graze as you find pasture.

Pasture.etym: [OF. pasture, F. pâture, L. pastura, fr. pascere, pastum, to pasture, to feed. See Pastor.]

senses.d: To feed, esp. to feed on growing grass; to supply grass as food for; as, the farmer pastures fifty oxen; the land will pasture forty cows.
To feed on growing grass; to graze.
The head of a person; the top, or crown, of the head.
q: His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.
Fat paunches have lean pate.

senses.d: The skin of a calf's head.

Pate.etym: [Cf. LG. & Prov. G. pattkopf, patzkopf, scabby head; patt, patz, scab + kopf head.]

senses.d: A trodden way; a footway.
q: The dewy paths of meadows we will tread.

senses.d: A way, course, or track, in which anything moves or has moved; route; passage; an established way; as, the path of a meteor, of a caravan, of a storm, of a pestilence. Also used figuratively, of a course of life or action.
q: All the paths of the Lord are mercy and truth.
The paths of glory lead but to the grave.

Path.etym: [AS. pæð, pað; akin to D. pad, G. pfad, of uncertain origin; cf. Gr. πάτοσ, Skr. patha, path. √21.]

senses.d: To make a path in, or on (something), or for (some one).
To walk or go.
A footpath; a beaten track; any path or course. Also used figuratively.
q: In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof is no death.
We tread the pathway arm in arm.

senses.d: The state or quality of being patient; the power of suffering with fortitude; uncomplaining endurance of evils or wrongs, as toil, pain, poverty, insult, oppression, calamity, etc.
q: Strengthened with all might, . . . unto all patience and long-suffering.
I must have patience to endure the load.
Who hath learned lowliness From his Lord's cradle, patience from his cross.

senses.d: The act or power of calmly or contentedly waiting for something due or hoped for; forbearance.
q: Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.

senses.d: Constancy in labor or application; perseverance.
q: He learned with patience, and with meekness taught.

senses.d: Sufferance; permission.
q: They stay upon your patience.

senses.d: A kind of dock (Rumex Patientia), less common in America than in Europe; monk's rhubarb.
Solitaire.

Patience.etym: [F. patience, fr. L. patientia. See Patient.]

senses.d: Having the quality of enduring; physically able to suffer or bear.
q: Patient of severest toil and hardship.

senses.d: Undergoing pains, trials, or the like, without murmuring or fretfulness; bearing up with equanimity against trouble; long-suffering.
Constant in pursuit or exertion; persevering; calmly diligent; as, patient endeavor.
q: Whatever I have done is due to patient thought.

senses.d: Expectant with calmness, or without discontent; not hasty; not overeager; composed.
q: Not patient to expect the turns of fate.

senses.d: Forbearing; long-suffering.
q: Be patient toward all men.

Patient.etym: [F., fr. L. patiens, -entis, p. pr. of pati to suffer. Cf. Pathos, Passion.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, is passively affected; a passive recipient.
q: Malice is a passion so impetuous and precipitate that it often involves the agent and the patient.

senses.d: A person under medical or surgical treatment; — correlative to physician or nurse.
q: Like a physician, . . . seeing his patient in a pestilent fever.

senses.d: To compose, to calm.
In a patient manner.

The father and ruler of a family; one who governs his family or descendants by paternal right; — usually applied to heads of families in ancient history, especially in Biblical and Jewish history to those who lived before the time of Moses.
A dignitary superior to the order of archbishops; as, the patriarch of Constantinople, of Alexandria, or of Antioch.
A venerable old man; an elder. Also used figuratively.
q: The patriarch hoary, the sage of his kith and the hamlet.
The monarch oak, the partiarch of trees.

Patriarch.etym: [F. patriarche, L. patriarcha, Gr. παριάρχησ, fr. παριά lineage, especially on the father's side, race; πατήρ father + αρχὄσ a leader, chief, fr. ἄρχειν to lead, rule. See Father, Archaic.]

senses.d: A right or estate inherited from one's father; or, in a larger sense, from any ancestor.
Formerly, a church estate or endowment.

Patrimony.etym: [L. patrimonium, fr. pater father: cf. F. patrimoine. See Paternal.]

senses.d: Anything proposed for imitation; an archetype; an exemplar; that which is to be, or is worthy to be, copied or imitated; as, a pattern of a machine.
q: I will be the pattern of all patience.

senses.d: A part showing the figure or quality of the whole; a specimen; a sample; an example; an instance.
q: He compares the pattern with the whole piece.

senses.d: Stuff sufficient for a garment; as, a dress pattern.
Figure or style of decoration; design; as, wall paper of a beautiful pattern.
Something made after a model; a copy.
q: The patterns of things in the heavens.

senses.d: Anything cut or formed to serve as a guide to cutting or forming objects; as, a dressmaker's pattern.
A full-sized model around which a mold of sand is made, to receive the melted metal. It is usually made of wood and in several parts, so as to be removed from the mold without injuring it.

Pattern.etym: [OE. patron, F. patron, a patron, also, a pattern. See Patron.]

senses.d: To make or design (anything) by, from, or after, something that serves as a pattern; to copy; to model; to imitate.
q: patterned from that which Adam reared in Paradise.

senses.d: To serve as an example for; also, to parallel.
A diagram showing the distribution of the pellets of a shotgun on a vertical target perpendicular to the plane of fire.
An Italian silver coin. See Paolo.

To lay or cover with stone, brick, or other material, so as to make a firm, level, or convenient surface for horses, carriages, or persons on foot, to travel on; to floor with brick, stone, or other solid material; as, to pave a street; to pave a court.
q: With silver paved, and all divine with gold.
To pave thy realm, and smooth the broken ways.

senses.d: Fig.: To make smooth, easy, and safe; to prepare, as a path or way; as, to pave the way to promotion; to pave the way for an enterprise.
q: It might open and pave a prepared way to his own title.

Pave.etym: [F. paver to pave, LL. pavare, from L. pavire to beat, ram, or tread down; cf. Gr. παίειν to beat, strike.]

senses.d: That with which anything is paved; a floor or covering of solid material, laid so as to make a hard and convenient surface for travel; a paved road or sidewalk; a decorative interior floor of tiles or colored bricks.
q: The riches of heaven's pavement, trodden gold.

Pavement.etym: [F., fr. LL. pavamentum, L. pavimentum. See Pave.]

senses.d: To furnish with a pavement; to pave.
A temporary movable habitation; a large tent; a marquee; esp., a tent raised on posts.

A single body or mass of building, contained within simple walls and a single roof, whether insulated, as in the park or garden of a larger edifice, or united with other parts, and forming an angle or central feature of a large pile.
A flag, colors, ensign, or banner.
Same as Tent (Her.)
That part of a brilliant which lies between the girdle and collet. See Illust. of Brilliant.
The auricle of the ear; also, the fimbriated extremity of the Fallopian tube.
A covering; a canopy; figuratively, the sky.
q: The pavilion of heaven is bare.

Pavilion.etym: [F. pavillon, fr. L. pavilio a butterfly, also, a tent, because spread out like a butterfly's wings.]

senses.d: To furnish or cover with, or shelter in, a tent or tents.
q: The field pavilioned with his guardians bright.

senses.d: The foot of a quadruped having claws, as the lion, dog, cat, etc.
The hand.

Paw.etym: [OE. pawe, poue, OF. poe: cf. patte, LG. pote, D. poot, G. pfote.]

senses.d: To draw the forefoot along the ground; to beat or scrape with the forefoot.
To pass the paw over; to stroke or handle with the paws; hence, to handle fondly or rudely.
To scrape or beat with the forefoot.
q: His hot courser pawed the Hungarian plane.

senses.d: To cover, as bottom of a vessel, a seam, a spar, etc., with tar or pitch, or waterproof composition of tallow, resin, etc.; to smear.

Pay.etym: [OF. peier, fr. L. picare to pitch, pix pitch: cf. OF. peiz pitch, F. poix. See Pitch a black substance.]

senses.d: To satisfy, or content; specifically, to satisfy (another person) for service rendered, property delivered, etc.; to discharge one's obligation to; to make due return to; to compensate; to remunerate; to recompense; to requite; as, to pay workmen or servants.
q: May no penny ale them pay [i.e., satisfy].
pays me with disdain.

senses.d: Hence, figuratively: To compensate justly; to requite according to merit; to reward; to punish; to retort or retaliate upon.
q: For which, or pay me quickly, or I'll pay you.

senses.d: To discharge, as a debt, demand, or obligation, by giving or doing what is due or required; to deliver the amount or value of to the person to whom it is owing; to discharge a debt by delivering (money owed).
q: Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.
If they pay this tax, they starve.

senses.d: To discharge or fulfill, as a duy; to perform or render duty, as that which has been promised.
q: This day have I paid my vows.

senses.d: To give or offer, without an implied obligation; as, to pay attention; to pay a visit.
q: Not paying me a welcome.

Pay.etym: [OE. paien, F. payer, fr. L. pacare to pacify, appease, fr. pax, pacis, peace. See Peace.]

senses.d: To give a recompense; to make payment, requital, or satisfaction; to discharge a debt.
q: The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again.

senses.d: Hence, to make or secure suitable return for expense or trouble; to be remunerative or profitable; to be worth the effort or pains required; as, it will pay to ride; it will pay to wait; politeness always pays.
Satisfaction; content.

An equivalent or return for money due, goods purchased, or services performed; salary or wages for work or service; compensation; recompense; payment; hire; as, the pay of a clerk; the pay of a soldier.
q: Where only merit constant pay receives.
There is neither pay nor plunder to be got.

senses.d: The act of paying, or giving compensation; the discharge of a debt or an obligation.
q: No man envieth the payment of a debt.

senses.d: That which is paid; the thing given in discharge of a debt, or an obligation, or in fulfillment of a promise; reward; recompense; requital; return.
Punishment; chastisement.

Payment.etym: [F. payment, paiement. See Pay to requite.]

senses.d: A state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation; calm; repose
Exemption from, or cessation of, war with public enemies.
Public quiet, order, and contentment in obedience to law.
Exemption from, or subjection of, agitating passions; tranquillity of mind or conscience.
Reconciliation; agreement after variance; harmony; concord.

Peace.etym: [OE. pees, pais, OF. pais, paiz, pes, F. paix, L. pax, pacis, akin to pacere, paciscere, pacisci, to make an agreement, and prob. also pangere to fasten. Cf. Appease, Fair, a., Fay, v., Fang, Pacify, Pact, Pay to requite.]

senses.d: To make or become quiet; to be silent; to stop.
q: When the thunder would not peace at my bidding.

senses.d: Begin in or at peace; tranquil; quiet; free from, or not disposed to, war, disorder, or excitement; not quarrelsome.

Peaceable.syn: Peaceful; pacific; tranquil; quiet; mild; undisturbed; serene; still.

senses.d: One who makes peace by reconciling parties that are at variance.
The male of any pheasant of the genus Pavo, of which at least two species are known, native of Southern Asia and the East Indies.
In common usage, the species in general or collectively; a peafowl.

Peacock.etym: [OE. pecok. Pea- in this word is from AS. peá, pāwa, peacock, fr. L. pavo, prob. of Oriental origin; cf. Gr. ταώσ, ταω̑σ, Per. tāus, tāwus, Ar. tāwūs. See Cock the bird.]

senses.d: A fringe or border.
To fringe; to border.

A shelly concretion, usually rounded, and having a brilliant luster, with varying tints, found in the mantle, or between the mantle and shell, of certain bivalve mollusks, especially in the pearl oysters and river mussels, and sometimes in certain univalves. It is usually due to a secretion of shelly substance around some irritating foreign particle. Its substance is the same as nacre, or mother-of-pearl. Pearls which are round, or nearly round, and of fine luster, are highly esteemed as jewels, and compare in value with the precious stones.
Hence, figuratively, something resembling a pearl; something very precious.
q: I see thee compassed with thy kingdom's pearl.
And those pearls of dew she wears.

senses.d: Nacre, or mother-of-pearl.
A fish allied to the turbot; the brill.
A light-colored tern.
One of the circle of tubercles which form the bur on a deer's antler.
A whitish speck or film on the eye.
A capsule of gelatin or similar substance containing some liquid for medicinal application, as ether.
A size of type, between agate and diamond.

Pearl.etym: [OE. perle, F. perle, LL. perla, perula, probably fr. (assumed) L. pirulo, dim. of L. pirum a pear. See Pear, and cf. Purl to mantle.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to pearl or pearls; made of pearls, or of mother-of-pearl.
To set or adorn with pearls, or with mother-of-pearl. Used also figuratively.
To cause to resemble pearls; to make into small round grains; as, to pearl barley.
To resemble pearl or pearls.
To dive or hunt for pearls; as, to go pearling.
One's own; belonging solely or especially to an individual; not possessed by others; of private, personal, or characteristic possession and use; not owned in common or in participation.
q: And purify unto himself a peculiar people.
Hymns . . . that Christianity hath peculiar unto itself.

senses.d: Particular; individual; special; appropriate.
q: While each peculiar power forgoes his wonted seat.
My fate is Juno's most peculiar care.

senses.d: Unusual; singular; rare; strange; as, the sky had a peculiar appearance.
q: Beauty, which, either walking or asleep, Shot forth peculiar graces.
For naught so vile that on the earth doth live, But to the earth some special good doth give.

Peculiar.etym: [L. peculiaris, fr. peculium private property, akin to pecunia money: cf. OF. peculier. See Pecuniary.]

senses.d: That which is peculiar; a sole or exclusive property; a prerogative; a characteristic.
q: Revenge is . . . the peculiar of Heaven.

senses.d: A particular parish or church which is exempt from the jurisdiction of the ordinary.
A line of ancestors; descent; lineage; genealogy; a register or record of a line of ancestors.
q: Alterations of surnames . . . have obscured the truth of our pedigrees.
His vanity labored to contrive us a pedigree.
I am no herald to inquire of men's pedigrees.
The Jews preserved the pedigrees of their tribes.

senses.d: A record of the lineage or strain of an animal, as of a horse.

Pedigree.etym: [Of unknown origin; possibly fr. F. par degrés by degrees, — for a pedigree is properly a genealogical table which records the relationship of families by degrees; or, perh., fr. F. pied de grue crane's foot, from the shape of the heraldic genealogical trees.]

senses.d: A small tower, fort, or castle; a keep.

A spadelike implement, variously used, as for removing loaves of bread from a baker's oven; also, a T-shaped implement used by printers and bookbinders for hanging wet sheets of paper on lines or poles to dry. Also, the blade of an oar.
To plunder; to pillage; to rob.
q: But govern ill the nations under yoke, Peeling their provinces.

Peel.etym: [Confused with peel to strip, but fr. F. piller to pillage. See Pill to rob, Pillage.]

senses.d: To strip off the skin, bark, or rind of; to strip by drawing or tearing off the skin, bark, husks, etc.; to flay; to decorticate; as, to peel an orange.
q: The skillful shepherd peeled me certain wands.

senses.d: To strip or tear off; to remove by stripping, as the skin of an animal, the bark of a tree, etc.

Peel.etym: [F. peler to pull out the hair, to strip, to peel, fr. L. pilare to deprive of hair, fr. pilus a hair; or perh. partly fr. F. peler to peel off the skin, perh. fr. L. pellis skin (cf. Fell skin). Cf. Peruke.]

senses.d: To lose the skin, bark, or rind; to come off, as the skin, bark, or rind does; — often used with an adverb; as, the bark peels easily or readily.
The skin or rind; as, the peel of an orange.

A graceful and swift South African antelope (Pelea capreola). The hair is woolly, and ash-gray on the back and sides. The horns are black, long, slender, straight, nearly smooth, and very sharp. Called also rheeboc, and rehboc.
To cry, as a chicken hatching or newly hatched; to chirp; to cheep.
q: There was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped.

senses.d: To begin to appear; to look forth from concealment; to make the first appearance.
q: When flowers first peeped, and trees did blossoms bear.

senses.d: To look cautiously or slyly; to peer, as through a crevice; to pry.
q: Peep through the blanket of the dark.
From her cabined loophole peep.

Peep.etym: [Of imitative origin; cf. OE. pipen, F. piper, pépier, L. pipire, pipare, pipiare, D. & G. piepen. Senses 2 and 3 perhaps come from a transfer of sense from the sound which chickens make upon the first breaking of the shell to the act accompanying it; or perhaps from the influence of peek, or peak.

senses.d: The cry of a young chicken; a chirp.
First outlook or appearance.
q: Oft have we seen him at the peep of dawn.

senses.d: A sly look; a look as through a crevice, or from a place of concealment.
q: To take t' other peep at the stars.

senses.d: Any small sandpiper, as the least sandpiper (Trigna minutilla).

Any large webfooted bird of the genus Pelecanus, of which about a dozen species are known. They have an enormous bill, to the lower edge of which is attached a pouch in which captured fishes are temporarily stored.
A retort or still having a curved tube or tubes leading back from the head to the body for continuous condensation and redistillation.

Pelican.etym: [F. pélican, L. pelicanus, pelecanus, Gr. πελεκάν, πελεκα̑σ, πελέκανοσ, the woodpecker, and also a water bird of the pelican kind, fr. πελεκα̑ν to hew with an ax, fr. πέλεκυσ an ax, akin to Skr. paraçu.]

senses.d: A feather.
A wing.

An instrument used for writing with ink, formerly made of a reed, or of the quill of a goose or other bird, but now also of other materials, as of steel, gold, etc. Also, originally, a stylus or other instrument for scratching or graving.
q: Graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock.

senses.d: Fig.: A writer, or his style; as, he has a sharp pen.
The internal shell of a squid.
A female swan.

Pen.etym: [OE. penne, OF. penne, pene, F. penne, fr. L. penna.]

senses.d: To write; to compose and commit to paper; to indite; to compose; as, to pen a sonnet.
To shut up, as in a pen or cage; to confine in a small inclosure or narrow space; to coop up, or shut in; to inclose.
q: Watching where shepherds pen their flocks at eve.

Pen.etym: [OE. pennen, AS. pennan in on-pennan to unfasten, prob. from the same source as pin, and orig. meaning, to fasten with a peg.See Pin, n. & v.]

senses.d: A small inclosure; as, a pen for sheep or for pigs.
q: My father stole two geese out of a pen.

senses.d: A small pocketknife; formerly, a knife used for making and mending quill pens.
Denoting pound weight for one thousand; — used in combination, with respect to nails; as, tenpenny nails, nails of which one thousand weight ten pounds.

Penny.etym: [Perh. a corruption of pun, for pound.]

senses.d: An English coin, formerly of copper, now of bronze, the twelfth part of an English shilling in account value, and equal to four farthings, or about two cents; — usually indicated by the abbreviation d. (the initial of denarius).
Any small sum or coin; a groat; a stiver.
Money, in general; as, to turn an honest penny.
q: What penny hath Rome borne, What men provided, what munition sent?

Penny.etym: [OE. peni, AS. penig, pening, pending; akin to D. penning, OHG. pfenning, pfenting, G. pfennig, Icel. penningr; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: Worth or costing one penny.
A penny's worth; as much as may be bought for a penny.
Hence: The full value of one's penny expended; due return for money laid out; a good bargain; a bargain.
q: The priests sold the better pennyworths.

senses.d: A small quantity; a trifle.

A solemn festival of the Jews; — so called because celebrated on the fiftieth day (seven weeks) after the second day of the Passover (which fell on the sixteenth of the Jewish month Nisan); — hence called, also, the Feast of Weeks. At this festival an offering of the first fruits of the harvest was made. By the Jews it was generally regarded as commemorative of the gift of the law on the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt.
A festival of the Roman Catholic and other churches in commemoration of the descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles; which occurred on the day of Pentecost; — called also Whitsunday.

Pentecost.etym: [L. pentecoste, Gr. � (sc. �) the fiftieth day, Pentecost, fr. � fiftieth, fr. � fifty, fr. � five. See Five, and cf. Pingster.]

senses.d: Absence of resources; want; privation; indigence; extreme poverty; destitution.
q: They were exposed to hardship and penury.
It arises in neither from penury of thought.

senses.d: Penuriousness; miserliness.

Penury.etym: [L. penuria; cf. Gr. � hunger, � poverty, need, � one who works for his daily bread, a poor man, � to work for one's daily bread, to be poor: cf. F. pénurie.]

senses.d: The body of persons who compose a community, tribe, nation, or race; an aggregate of individuals forming a whole; a community; a nation.
q: Unto him shall the gathering of the people be.
The ants are a people not strong.
Before many peoples, and nations, and tongues.
Earth's monarchs are her peoples.
A government of all the people, by all the people, for all the people.

senses.d: Persons, generally; an indefinite number of men and women; folks; population, or part of population; as, country people; — sometimes used as an indefinite subject or verb, like on in French, and man in German; as, people in adversity.
q: People were tempted to lend by great premiums.
People have lived twenty-four days upon nothing but water.

senses.d: The mass of community as distinguished from a special class; the commonalty; the populace; the vulgar; the common crowd; as, nobles and people.
q: And strive to gain his pardon from the people.

senses.d: One's ancestors or family; kindred; relations; as, my people were English.

People.etym: [OE. peple, people, OF. pueple, F. peuple, fr. L. populus. Cf. Populage, Public, Pueblo.]

senses.d: To stock with people or inhabitants; to fill as with people; to populate.
q: As the gay motes that people the sunbeams.

People.etym: [Cf. OF. popler, puepler, F. puepler. Cf. Populate.]

senses.d: Through; by means of; through the agency of; by; for; for each; as, per annum; per capita, by heads, or according to individuals; per curiam, by the court; per se, by itself, of itself. Per is also sometimes used with English words.

Per.etym: [L. Cf. Far, For-, Pardon, and cf. Par, prep.]

senses.d: By chance; perhaps; it may be; if; supposing.
q: Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city.

Peradventure.etym: [OE. per aventure, F. par aventure. See Per, and Adventure.]

senses.d: Chance; hap; hence, doubt; question; as, proved beyond peradventure.

To obtain knowledge of through the senses; to receive impressions from by means of the bodily organs; to take cognizance of the existence, character, or identity of, by means of the senses; to see, hear, or feel; as, to perceive a distant ship; to perceive a discord.
To take intellectual cognizance of; to apprehend by the mind; to be convinced of by direct intuition; to note; to remark; to discern; to see; to understand.
q: Jesus perceived their wickedness.
You may, fair lady, Perceive I speak sincerely.
Till we ourselves see it with our own eyes, and perceive it by our own understandings, we are still in the dark.

senses.d: To be affected of influented by.
q: The upper regions of the air perceive the collection of the matter of tempests before the air here below.

Perceive.syn: To discern; distinguish; observe; see; feel; know; understand.
Perceive.etym: [OF. percevoir, perceveir, L. percipere, perceptum; per (see Per-) + capere to take, receive. See Capacious, and cf. Perception.]

senses.d: Entire loss; utter destruction; ruin; esp., the utter loss of the soul, or of final happiness in a future state; future misery or eternal death.
q: The mere perdition of the Turkish fleet.
If we reject the truth, we seal our own perdition.

senses.d: Loss or diminution.

Perdition.etym: [F., fr. L. perditio, fr. perdere, perditum, to ruin, to lose; per (cf. Skr. parā away) + -dere (only in comp.) to put; akin to Gr. τιθέναι, E. do. See Do.]

senses.d: A peer.

Brought to consummation or completeness; completed; not defective nor redundant; having all the properties or qualities requisite to its nature and kind; without flaw, fault, or blemish; without error; mature; whole; pure; sound; right; correct.
q: My strength is made perfect in weakness.
Three glorious suns, each one a perfect sun.
I fear I am not in my perfect mind.
O most entire perfect sacrifice!
God made thee perfect, not immutable.

senses.d: Well informed; certain; sure.
q: I am perfect that the Pannonians are now in arms.

senses.d: Hermaphrodite; having both stamens and pistils; — said of a flower.

Perfect.syn: Finished; consummate; complete; entire; faultless; blameless; unblemished.
Perfect.etym: [OE. parfit, OF. parfit, parfet, parfait, F. parfait, L. perfectus, p. p. of perficere to carry to the end, to perform, finish, perfect; per (see Per-) + facere to make, do. See Fact.]

senses.d: The perfect tense, or a form in that tense.
To make perfect; to finish or complete, so as to leave nothing wanting; to give to anything all that is requisite to its nature and kind.
q: God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfect in us.
Inquire into the nature and properties of the things, . . . and thereby perfect our ideas of their distinct species.

Perfect.etym: [L. perfectus, p. p. of perficere. See Perfect, a.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being perfect or complete, so that nothing requisite is wanting; entire development; consummate culture, skill, or moral excellence; the highest attainable state or degree of excellence; maturity; as, perfection in an art, in a science, or in a system; perfection in form or degree; fruits in perfection.
