q: If the plot or intrigue must be natural, and such as springs from the subject, then the winding up of the plot must be a probable consequence of all that went before.

Plot.syn: Intrigue; stratagem; conspiracy; cabal; combination; contrivance.

senses.d: To form a scheme of mischief against another, especially against a government or those who administer it; to conspire.
q: The wicked plotteth against the just.

senses.d: To contrive a plan or stratagem; to scheme.
q: The prince did plot to be secretly gone.

senses.d: To plan; to scheme; to devise; to contrive secretly.

A well-known implement, drawn by horses, mules, oxen, or other power, for turning up the soil to prepare it for bearing crops; also used to furrow or break up the soil for other purposes; as, the subsoil plow; the draining plow.
q: Where fern succeeds ungrateful to the plow.

senses.d: Fig.: Agriculture; husbandry.
A carucate of land; a plowland.
q: Johan, mine eldest son, shall have plowes five.

senses.d: A joiner's plane for making grooves; a grooving plane.
An implement for trimming or shaving off the edges of books.
Same as Charles's Wain.

Plow.etym: [OE. plouh, plou, AS. plōh; akin to D. ploeg, G. pflug, OHG. pfluog, pfluoh, Icel. plōgr, Sw. plog, Dan. ploug, plov, Russ. plug', Lith. plugas.]

senses.d: To turn up, break up, or trench, with a plow; to till with, or as with, a plow; as, to plow the ground; to plow a field.
To furrow; to make furrows, grooves, or ridges in; to run through, as in sailing.
q: Let patient Octavia plow thy visage up With her prepared nails.
With speed we plow the watery way.

senses.d: To trim, or shave off the edges of, as a book or paper, with a plow. See Plow, n., 5.
To cut a groove in, as in a plank, or the edge of a board; especially, a rectangular groove to receive the end of a shelf or tread, the edge of a panel, a tongue, etc.
To labor with, or as with, a plow; to till or turn up the soil with a plow; to prepare the soil or bed for anything.
q: Doth the plowman plow all day to sow ?

senses.d: One who plows; a plowman; a cultivator.
One who plows, or who holds and guides a plow; hence, a husbandman.
A rustic; a countryman; a field laborer.
The share of a plow, or that part which cuts the slice of earth or sod at the bottom of the furrow.
To pull; to draw.
q: Its own nature . . . plucks on its own dissolution.

senses.d: Especially, to pull with sudden force or effort, or to pull off or out from something, with a twitch; to twitch; also, to gather, to pick; as, to pluck feathers from a fowl; to pluck hair or wool from a skin; to pluck grapes.
q: I come to pluck your berries harsh and crude.
E'en children followed, with endearing wile, And plucked his gown to share the good man's smile.

senses.d: To strip of, or as of, feathers; as, to pluck a fowl.
q: They which pass by the way do pluck her.

senses.d: To reject at an examination for degrees.

Pluck.etym: [AS. pluccian; akin to LG. & D. plukken, G. pflücken, Icel. plokka, plukka, Dan. plukke, Sw. plocka. �27.]

senses.d: To make a motion of pulling or twitching; — usually with at; as, to pluck at one's gown.
The act of plucking; a pull; a twitch.
The heart, liver, and lights of an animal.
Spirit; courage; indomitable resolution; fortitude.
q: Decay of English spirit, decay of manly pluck.

senses.d: The act of plucking, or the state of being plucked, at college. See Pluck, v. t., 4.
The lyrie.
Having courage and spirit.
A piece of lead attached to a line, used in sounding the depth of water.
q: I'll sink him deeper than e'er plummet sounded.

senses.d: A plumb bob or a plumb line. See under Plumb, n.
Hence, any weight.
A piece of lead formerly used by school children to rule paper for writing.

Plummet.etym: [OE. plommet, OF. plommet, fr. plom, plum, lead, F. plomb. See Plumb.]

senses.d: To thrust into water, or into any substance that is penetrable; to immerse; to cause to penetrate or enter quickly and forcibly; to thrust; as, to plunge the body into water; to plunge a dagger into the breast. Also used figuratively; as, to plunge a nation into war.
q: Bound and plunged him into a cell.
We shall be plunged into perpetual errors.

senses.d: To baptize by immersion.
To entangle; to embarrass; to overcome.
q: Plunged and graveled with three lines of Seneca.

Plunge.etym: [OE. ploungen, OF. plongier, F. plonger, fr. (assumed) LL. plumbicare, fr. L. plumbum lead. See Plumb.]

senses.d: To thrust or cast one's self into water or other fluid; to submerge one's self; to dive, or to rush in; as, he plunged into the river. Also used figuratively; as, to plunge into debt.
q: Forced to plunge naked in the raging sea.
To plunge into guilt of a murther.

senses.d: To pitch or throw one's self headlong or violently forward, as a horse does.
q: Some wild colt, which . . . flings and plunges.

senses.d: To bet heavily and with seeming recklessness on a race, or other contest; in an extended sense, to risk large sums in hazardous speculations.
The act of thrusting into or submerging; a dive, leap, rush, or pitch into, or as into, water; as, to take the water with a plunge.
Hence, a desperate hazard or act; a state of being submerged or overwhelmed with difficulties.
q: She was brought to that plunge, to conceal her husband's murder or accuse her son.
And with thou not reach out a friendly arm, To raise me from amidst this plunge of sorrows?

senses.d: The act of pitching or throwing one's self headlong or violently forward, like an unruly horse.
Heavy and reckless betting in horse racing; hazardous speculation.
One skilled in making poetry; one who has a particular genius for metrical composition; the author of a poem; an imaginative thinker or writer.
q: The poet's eye, in a fine frenzy rolling, Doth glance from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven.
A poet is a maker, as the word signifies.

Poet.etym: [F. poëte, L. poëta, fr. Gr. �, fr. � to make. Cf. Poem.]

senses.d: To appoint.
That which pricks or pierces; the sharp end of anything, esp. the sharp end of a piercing instrument, as a needle or a pin.
An instrument which pricks or pierces, as a sort of needle used by engravers, etchers, lace workers, and others; also, a pointed cutting tool, as a stone cutter's point; — called also pointer.
Anything which tapers to a sharp, well-defined termination. Specifically: A small promontory or cape; a tract of land extending into the water beyond the common shore line.
The mark made by the end of a sharp, piercing instrument, as a needle; a prick.

An indefinitely small space; a mere spot indicated or supposed. Specifically: (Geom.) That which has neither parts nor magnitude; that which has position, but has neither length, breadth, nor thickness, — sometimes conceived of as the limit of a line; that by the motion of which a line is conceived to be produced.
An indivisible portion of time; a moment; an instant; hence, the verge.
q: When time's first point begun Made he all souls.

senses.d: A mark of punctuation; a character used to mark the divisions of a composition, or the pauses to be observed in reading, or to point off groups of figures, etc.; a stop, as a comma, a semicolon, and esp. a period; hence, figuratively, an end, or conclusion.
q: And there a point, for ended is my tale.
Commas and points they set exactly right.

senses.d: Whatever serves to mark progress, rank, or relative position, or to indicate a transition from one state or position to another, degree; step; stage; hence, position or condition attained; as, a point of elevation, or of depression; the stock fell off five points; he won by tenpoints.
q: A lord full fat and in good point.

senses.d: That which arrests attention, or indicates qualities or character; a salient feature; a characteristic; a peculiarity; hence, a particular; an item; a detail; as, the good or bad points of a man, a horse, a book, a story, etc.
q: He told him, point for point, in short and plain.
In point of religion and in point of honor.
Shalt thou dispute With Him the points of liberty ?

senses.d: Hence, the most prominent or important feature, as of an argument, discourse, etc.; the essential matter; esp., the proposition to be established; as, the point of an anecdote.
q: They will hardly prove his point.

senses.d: A small matter; a trifle; a least consideration; a punctilio.
q: This fellow doth not stand upon points.
cared not for God or man a point.

senses.d: A dot or mark used to designate certain tones or time

Point.etym: [F. point, and probably also pointe, L. punctum, puncta, fr. pungere, punctum, to prick. See Pungent, and cf. Puncto, Puncture.]

senses.d: To give a point to; to sharpen; to cut, forge, grind, or file to an acute end; as, to point a dart, or a pencil. Used also figuratively; as, to point a moral.
To direct toward an abject; to aim; as, to point a gun at a wolf, or a cannon at a fort.
Hence, to direct the attention or notice of.
q: Whosoever should be guided through his battles by Minerva, and pointed to every scene of them.

senses.d: To supply with punctuation marks; to punctuate; as, to point a composition.
To mark (as Hebrew) with vowel points.
To give particular prominence to; to designate in a special manner; to indicate, as if by pointing; as, the error was pointed out.
q: He points it, however, by no deviation from his straightforward manner of speech.

senses.d: To indicate or discover by a fixed look, as game.
To fill up and finish the joints of (a wall), by introducing additional cement or mortar, and bringing it to a smooth surface.
To cut, as a surface, with a pointed tool.
To direct the point of something, as of a finger, for the purpose of designating an object, and attracting attention to it; — with at.
q: Now must the world point at poor Katharine.
Point at the tattered coat and ragged shoe.

senses.d: To indicate the presence of game by fixed and steady look, as certain hunting dogs do.
q: He treads with caution, and he points with fear.

senses.d: To approximate to the surface; to head; — said of an abscess.
A pointed piece of quill or bone covered at one end with vaccine matter; — called also vaccine point.

One of the raised dots used in certain systems of printing and writing for the blind. The first practical system was that devised by Louis Braille in 1829, and still used in Europe (see Braille). Two modifications of this are current in the United States: New York point founded on three bases of equidistant points arranged in two lines (viz., : :: :::), and a later improvement, American Braille, embodying the Braille base (:::) and the New-York-point principle of using the characters of few points for the commonest letters.
In various games, a position of a certain player, or, by extension, the player himself;
Sharp; having a sharp point; as, a pointed rock.
Characterized by sharpness, directness, or pithiness of expression; terse; epigrammatic; especially, directed to a particular person or thing.
q: His moral pleases, not his pointed wit.

senses.d: Any agent which, when introduced into the animal organism, is capable of producing a morbid, noxious, or deadly effect upon it; as, morphine is a deadly poison; the poison of pestilential diseases.
That which taints or destroys moral purity or health; as, the poison of evil example; the poison of sin.

Poison.etym: [F. poison, in Old French also, a potion, fr. L. potio a drink, draught, potion, a poisonous draught, fr. potare to drink. See Potable, and cf. Potion.]

senses.d: To put poison upon or into; to infect with poison; as, to poison an arrow; to poison food or drink.
To injure or kill by poison; to administer poison to.
q: If you poison us, do we not die ?

senses.d: To taint; to corrupt; to vitiate; as, vice poisons happiness; slander poisoned his mind.
q: Whispering tongues can poison truth.

Poison.etym: [Cf. OF. poisonner, F. empoissoner, L. potionare to give to drink. See Poison, n.]

senses.d: To act as, or convey, a poison.
q: Tooth that poisons if it bite.

senses.d: A native or inhabitant of Poland; a Polander.

Pole.etym: [Cf. G. Pole a Pole, Polen Poland.]

senses.d: A long, slender piece of wood; a tall, slender piece of timber; the stem of a small tree whose branches have been removed; as, specifically: (a) A carriage pole, a wooden bar extending from the front axle of a carriage between the wheel horses, by which the carriage is guided and held back. (b) A flag pole, a pole on which a flag is supported. (c) A Maypole. See Maypole. (d) A barber's pole, a pole painted in stripes, used as a sign by barbers and hairdressers. (e) A pole on which climbing beans, hops, or other vines, are trained.
A measuring stick; also, a measure of length equal to 5� yards, or a square measure equal to 30� square yards; a rod; a perch.

Pole.etym: [As. pāl, L. palus, akin to pangere to make fast. Cf. Pale a stake, Pact.]

senses.d: To furnish with poles for support; as, to pole beans or hops.
To convey on poles; as, to pole hay into a barn.
To impel by a pole or poles, as a boat.
To stir, as molten glass, with a pole.
Either extremity of an axis of a sphere; especially, one of the extremities of the earth's axis; as, the north pole.

A point upon the surface of a sphere equally distant from every part of the circumference of a great circle; or the point in which a diameter of the sphere perpendicular to the plane of such circle meets the surface. Such a point is called the pole of that circle; as, the pole of the horizon; the pole of the ecliptic; the pole of a given meridian.

One of the opposite or contrasted parts or directions in which a polar force is manifested; a point of maximum intensity of a force which has two such points, or which has polarity; as, the poles of a magnet; the north pole of a needle.
The firmament; the sky.
q: Shoots against the dusky pole.

Pole.etym: [L. polus, Gr. � a pivot or hinge on which anything turns, an axis, a pole; akin to � to move: cf. F. pôle.]

senses.d: Civil polity.

The settled method by which the government and affairs of a nation are, or may be, administered; a system of public or official administration, as designed to promote the external or internal prosperity of a state.
The method by which any institution is administered; system of management; course.
Management or administration based on temporal or material interest, rather than on principles of equity or honor; hence, worldly wisdom; dexterity of management; cunning; stratagem.
Prudence or wisdom in the management of public and private affairs; wisdom; sagacity; wit.
q: The very policy of a hostess, finding his purse so far above his clothes, did detect him.

senses.d: Motive; object; inducement.
q: What policy have you to bestow a benefit where it is counted an injury?

Policy.etym: [L. politia, Gr. �; cf. F. police, Of. police. See Police, n.]

senses.d: To regulate by laws; to reduce to order.
A ticket or warrant for money in the public funds.

The writing or instrument in which a contract of insurance is embodied; an instrument in writing containing the terms and conditions on which one party engages to indemnify another against loss arising from certain hazards, perils, or risks to which his person or property may be exposed. See Insurance.
A method of gambling by betting as to what numbers will be drawn in a lottery; as, to play policy.

Policy.etym: [F. police; cf. Pr. polissia, Sp. pólizia, It. pólizza; of uncertain origin; cf. L. pollex thumb (as being used in pressing the seal), in LL. also, seal; or cf. LL. politicum, poleticum, polecticum, L. polyptychum, account book, register, fr. Gr. � having many folds or leaves; � many + � fold, leaf,

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Poland or its inhabitants.
The language of the Poles.
To make smooth and glossy, usually by friction; to burnish; to overspread with luster; as, to polish glass, marble, metals, etc.
Hence, to refine; to wear off the rudeness, coarseness, or rusticity of; to make elegant and polite; as, to polish life or manners.
To become smooth, as from friction; to receive a gloss; to take a smooth and glossy surface; as, steel polishes well.
A smooth, glossy surface, usually produced by friction; a gloss or luster.
q: Another prism of clearer glass and better polish.

senses.d: Anything used to produce a gloss.
Fig.: Refinement; elegance of manners.
q: This Roman polish and this smooth behavior.

senses.d: Made smooth and glossy, as by friction; hence, highly finished; refined; polite; as, polished plate; polished manners; polished verse.
A parrot; — familiarly so called.
One who does not try for honors, but is content to take a degree merely; a passman.
The head; the back part of the head.
A number or aggregate of heads; a list or register of heads or individuals.
q: We are the greater poll, and in true fear They gave us our demands.
The muster file, rotten and sound, upon my life, amounts not to fifteen thousand poll.

senses.d: Specifically, the register of the names of electors who may vote in an election.
The casting or recording of the votes of registered electors; as, the close of the poll.
q: All soldiers quartered in place are to remove . . . and not to return till one day after the poll is ended.

senses.d: The place where the votes are cast or recorded; as, to go to the polls.
The broad end of a hammer; the but of an ax.
The European chub. See Pollard, 3 (a).

Poll.etym: [Akin to LG. polle the head, the crest of a bird, the top of a tree, OD. pol, polle, Dan. puld the crown of a hat.]

senses.d: To remove the poll or head of; hence, to remove the top or end of; to clip; to lop; to shear; as, to poll the head; to poll a tree.
q: When he pollled his head.
His death did so grieve them that they polled themselves; they clipped off their horse and mule's hairs.

senses.d: To cut off; to remove by clipping, shearing, etc.; to mow or crop; — sometimes with off; as, to poll the hair; to poll wool; to poll grass.
q: Who, as he polled off his dart's head, so sure he had decreed That all the counsels of their war he would poll off like it.

senses.d: To extort from; to plunder; to strip.
q: Which polls and pills the poor in piteous wise.

senses.d: To impose a tax upon.
To pay as one's personal tax.
q: The man that polled but twelve pence for his head.

senses.d: To enter, as polls or persons, in a list or register; to enroll, esp. for purposes of taxation; to enumerate one by one.
q: Polling the reformed churches whether they equalize in number those of his three kingdoms.

senses.d: To register or deposit, as a vote; to elicit or call forth, as votes or voters; as, he polled a hundred votes more than his opponent.
q: And poll for points of faith his trusty vote.

senses.d: To cut or shave smooth or even; to cut in a straight line without indentation; as, a polled deed. See Dee� poll.
To vote at an election.

Deprived of a poll, or of something belonging to the poll. Specifically: (a) Lopped; — said of trees having their tops cut off. (b) Cropped; hence, bald; — said of a person. “The polled bachelor.” Beau. & Fl. (c) Having cast the antlers; — said of a stag. (d) Without horns; as, polled cattle; polled sheep.
To make foul, impure, or unclean; to defile; to taint; to soil; to desecrate; — used of physical or moral defilement.
q: The land was polluted with blood.
Wickedness . . . hath polluted the whole earth.

senses.d: To violate sexually; to debauch; to dishonor.
To render ceremonially unclean; to disqualify or unfit for sacred use or service, or for social intercourse.
q: Neither shall ye pollute the holy things of the children of Israel, lest ye die.
They have polluted themselves with blood.

Pollute.syn: To defile; soil; contaminate; corrupt; taint; vitiate; debauch; dishonor; ravish.
Pollute.etym: [L. pollutus, p. p. of polluere to defile, to pollute, from a prep. appearing only in comp. + luere to wash. See Position, Lave.]

senses.d: Polluted.
Defiled; made unclean or impure; debauched.
Adapted or tending to pollute; causing defilement or pollution.
The act of polluting, or the state of being polluted (in any sense of the verb); defilement; uncleanness; impurity.
The emission of semen, or sperm, at other times than in sexual intercourse.
A fixed star of the second magnitude, in the constellation Gemini. Cf. 3d Castor.
Same as Pollucite.

The fruit of the tree Punica Granatum; also, the tree itself (see Balaustine), which is native in the Orient, but is successfully cultivated in many warm countries, and as a house plant in colder climates. The fruit is as large as an orange, and has a hard rind containing many rather large seeds, each one separately covered with crimson, acid pulp.
A carved or embroidered ornament resembling a pomegranate.

Pomegranate.etym: [OE. pomgarnet, OF. pome de grenate, F. grenade, L. pomum a fruit + granatus grained, having many grains or seeds. See Pome, and Garnet, Grain.]

senses.d: A knob or ball; an object resembling a ball in form
The knob on the hilt of a sword.
The knob or protuberant part of a saddlebow.
The top (of the head).
A knob forming the finial of a turret or pavilion.

Pommel.etym: [OE. pomel, OF. pomel, F. pommeau, LL. pomellus, fr. L. pomum fruit, LL. also, an apple. See Pome.]

senses.d: To beat soundly, as with the pommel of a sword, or with something knoblike; hence, to beat with the fists.
A procession distinguished by ostentation and splendor; a pageant.
Show of magnificence; parade; display; power.

Pomp.syn: Display; parade; pageant; pageantry; splendor; state; magnificence; ostentation; grandeur; pride.
Pomp.etym: [OE. pompe, F. pompe, L. pompa, fr. Gr. � a sending, a solemn procession, pomp, fr. � to send. Cf. Pump a shoe.]

senses.d: To make a pompons display; to conduct.
A body of water, naturally or artificially confined, and usually of less extent than a lake.

Pond.etym: [Probably originally, an inclosed body of water, and the same word as pound. See Pound an inclosure.]

senses.d: To make into a pond; to collect, as water, in a pond by damming.
To ponder.
q: Pleaseth you, pond your suppliant's plaint.

senses.d: To weigh.
To weigh in the mind; to view with deliberation; to examine carefully; to consider attentively.
q: Ponder the path of thy feet.

Ponder.etym: [L. ponderare, fr. pondus, ponderis, a weight, fr. pendere to weigh: cf. F. pondérer. See Pendant, and cf. Pound a weight.]

senses.d: To think; to deliberate; to muse; — usually followed by on or over.
A small and rather deep collection of (usually) fresh water, as one supplied by a spring, or occurring in the course of a stream; a reservoir for water; as, the pools of Solomon.
q: Charity will hardly water the ground where it must first fill a pool.
The sleepy pool above the dam.

senses.d: A small body of standing or stagnant water; a puddle.

Pool.etym: [AS. pōl; akin to LG. pool, pohl, D. poel, G. pfuhl; cf. Icel. pollr, also W. pwll, Gael. poll.]

senses.d: The stake played for in certain games of cards, billiards, etc.; an aggregated stake to which each player has contributed a snare; also, the receptacle for the stakes.

A game at billiards, in which each of the players stakes a certain sum, the winner taking the whole; also, in public billiard rooms, a game in which the loser pays the entrance fee for all who engage in the game; a game of skill in pocketing the balls on a pool table.
q: He plays pool at the billiard houses.

senses.d: In rifle shooting, a contest in which each competitor pays a certain sum for every shot he makes, the net proceeds being divided among the winners.
Any gambling or commercial venture in which several persons join.

A combination of persons contributing money to be used for the purpose of increasing or depressing the market price of stocks, grain, or other commodities; also, the aggregate of the sums so contributed; as, the pool took all the wheat offered below the limit; he put $10,000 into the pool.
A mutual arrangement between competing lines, by which the receipts of all are aggregated, and then distributed pro rata according to agreement.
An aggregation of properties or rights, belonging to different people in a community, in a common fund, to be charged with common liabilities.

Pool.etym: [F. poule, properly, a hen. See Pullet.]

senses.d: To put together; to contribute to a common fund, on the basis of a mutual division of profits or losses; to make a common interest of; as, the companies pooled their traffic.
q: Finally, it favors the poolingof all issues.

senses.d: To combine or contribute with others, as for a commercial, speculative, or gambling transaction.
Destitute of property; wanting in material riches or goods; needy; indigent.
So completely destitute of property as to be entitled to maintenance from the public.
Destitute of such qualities as are desirable, or might naturally be expected
q: That I have wronged no man will be a poor plea or apology at the last day.

senses.d: Worthy of pity or sympathy; — used also sometimes as a term of endearment, or as an expression of modesty, and sometimes as a word of contempt.
q: And for mine own poor part, Look you, I'll go pray.
Poor, little, pretty, fluttering thing.

senses.d: Free from self-assertion; not proud or arrogant; meek.

Poor.etym: [OE. poure or povre, OF. povre, F. pauvre, L. pauper; the first syllable of which is probably akin to paucus few (see Paucity, Few), and the second to parare to prepare, procure. See Few, and cf. Parade, Pauper, Poverty.]

senses.d: A small European codfish (Gadus minutus); — called also power cod.
Any tree of the genus Populus; also, the timber, which is soft, and capable of many uses.
The timber of the tulip tree; — called also white poplar.

Poplar.etym: [OE. popler, OF. poplier, F. peuplier, fr. L. populus poplar.]

senses.d: Abounding in people; full of inhabitants; containing many inhabitants in proportion to the extent of the country.
q: Heaven, yet populous, retains Number sufficient to possess her realms.

senses.d: Popular; famous.
Common; vulgar.
Numerous; in large number.

Populous.etym: [L. populosus, fr. populus people: cf. F. populeux.]

senses.d: A covered and inclosed entrance to a building, whether taken from the interior, and forming a sort of vestibule within the main wall, or projecting without and with a separate roof. Sometimes the porch is large enough to serve as a covered walk. See also Carriage porch, under Carriage, and Loggia.
q: The graceless Helen in the porch I spied Of Vesta's temple.

senses.d: A portico; a covered walk.
q: Repair to Pompey's porch, where you shall find find us.

Porch.etym: [F. porche, L. porticus, fr. porta a gate, entrance, or passage. See Port a gate, and cf. Portico.]

senses.d: A dark red or purple astringent wine made in Portugal. It contains a large percentage of alcohol.

Port.etym: [From Oporto, in Portugal, i.e., � porto the port, L. portus. See Port harbor.]

senses.d: A place where ships may ride secure from storms; a sheltered inlet, bay, or cove; a harbor; a haven. Used also figuratively.
q: Peering in maps for ports and piers and roads.
We are in port if we have Thee.

senses.d: In law and commercial usage, a harbor where vessels are admitted to discharge and receive cargoes, from whence they depart and where they finish their voyages.

Port.etym: [AS. port, L. portus: cf. F. port. See Farm, v., Ford, and 1st, 3d, & 4h Port.]

senses.d: A passageway; an opening or entrance to an inclosed place; a gate; a door; a portal.
q: Him I accuse The city ports by this hath entered.
Form their ivory port the cherubim Forth issuing.

senses.d: An opening in the side of a vessel; an embrasure through which cannon may be discharged; a porthole; also, the shutters which close such an opening.
q: Her ports being within sixteen inches of the water.

senses.d: A passageway in a machine, through which a fluid, as steam, water, etc., may pass, as from a valve to the interior of the cylinder of a steam engine; an opening in a valve seat, or valve face.

Port.etym: [F. porte, L. porta, akin to portus; cf. AS. porte, fr. L. porta. See Port a harbor, and cf. Porte.]

senses.d: To carry; to bear; to transport.
q: They are easily ported by boat into other shires.

senses.d: To throw, as a musket, diagonally across the body, with the lock in front, the right hand grasping the small of the stock, and the barrel sloping upward and crossing the point of the left shoulder; as, to port arms.
q: Began to hem him round with ported spears.

Port.etym: [F. porter, L. portare to carry. See Port demeanor.]

senses.d: The manner in which a person bears himself; deportment; carriage; bearing; demeanor; hence, manner or style of living; as, a proud port.
q: And of his port as meek as is a maid.
The necessities of pomp, grandeur, and a suitable port in the world.

Port.etym: [F. port, fr. porter to carry, L. portare, prob. akin to E. fare, v. See Port harbor, and cf. Comport, Export, Sport.]

senses.d: The larboard or left side of a ship (looking from the stern toward the bow); as, a vessel heels to port. See Note under Larboard. Also used adjectively.
To turn or put to the left or larboard side of a ship; — said of the helm, and used chiefly in the imperative, as a command; as, port your helm.
The Ottoman court; the government of the Turkish empire, officially called the Sublime Porte, from the gate (port) of the sultan's palace at which justice was administered.

Porte.etym: [F. porte a gate, L. porta. See Port a gate.]

senses.d: A man who has charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper; one who waits at the door to receive messages.
q: To him the porter openeth.

Porter.etym: [F. portier, L. portarius, from porta a gate, door. See Port a gate.]

senses.d: A carrier; one who carries or conveys burdens, luggage, etc.; for hire.

A bar of iron or steel at the end of which a forging is made; esp., a long, large bar, to the end of which a heavy forging is attached, and by means of which the forging is lifted and handled in hammering and heating; — called also porter bar.
A malt liquor, of a dark color and moderately bitter taste, possessing tonic and intoxicating qualities.

Porter.etym: [F. porteur, fr. porter to carry, L. portare. See Port to carry.]

senses.d: That which is divided off or separated, as a part from a whole; a separated part of anything.
A part considered by itself, though not actually cut off or separated from the whole.
q: These are parts of his ways; but how little a portion is heard of him!
Portions and parcels of the dreadful past.

senses.d: A part assigned; allotment; share; fate.
q: The lord of that servant . . . will appoint him his portion with the unbelievers.
Man's portion is to die and rise again.

senses.d: The part of an estate given to a child or heir, or descending to him by law, and distributed to him in the settlement of the estate; an inheritance.
q: Give me the portion of goods that falleth to me.

senses.d: A wife's fortune; a dowry.

Portion.syn: Division; share; parcel; quantity; allotment; dividend.
Portion.etym: [F., from L. portio, akin to pars, partis, a part. See Part, n.]

senses.d: To separate or divide into portions or shares; to parcel; to distribute.
q: And portion to his tribes the wide domain.

senses.d: To endow with a portion or inheritance.
q: Him portioned maids, apprenticed orphans, blest.

senses.d: To occupy in person; to hold or actually have in one's own keeping; to have and to hold.
q: Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
Yet beauty, though injurious, hath strange power, After offense returning, to regain Love once possessed.

senses.d: To have the legal title to; to have a just right to; to be master of; to own; to have; as, to possess property, an estate, a book.
q: I am yours, and all that I possess.

senses.d: To obtain occupation or possession of; to accomplish; to gain; to seize.
q: How . . . to possess the purpose they desired.

senses.d: To enter into and influence; to control the will of; to fill; to affect; — said especially of evil spirits, passions, etc.
q: Those which were possessed with devils.
For ten inspired, ten thousand are possessed.

senses.d: To put in possession; to make the owner or holder of property, power, knowledge, etc.; to acquaint; to inform; — followed by of or with before the thing possessed, and now commonly used reflexively.
q: I have possessed your grace of what I purpose.
Record a gift . . . of all he dies possessed Unto his son.
We possessed our selves of the kingdom of Naples.
To possess our minds with an habitual good intention.

Possess.syn: To have; hold; occupy; control; own.
Possess.etym: [L. possessus, p. p. of possidere to have, possess, from an inseparable prep. (cf. Position) + sedere to sit. See Sit.]

senses.d: The act or state of possessing, or holding as one's own.
The having, holding, or detention of property in one's power or command; actual seizin or occupancy; ownership, whether rightful or wrongful.
The thing possessed; that which any one occupies, owns, or controls; in the plural, property in the aggregate; wealth; dominion; as, foreign possessions.
q: When the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession.
The house of Jacob shall possess their possessions.

senses.d: The state of being possessed or controlled, as by an evil spirit, or violent passions; madness; frenzy; as, demoniacal possession.
q: How long hath this possession held the man?

senses.d: To invest with property.
One who possesses; one who occupies, holds, owns, or controls; one who has actual participation or enjoyment, generally of that which is desirable; a proprietor.
q: As if he had been possessor of the whole world.

senses.d: Capable of existing or occurring, or of being conceived or thought of; able to happen; capable of being done; not contrary to the nature of things; — sometimes used to express extreme improbability; barely able to be, or to come to pass; as, possibly he is honest, as it is possible that Judas meant no wrong.
q: With God all things are possible.

Possible.etym: [F., fr. L. possibilis, fr. posse to be able, to have power; potis able, capable + esse to be. See Potent, Am, and cf. Host a landlord.]

senses.d: Hired to do what is wrong; suborned.

Post.etym: [F. aposter to place in a post or position, generally for a bad purpose.]

senses.d: A piece of timber, metal, or other solid substance, fixed, or to be fixed, firmly in an upright position, especially when intended as a stay or support to something else; a pillar; as, a hitching post; a fence post; the posts of a house.
q: They shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper doorpost of the houses.
Then by main force pulled up, and on his shoulders bore, The gates of Azza, post and massy bar.
Unto his order he was a noble post.

senses.d: The doorpost of a victualer's shop or inn, on which were chalked the scores of customers; hence, a score; a debt.
q: When God sends coin I will discharge your post.

Post.etym: [AS., fr. L. postis, akin to ponere, positum, to place. See Position, and cf. 4th Post.]

senses.d: The place at which anything is stopped, placed, or fixed; a station.
A messenger who goes from station; an express; especially, one who is employed by the government to carry letters and parcels regularly from one place to another; a letter carrier; a postman.
q: In certain places there be always fresh posts, to carry that further which is brought unto them by the other.
I fear my Julia would not deign my lines, Receiving them from such a worthless post.

senses.d: An established conveyance for letters from one place or station to another; especially, the governmental system in any country for carrying and distributing letters and parcels; the post office; the mail; hence, the carriage by which the mail is transported.
q: I send you the fair copy of the poem on dullness, which I should not care to hazard by the common post.

senses.d: Haste or speed, like that of a messenger or mail carrier.
One who has charge of a station, especially of a postal station.
q: He held office of postmaster, or, as it was then called, post, for several years.

senses.d: A station, office, or position of service, trust, or emolument; as, the post of duty; the post of danger.
q: The post of honor is a private station.

senses.d: A size of printing and writing paper. See the Table under Paper.

Post.etym: [F. poste, LL. posta station, post (where horses were kept), properly, a fixed or set place, fem. fr. L. positus placed, p. p. of ponere. See Position, and cf. Post a pillar.]

senses.d: To attach to a post, a wall, or other usual place of affixing public notices; to placard; as, to post a notice; to post playbills.
To hold up to public blame or reproach; to advertise opprobriously; to denounce by public proclamation; as, to post one for cowardice.
q: On pain of being posted to your sorrow Fail not, at four, to meet me.

senses.d: To enter (a name) on a list, as for service, promotion, or the like.
To assign to a station; to set; to place; as, to post a sentinel.
To carry, as an account, from the journal to the ledger; as, to post an account; to transfer, as accounts, to the ledger.
q: You have not posted your books these ten years.

senses.d: To place in the care of the post; to mail; as, to post a letter.
To inform; to give the news to; to make (one) acquainted with the details of a subject; — often with up.
q: Thoroughly posted up in the politics and literature of the day.

senses.d: To travel with post horses; figuratively, to travel in haste.
q: And post o'er land and ocean without rest.

senses.d: To rise and sink in the saddle, in accordance with the motion of the horse, esp. in trotting.
With post horses; hence, in haste; as, to travel post.

The race that proceeds from a progenitor; offspring to the furthest generation; the aggregate number of persons who are descended from an ancestor of a generation; descendants; — contrasted with ancestry; as, the posterity of Abraham.
q: If should not stand in thy posterity.

senses.d: Succeeding generations; future times.
q: Their names shall be transmitted to posterity.
Their names shall be transmitted to posterity.

Posterity.etym: [L. posteritas: cf. F. postérité. See Posterior.]

senses.d: A metallic or earthen vessel, appropriated to any of a great variety of uses, as for boiling meat or vegetables, for holding liquids, for plants, etc.; as, a quart pot; a flower pot; a bean pot.
An earthen or pewter cup for liquors; a mug.
The quantity contained in a pot; a potful; as, a pot of ale.
A metal or earthenware extension of a flue above the top of a chimney; a chimney pot.
A crucible; as, a graphite pot; a melting pot.
A wicker vessel for catching fish, eels, etc.
A perforated cask for draining sugar.
A size of paper. See Pott.

Pot.etym: [Akin to LG. pott, D. pot, Dan. potte, Sw. potta, Icel. pottr, F. pot; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To place or inclose in pots
To preserve seasoned in pots.
To set out or cover in pots; as, potted plants or bulbs.
To drain; as, to pot sugar, by taking it from the cooler, and placing it in hogsheads, etc., having perforated heads, through which the molasses drains off.
To pocket.
To tipple; to drink.
q: It is less labor to plow than to pot it.

senses.d: To shoot for the pot, i.e., cooking; to secure or hit by a pot shot; to shoot when no special skill is needed.
q: When hunted, it takes refuge in trees, and this habit is well known to hunters, who pursue it with dogs and pot it when treed.

senses.d: To secure; gain; win; bag.
To take a pot shot or shots, as at game or an enemy.
The total of the bets at stake at one time, as in racing or card playing; the pool;
A plain defensive headpiece; later, and perhaps in a jocose sense, any helmet; — called also pot helmet.
The total of the bets at one time; the pool.
One who is potent; one who possesses great power or sway; a prince, sovereign, or monarch.
q: The blessed and only potentate.
Cherub and seraph, potentates and thrones.

Potentate.etym: [LL. potentatus, fr. potentare to exercise power: cf. F. potentat. See Potent, a.]

senses.d: A piece or fragment of a broken pot.
A size of paper. See under Paper.
A kind of food made by boiling vegetables or meat, or both together, in water, until soft; a thick soup or porridge.
q: Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentils.

Pottage.etym: [F. potage, fr. pot pot. See Pot, and cf. Porridge, Porringer.]

senses.d: One whose occupation is to make earthen vessels.
q: The potter heard, and stopped his wheel.

senses.d: One who hawks crockery or earthenware.
One who pots meats or other eatables.
The red-bellied terrapin. See Terrapin.
To busy one's self with trifles; to labor with little purpose, energy, of effect; to trifle; to pother.
q: Pottering about the Mile End cottages.

senses.d: To walk lazily or idly; to saunter.

Potter.etym: [Cf. W. pwtio to poke, or OD. poteren to search one thoroughly, Sw. påta, peta, to pick, E. pother, put.]

senses.d: To poke; to push; also, to disturb; to confuse; to bother.
To strike repeatedly with some heavy instrument; to beat.
q: With cruel blows she pounds her blubbered cheeks.

senses.d: To comminute and pulverize by beating; to bruise or break into fine particles with a pestle or other heavy instrument; as, to pound spice or salt.

Pound.etym: [OE. pounen, AS. punian to bruise. Cf. Pun a play on words.]

senses.d: To strike heavy blows; to beat.
To make a jarring noise, as in running; as, the engine pounds.
An inclosure, maintained by public authority, in which cattle or other animals are confined when taken in trespassing, or when going at large in violation of law; a pinfold.
A level stretch in a canal between locks.
A kind of net, having a large inclosure with a narrow entrance into which fish are directed by wings spreading outward.

Pound.etym: [AS. pund an inclosure: cf. forpyndan to turn away, or to repress, also Icel. pynda to extort, torment, Ir. pont, pond, pound. Cf. Pinder, Pinfold, Pin to inclose, Pond.]

senses.d: To confine in, or as in, a pound; to impound.
A certain specified weight; especially, a legal standard consisting of an established number of ounces.

A British denomination of money of account, equivalent to twenty shillings sterling, and equal in value to about $4.86. There is no coin known by this name, but the gold sovereign is of the same value.

Pound.etym: [AS. pund, fr. L. pondo, akin to pondus a weight, pendere to weigh. See Pendant.]

senses.d: Poor.
To pore.

To cause to flow in a stream, as a liquid or anything flowing like a liquid, either out of a vessel or into it; as, to pour water from a pail; to pour wine into a decanter; to pour oil upon the waters; to pour out sand or dust.
To send forth as in a stream or a flood; to emit; to let escape freely or wholly.
q: I . . . have poured out my soul before the Lord.
Now will I shortly pour out my fury upon thee.
London doth pour out her citizens !
Wherefore did Nature pour her bounties forth With such a full and unwithdrawing hand ?

senses.d: To send forth from, as in a stream; to discharge uninterruptedly.
q: Is it for thee the linnet pours his throat ?

Pour.etym: [OE. pouren, of uncertain origin; cf. W. bwrw to cast, throw, shed, bwrw gwlaw to rain.]

senses.d: To flow, pass, or issue in a stream, or as a stream; to fall continuously and abundantly; as, the rain pours; the people poured out of the theater.
q: In the rude throng pour on with furious pace.

senses.d: A stream, or something like a stream; a flood.
The quality or state of being poor or indigent; want or scarcity of means of subsistence; indigence; need.
q: The drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty.

senses.d: Any deficiency of elements or resources that are needed or desired, or that constitute richness; as, poverty of soil; poverty of the blood; poverty of ideas.

Poverty.syn: Indigence; penury; beggary; need; lack; want; scantiness; sparingness; meagerness; jejuneness.
Poverty.etym: [OE. poverte, OF. poverté, F. pauvreté, fr. L. paupertas, fr. pauper poor. See Poor.]

senses.d: The fine particles to which any dry substance is reduced by pounding, grinding, or triturating, or into which it falls by decay; dust.
q: Grind their bones to powder small.

senses.d: An explosive mixture used in gunnery, blasting, etc.; gunpowder. See Gunpowder.

Powder.etym: [OE. poudre, pouldre, F. poudre, OF. also poldre, puldre, L. pulvis, pulveris: cf. pollen fine flour, mill dust, E. pollen. Cf. Polverine, Pulverize.]

senses.d: To reduce to fine particles; to pound, grind, or rub into a powder; to comminute; to pulverize; to triturate.
To sprinkle with powder, or as with powder; to be sprinkle; as, to powder the hair.
q: A circling zone thou seest Powdered with stars.

senses.d: To sprinkle with salt; to corn, as meat.
To be reduced to powder; to become like powder; as, some salts powder easily.
To use powder on the hair or skin; as, she paints and powders.
Same as Poor, the fish.

Ability to act, regarded as latent or inherent; the faculty of doing or performing something; capacity for action or performance; capability of producing an effect, whether physical or moral: potency; might; as, a man of great power; the power of capillary attraction; money gives power.

Ability, regarded as put forth or exerted; strength, force, or energy in action; as, the power of steam in moving an engine; the power of truth, or of argument, in producing conviction; the power of enthusiasm.
Capacity of undergoing or suffering; fitness to be acted upon; susceptibility; — called also passive power; as, great power of endurance.
q: Power, then, is active and passive; faculty is active power or capacity; capacity is passive power.

senses.d: The exercise of a faculty; the employment of strength; the exercise of any kind of control; influence; dominion; sway; command; government.
q: Power is no blessing in itself but when it is employed to protect the innocent.

senses.d: The agent exercising an ability to act; an individual invested with authority; an institution, or government, which exercises control; as, the great powers of Europe; hence, often, a superhuman agent; a spirit; a divinity.
q: And the powers of the heavens shall be shaken.

senses.d: A military or naval force; an army or navy; a great host.
q: Never such a power . . . Was levied in the body of a land.

senses.d: A large quantity; a great number; as, a power o� good things.
The rate at which mechanical energy is exerted or mechanical work performed, as by an engine or other machine, or an animal, working continuously; as, an engine of twenty horse power.
A mechanical agent; that from which useful mechanical energy is derived; as, water power; steam power; hand power, etc.
Applied force; force producing motion or pressure; as, the power applied at one and of a lever to lift a weight at the other end.
A machine acted upon by an animal, and serving as a motor to drive other machinery; as, a dog power.
The product arising from the multiplication of a number into itself; as, a square is the second power, and a cube is third power, of a number.

Power.etym: [OE. pouer, poer, OF. poeir, pooir, F. pouvoir, n. & v., fr. LL. potere, for L. posse, potesse, to be able, to have power. See Possible, Potent, and cf. Posse comitatus.]

senses.d: Full of power; capable of producing great effects of any kind; potent; mighty; efficacious; intense; as, a powerful man or beast; a powerful engine; a powerful argument; a powerful light; a powerful vessel.
q: The powerful grace that lies In herbs, plants, stones, and their true qualities.

senses.d: Large; capacious; — said of veins of ore.

Powerful.syn: Mighty; strong; potent; forcible; efficacious; energetic; intense.

senses.d: Practical.
Artful; deceitful; skillful.

Frequently repeated or customary action; habitual performance; a succession of acts of a similar kind; usage; habit; custom; as, the practice of rising early; the practice of making regular entries of accounts; the practice of daily exercise.
q: A heart . . . exercised with covetous practices.

senses.d: Customary or constant use; state of being used.
q: Obsolete words may be revived when they are more sounding or more significant than those in practice.

senses.d: Skill or dexterity acquired by use; expertness.
Actual performance; application of knowledge; — opposed to theory.
q: There are two functions of the soul, — contemplation and practice.
There is a distinction, but no opposition, between theory and practice; each, to a certain extent, supposes the other; theory is dependent on practice; practice must have preceded theory.

senses.d: Systematic exercise for instruction or discipline; as, the troops are called out for practice; she neglected practice in music.
Application of science to the wants of men; the exercise of any profession; professional business; as, the practice of medicine or law; a large or lucrative practice.
q: Practice is exercise of an art, or the application of a science in life, which application is itself an art.

senses.d: Skillful or artful management; dexterity in contrivance or the use of means; art; stratagem; artifice; plot; — usually in a bad sense.
q: He sought to have that by practice which he could not by prayer.

senses.d: A easy and concise method of applying the rules of arithmetic to questions which occur in trade and business.
The form, manner, and order of conducting and carrying on suits and prosecutions through their various stages, according to the principles of law and the rules laid down by the courts.

Practice.etym: [OE. praktike, practique, F. pratique, formerly also, practique, LL. practica, fr. Gr. �, fr. � practical. See Practical, and cf. Pratique, Pretty.]

senses.d: To do or perform frequently, customarily, or habitually; to make a practice of; as, to practice gaming.
To exercise, or follow, as a profession, trade, art, etc., as, to practice law or medicine.
To exercise one's self in, for instruction or improvement, or to acquire discipline or dexterity; as, to practice gunnery; to practice music.
To put into practice; to carry out; to act upon; to commit; to execute; to do.
q: As this advice ye practice or neglect.

senses.d: To make use of; to employ.
q: In malice to this good knight's wife, I practiced Ubaldo and Ricardo to corrupt her.

senses.d: To teach or accustom by practice; to train.
q: In church they are taught to love God; after church they are practiced to love their neighbor.

senses.d: To perform certain acts frequently or customarily, either for instruction, profit, or amusement; as, to practice with the broadsword or with the rifle; to practice on the piano.
To learn by practice; to form a habit.
q: They shall practice how to live secure.
Practice first over yourself to reign.

senses.d: To try artifices or stratagems.
q: He will practice against thee by poison.

senses.d: To apply theoretical science or knowledge, esp. by way of experiment; to exercise or pursue an employment or profession, esp. that of medicine or of law.
q: little inclined to practice on others, and as little that others should practice on me.

senses.d: To commend; to applaud; to express approbation of; to laud; — applied to a person or his acts.
q: Let her own works praise her in the gates.
We praise not Hector, though his name, we know, Is great in arms; 't is hard to praise a foe.

senses.d: To extol in words or song; to magnify; to glorify on account of perfections or excellent works; to do honor to; to display the excellence of; — applied especially to the Divine Being.
q: Praise ye him, all his angels; praise ye him, all his hosts!

senses.d: To value; to appraise.

Praise.syn: To commend; laud; eulogize; celebrate; glorify; magnify.
Praise.etym: [OE. preisen, OF. preisier, prisier, F. priser, L. pretiare to prize, fr. pretium price. See Price, n., and cf. Appreciate, Praise, n., Prize, v.]

senses.d: Commendation for worth; approval expressed; honor rendered because of excellence or worth; laudation; approbation.
q: There are men who always confound the praise of goodness with the practice.

senses.d: Especially, the joyful tribute of gratitude or homage rendered to the Divine Being; the act of glorifying or extolling the Creator; worship, particularly worship by song, distinction from prayer and other acts of worship; as, a service of praise.
The object, ground, or reason of praise.
q: He is thy praise, and he is thy God.

Praise.syn: Encomium; honor; eulogy; panegyric; plaudit; applause; acclaim; eclat; commendation; laudation.
Praise.etym: [OE. preis, OF. preis price, worth, value, estimation. See Praise, v., Price.]

senses.d: To talk much and to little purpose; to be loquacious; to speak foolishly; to babble.
q: To prate and talk for life and honor.
And make a fool presume to prate of love.

Prate.etym: [Akin to LG. & D. praten, Dan. prate, Sw. & Icel. prata.]

senses.d: To utter foolishly; to speak without reason or purpose; to chatter, or babble.
q: What nonsense would the fool, thy master, prate, When thou, his knave, canst talk at such a rate !

senses.d: Talk to little purpose; trifling talk; unmeaning loquacity.
q: Sick of tops, and poetry, and prate.

Prate.etym: [Akin to LG. & D. praat, Sw. prat.]

senses.d: To make request with earnestness or zeal, as for something desired; to make entreaty or supplication; to offer prayer to a deity or divine being as a religious act; specifically, to address the Supreme Being with adoration, confession, supplication, and thanksgiving.
q: And to his goddess pitously he preyde.
When thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
I pray, sir. why am I beaten?

Pray.syn: To entreat; supplicate; beg; implore; invoke; beseech; petition.
Pray.etym: [OE. preien, OF. preier, F. prier, L. precari, fr. prex, precis, a prayer, a request; akin to Skr. prach to ask, AS. frignan, frīnan, fricgan, G. fragen, Goth. fraíhnan. Cf. Deprecate, Imprecate, Precarious.]

senses.d: To address earnest request to; to supplicate; to entreat; to implore; to beseech.
q: And as this earl was preyed, so did he.
We pray you . . . by ye reconciled to God.

senses.d: To ask earnestly for; to seek to obtain by supplication; to entreat for.
q: I know not how to pray your patience.

senses.d: To effect or accomplish by praying; as, to pray a soul out of purgatory.
One who prays; a supplicant.
The act of praying, or of asking a favor; earnest request or entreaty; hence, a petition or memorial addressed to a court or a legislative body.

The act of addressing supplication to a divinity, especially to the true God; the offering of adoration, confession, supplication, and thanksgiving to the Supreme Being; as, public prayer; secret prayer.
q: As he is famed for mildness, peace, and prayer.

senses.d: The form of words used in praying; a formula of supplication; an expressed petition; especially, a supplication addressed to God; as, a written or extemporaneous prayer; to repeat one's prayers.
q: He made those excellent prayers which were published immediately after his death.

Prayer.etym: [OE. preiere, OF. preiere, F. prière, fr. L. precarius obtained by prayer, fr. precari to pray. See Pray, v. i.]

senses.d: To proclaim or publish tidings; specifically, to proclaim the gospel; to discourse publicly on a religious subject, or from a text of Scripture; to deliver a sermon.
q: How shall they preach, except they be sent?
From that time Jesus began to preach.

senses.d: To give serious advice on morals or religion; to discourse in the manner of a preacher.

Preach.etym: [OE. prechen, OF. preechier, F. prêcher, fr. L. praedicare to cry in public, to proclaim; prae before + dicare to make known, dicere to say; or perhaps from (assumed) LL. praedictare. See Diction, and cf. Predicate, Predict.]

senses.d: To proclaim by public discourse; to utter in a sermon or a formal religious harangue.
q: That Cristes gospel truly wolde preche.
The Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek.

senses.d: To inculcate in public discourse; to urge with earnestness by public teaching.
To deliver or pronounce; as, to preach a sermon.
To teach or instruct by preaching; to inform by preaching.
To advise or recommend earnestly.
q: My master preaches patience to him.

senses.d: A religious discourse.

Preach.etym: [Cf. F. prêche, fr. prêcher. See Preach, v.]

senses.d: One who preaches; one who discourses publicly on religious subjects.
q: How shall they hear without a preacher?

senses.d: One who inculcates anything with earnestness.
q: No preacher is listened to but Time.

Preacher.etym: [Cf. OF. preeschierre, prescheur, F. prêcheur, L. praedicator.]

senses.d: The act of delivering a religious discourse; the art of sermonizing; also, a sermon; a public religious discourse; serious, earnest advice.
Any commandment, instruction, or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; esp., a command respecting moral conduct; an injunction; a rule.
q: For precept must be upon precept.
No arts are without their precepts.

senses.d: A command in writing; a species of writ or process.

Precept.syn: Commandment; injunction; mandate; law; rule; direction; principle; maxim. See Doctrine.
Precept.etym: [L. praeceptum, from praecipere to take beforehand, to instruct, teach; prae before + capere to take: cf. F. précepte. See Pre-, and Capacious.]

senses.d: To teach by precepts.
Of great price; costly; as, a precious stone.
Of great value or worth; very valuable; highly esteemed; dear; beloved; as, precious recollections.
q: She is more precious than rules.
Many things which are most precious are neglected only because the value of them lieth hid.

senses.d: Particular; fastidious; overnice.
q: Lest that precious folk be with me wroth.

Precious.etym: [OF. precious, precius, precios, F. précieux, L. pretiosus, fr. pretium price, worth, value. See Price.]

senses.d: Particular; fastidious; overnice; overrefined. Cf. Précieuse, Preciosity.
q: Lest that precious folk be with me wroth.
Elaborate embroidery of precious language.

senses.d: Predestinated; foreordained; fated.

Predestinate.etym: [L. praedestinatus, p. p. of praedestinare to predestine; prae before + destinare to determine. See Destine.]

senses.d: To predetermine or foreordain; to appoint or ordain beforehand by an unchangeable purpose or decree; to preëlect.
q: Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son.

Predestinate.syn: To predetermine; foreordain; preordain; decree; predestine; foredoom.

senses.d: To carry or bring (something) forward, or before one; hence, to bring for consideration, acceptance, judgment, etc.; to offer; to present; to proffer; to address; — said especially of a request, prayer, petition, claim, charge, etc.
q: He spake, and to her hand preferred the bowl.
Presently prefer his suit to Cæsar.
Three tongues prefer strange orisons on high.

senses.d: To go before, or be before, in estimation; to outrank; to surpass.
To cause to go before; hence, to advance before others, as to an office or dignity; to raise; to exalt; to promote; as, to prefer an officer to the rank of general.
q: I would prefer him to a better place.

senses.d: To set above or before something else in estimation, favor, or liking; to regard or honor before another; to hold in greater favor; to choose rather; — often followed by to, before, or above.
q: If I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy.
Preferred an infamous peace before a most just war.

Prefer.etym: [F. préférer, L. praeferre; prae before + ferre to bear or carry. See 1st Bear.]

senses.d: To think on, and revolve in the mind, beforehand; to contrive and design previously; as, to premeditate robbery.
q: With words premeditated thus he said.

Premeditate.etym: [L. praemeditatus, p. p. of praemeditari; prae before + meditari to meditate. See Meditate.]

senses.d: To think, consider, deliberate, or revolve in the mind, beforehand.
Premeditated; deliberate.

The act of preparing or fitting beforehand for a particular purpose, use, service, or condition; previous arrangement or adaptation; a making ready; as, the preparation of land for a crop of wheat; the preparation of troops for a campaign.
The state of being prepared or made ready; preparedness; readiness; fitness; as, a nation in good preparation for war.
That which makes ready, prepares the way, or introduces; a preparatory act or measure.
q: I will show what preparations there were in nature for this dissolution.

senses.d: That which is prepared, made, or compounded by a certain process or for a particular purpose; a combination. Specifically: (a) Any medicinal substance fitted for use. (b) Anything treated for preservation or examination as a specimen. (c) Something prepared for use in cookery.
q: I wish the chemists had been more sparing who magnify their preparations.
In the preparations of cookery, the most volatile parts of vegetables are destroyed.

senses.d: An army or fleet.

The holding over of a note from one chord into the next chord, where it forms a temporary discord, until resolved in the chord that follows; the anticipation of a discordant note in the preceding concord, so that the ear is prepared for the shock. See Suspension.
Accomplishment; qualification.
To fit, adapt, or qualify for a particular purpose or condition; to make ready; to put into a state for use or application; as, to prepare ground for seed; to prepare a lesson.
q: Our souls, not yet prepared for upper light.

senses.d: To procure as suitable or necessary; to get ready; to provide; as, to prepare ammunition and provisions for troops; to prepare ships for defence; to prepare an entertainment.
q: That they may prepare a city for habitation.

Prepare.syn: To fit; adjust; adapt; qualify; equip; provide; form; make; make; ready.
Prepare.etym: [F. préparer, L. praeparare; prae before + parare to make ready. See Pare.]

senses.d: To make all things ready; to put things in order; as, to prepare for a hostile invasion.
To make one's self ready; to get ready; to take the necessary previous measures; as, to prepare for death.
Preparation.
Made fit or suitable; adapted; ready; as, prepared food; prepared questions.
A body of elders in the early Christian church.

A judicatory consisting of all the ministers within a certain district, and one layman, who is a ruling elder, from each parish or church, commissioned to represent the church in conjunction with the pastor. This body has a general jurisdiction over the churches under its care, and next below the provincial synod in authority.
The Presbyterian religion of polity.
That part of the church reserved for the officiating priest.

Presbytery.etym: [L. presbyterium, Gr. �. See Presbyter, and cf. Presbyterium.]

senses.d: To lay down authoritatively as a guide, direction, or rule of action; to impose as a peremptory order; to dictate; to appoint; to direct.
q: Prescribe not us our duties.
Let streams prescribe their fountains where to run.

senses.d: To direct, as a remedy to be used by a patient; as, the doctor prescribed quinine.

Prescribe.syn: To appoint; order; command; dictate; ordain; institute; establish.
Prescribe.etym: [L. praescribere, praescriptum; prae before + scriebe to write. See Scribe.]

senses.d: To give directions; to dictate.
q: A forwardness to prescribe to their opinions.

senses.d: To influence by long use
To write or to give medical directions; to indicate remedies; as, to prescribe for a patient in a fever.
To claim by prescription; to claim a title to a thing on the ground of immemorial use and enjoyment, that is, by a custom having the force of law.
The state of being present, or of being within sight or call, or at hand; — opposed to absence.
The place in which one is present; the part of space within one's ken, call, influence, etc.; neighborhood without the intervention of anything that forbids intercourse.
q: Wrath shell be no more Thenceforth, but in thy presence joy entire.

senses.d: Specifically, neighborhood to the person of one of superior of exalted rank; also, presence chamber.
q: In such a presence here to plead my thoughts.
An't please your grace, the two great cardinals. Wait in the presence.

senses.d: The whole of the personal qualities of an individual; person; personality; especially, the person of a superior, as a sovereign.
q: The Sovran Presence thus replied.

senses.d: An assembly, especially of person of rank or nobility; noble company.
q: Odmar, of all this presence does contain, Give her your wreath whom you esteem most fair.

senses.d: Port, mien; air; personal appearence.
q: A graceful presence bespeaks acceptance.

senses.d: Being at hand, within reach or call, within certain contemplated limits; — opposed to absent.
q: These things have I spoken unto you, being yet present with you.

senses.d: Now existing, or in process; begun but not ended; now in view, or under consideration; being at this time; not past or future; as, the present session of Congress; the present state of affairs; the present instance.
q: I'll bring thee to the present business

senses.d: Not delayed; immediate; instant; coincident.
q: An ambassador . . . desires a present audience.

senses.d: Ready; quick in emergency; as a present wit.
Favorably attentive; propitious.
q: To find a god so present to my prayer.

Present.etym: [F. présent, L. praesens,-entis, that is before one, in sight or at hand, p. p. of praeesse to be before; prae before + esse to be. See Essence.]

senses.d: Present time; the time being; time in progress now, or at the moment contemplated; as, at this present.
q: Past and present, wound in one.

senses.d: Present letters or instrument, as a deed of conveyance, a lease, letter of attorney, or other writing; as in the phrase, “ Know all men by these presents,” that is, by the writing itself, “ per has literas praesentes; ” — in this sense, rarely used in the singular.
A present tense, or the form of the verb denoting the present tense.

To bring or introduce into the presence of some one, especially of a superior; to introduce formally; to offer for acquaintance; as, to present an envoy to the king; (with the reciprocal pronoun) to come into the presence of a superior.
q: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the lord.

senses.d: To exhibit or offer to view or notice; to lay before one's perception or cognizance; to set forth; to present a fine appearance.
q: Lectorides's memory is ever . . . presenting him with the thoughts of other persons.

senses.d: To pass over, esp. in a ceremonious manner; to give in charge or possession; to deliver; to make over.
q: So ladies in romance assist their knight, Present the spear, and arm him for the fight.

senses.d: To make a gift of; to bestow; to give, generally in a formal or ceremonious manner; to grant; to confer.
q: My last, least offering, I present thee now.

senses.d: Hence: To endow; to bestow a gift upon; to favor, as with a donation; also, to court by gifts.
q: Octavia presented the poet for him admirable elegy on her son Marcellus.

senses.d: To present; to personate.
To nominate to an ecclesiastical benefice; to offer to the bishop or ordinary as a candidate for institution.
q: The patron of a church may present his clerk to a parsonage or vicarage; that is, may offer him to the bishop of the diocese to be instituted.

senses.d: To nominate for support at a public school or other institution .
To lay before a public body, or an official, for consideration, as before a legislature, a court of judicature, a corporation, etc.; as, to present a memorial, petition, remonstrance, or indictment.

To lay before a court as an object of inquiry; to give notice officially of, as a crime of offence; to find or represent judicially; as, a grand jury present certain offenses or nuisances, or whatever they think to be public injuries.
To bring an indictment against .
To aim, point, or direct, as a weapon; as, to present a pistol or the point of a sword to the breast of another.

Present.etym: [F. présenter, L. praesentare, fr. praesens, a. See Present, a.]

senses.d: To appear at the mouth of the uterus so as to be perceptible to the finger in vaginal examination; — said of a part of an infant during labor.
Anything presented or given; a gift; a donative; as, a Christmas present.

Present.syn: Gift; donation; donative; benefaction. See Gift.

senses.d: The position of a soldier in presenting arms; as, to stand at present.
At present; at this time; now.
q: The towns and forts you presently have.

senses.d: At once; without delay; forthwith; also, less definitely, soon; shortly; before long; after a little while; by and by.
q: And presently the fig tree withered away.

senses.d: With actual presence; actually .
q: His precious body and blood presently three.

senses.d: To keep or save from injury or destruction; to guard or defend from evil, harm, danger, etc.; to protect.
q: O Lord, thou preserved man and beast.
Now, good angels preserve the king.

senses.d: To save from decay by the use of some preservative substance, as sugar, salt, etc.; to season and prepare for remaining in a good state, as fruits, meat, etc.; as, to preserve peaches or grapes.
q: You can not preserve it from tainting.

senses.d: To maintain throughout; to keep intact; as, to preserve appearances; to preserve silence.

Preserve.syn: To keep; save; secure; uphold; sustain; defend; spare; protect; guard; shield. See Keep.
Preserve.etym: [F. préserver, from L. prae before + servare to save, preserve; cf. L. praeservare to observe beforehand. See Serve.]

senses.d: To make preserves.
To protect game for purposes of sport.
That which is preserved; fruit, etc., seasoned and kept by suitable preparation; esp., fruit cooked with sugar; — commonly in the plural.
A place in which game, fish, etc., are preserved for purposes of sport, or for food.
One who, or that which, preserves, saves, or defends, from destruction, injury, or decay; esp., one who saves the life or character of another.
One who makes preserves of fruit.
Precedent.
Occupying the first rank or chief place; having the highest authority; presiding.
q: His angels president In every province.

senses.d: One who is elected or appointed to preside; a presiding officer, as of a legislative body.
A protector; a guardian; a presiding genius.
q: Just Apollo, president of verse.

President.etym: [F. président, L. praesidens, -entis, p. pr. of praesidere. See Preside.]

senses.d: An East Indian insectivore (Tupaia ferruginea). It is arboreal in its habits, and has a bushy tail. The fur is soft, and varies from rusty red to maroon and to brownish black.
To force into service, particularly into naval service; to impress.
q: To peaceful peasant to the wars is pressed.

Press.etym: [Corrupt. fr. prest ready money advanced, a loan; hence, earnest money given soldiers on entering service. See Prest, n.]

senses.d: A commission to force men into public service, particularly into the navy.
q: I have misused the king's press.

senses.d: To urge, or act upon, with force, as weight; to act upon by pushing or thrusting, in distinction from pulling; to crowd or compel by a gradual and continued exertion; to bear upon; to squeeze; to compress; as, we press the ground with the feet when we walk; we press the couch on which we repose; we press substances with the hands, fingers, or arms; we are pressed in a crowd.
q: Good measure, pressed down, and shaken together.

senses.d: To squeeze, in order to extract the juice or contents of; to squeeze out, or express, from something.
q: From sweet kernels pressed, She tempers dulcet creams.
And I took the grapes, and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and I gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand.

senses.d: To squeeze in or with suitable instruments or apparatus, in order to compact, make dense, or smooth; as, to press cotton bales, paper, etc.; to smooth by ironing; as, to press clothes.
To embrace closely; to hug.
q: Leucothoe shook at these alarms, And pressed Palemon closer in her arms.

senses.d: To oppress; to bear hard upon.
q: Press not a falling man too far.

senses.d: To straiten; to distress; as, to be pressed with want or hunger.
To exercise very powerful or irresistible influence upon or over; to constrain; to force; to compel.
q: Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ.

senses.d: To try to force (something upon some one); to urge or inculcate with earnestness or importunity; to enforce; as, to press divine truth on an audience.
q: He pressed a letter upon me within this hour.
Be sure to press upon him every motive.

senses.d: To drive with violence; to hurry; to urge on; to ply hard; as, to press a horse in a race.
q: The posts . . . went cut, being hastened and pressed on, by the king's commandment.

Press.etym: [F. presser, fr. L. pressare to press, fr. premere, pressum, to press. Cf. Print, v.]

senses.d: To exert pressure; to bear heavily; to push, crowd, or urge with steady force.
To move on with urging and crowding; to make one's way with violence or effort; to bear onward forcibly; to crowd; to throng; to encroach.
q: They pressed upon him for to touch him.

senses.d: To urge with vehemence or importunity; to exert a strong or compelling influence; as, an argument presses upon the judgment.

An apparatus or machine by which any substance or body is pressed, squeezed, stamped, or shaped, or by which an impression of a body is taken; sometimes, the place or building containing a press or presses.
Specifically, a printing press.

The art or business of printing and publishing; hence, printed publications, taken collectively, more especially newspapers or the persons employed in writing for them; as, a free press is a blessing, a licentious press is a curse.
An upright case or closet for the safe keeping of articles; as, a clothes press.
The act of pressing or thronging forward.
q: In their throng and press to that last hold.

senses.d: Urgent demands of business or affairs; urgency; as, a press of engagements.
A multitude of individuals crowded together; � crowd of single things; a throng.
q: They could not come nigh unto him for the press.

senses.d: To assume or take beforehand; esp., to do or undertake without leave or authority previously obtained.
q: Dare he presume to scorn us in this manner?
Bold deed thou hast presumed, adventurous Eve.

senses.d: To take or suppose to be true, or entitled to belief, without examination or proof, or on the strength of probability; to take for granted; to infer; to suppose.
q: Every man is to be presumed innocent till he is proved to be guilty.
What rests but that the mortal sentence pass, . . . Which he presumes already vain and void, Because not yet inflicted?

Presume.etym: [F. présumer, L. praesumere, praesumptum; prae before + sumere to take. See Assume, Redeem.]

senses.d: To suppose or assume something to be, or to be true, on grounds deemed valid, though not amounting to proof; to believe by anticipation; to infer; as, we may presume too far.

To venture, go, or act, by an assumption of leave or authority not granted; to go beyond what is warranted by the circumstances of the case; to venture beyond license; to take liberties; — often with on or upon before the ground of confidence.
q: Do not presume too much upon my love.
This man presumes upon his parts.

senses.d: Full of presumption; presuming; overconfident or venturesome; audacious; rash; taking liberties unduly; arrogant; insolent; as, a presumptuous commander; presumptuous conduct.
q: A class of presumptuous men, whom age has not made cautious, nor adversity wise.

senses.d: Founded on presumption; as, a presumptuous idea.
Done with hold design, rash confidence, or in violation of known duty; willful.

Presumptuous.syn: Overconfident; foolhardy; rash; presuming; forward; arrogant; insolent.
Presumptuous.etym: [L. praesumptuosus: cf. F. présomptueux, OF. also presumptuous. See Presumption.]

senses.d: In a presumptuous manner; arrogantly.
The general's tent in a Roman camp; hence, a council of war, because held in the general's tent.
The official residence of a governor of a province; hence, a place; a splendid country seat.
To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to gain the advantage; to have the upper hand, or the mastery; to succeed; — sometimes with over or against.
q: When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.
So David prevailed over the Philistine.
This kingdom could never prevail against the united power of England.

senses.d: To be in force; to have effect, power, or influence; to be predominant; to have currency or prevalence; to obtain; as, the practice prevails this day.
q: This custom makes the short-sighted bigots, and the warier skeptics, as far as it prevails.

senses.d: To persuade or induce; — with on, upon, or with; as, I prevailedon him to wait.
q: He was prevailed with to restrain the Earl.
Prevail upon some judicious friend to be your constant hearer, and allow him the utmost freedom.

Prevail.etym: [F. prévaloir, OF. prevaleir, L. praevalere; prae before + valere to be strong, able, or worth. See Valiant.]

senses.d: To go before; to precede; hence, to go before as a guide; to direct.
q: We which are alive and remain unto the coming of the Lord shall not prevent them which are asleep.
We pray thee that thy grace may always prevent and follow us.
Then had I come, preventing Sheba's queen.

senses.d: To be beforehand with; to anticipate.
q: Their ready guilt preventing thy commands.

senses.d: To intercept; to hinder; to frustrate; to stop; to thwart.
q: Perhaps forestalling night prevented them.

Prevent.etym: [L. praevenire, praeventum; prae before + venire to come. See Come.]

senses.d: To come before the usual time.
q: Strawberries . . . will prevent and come early.

senses.d: Anything, as goods, etc., taken or got by violence; anything taken by force from an enemy in war; spoil; booty; plunder.
q: And they brought the captives, and the prey, and the spoil, unto Moses, and Eleazar the priest.

senses.d: That which is or may be seized by animals or birds to be devoured; hence, a person given up as a victim.
q: The old lion perisheth for lack of prey.
Already sees herself the monster's prey.

senses.d: The act of devouring other creatures; ravage.
q: Hog in sloth, fox in stealth, . . . lion in prey.

Prey.etym: [OF. preie, F. proie, L. praeda, probably for praeheda. See Prehensile, and cf. Depredate, Predatory.]

senses.d: To take booty; to gather spoil; to ravage; to take food by violence.
q: More pity that the eagle should be mewed, While kites and buzzards prey at liberty.

Prey.etym: [OF. preier, preer, L. praedari, fr. praeda. See Prey, n.]

senses.d: The sum or amount of money at which a thing is valued, or the value which a seller sets on his goods in market; that for which something is bought or sold, or offered for sale; equivalent in money or other means of exchange; current value or rate paid or demanded in market or in barter; cost.
q: We can afford no more at such a price.

senses.d: Value; estimation; excellence; worth.
q: Her price is far above rubies.
New treasures still, of countless price.

senses.d: Reward; recompense; as, the price of industry.
q: 'T is the price of toil, The knave deserves it when he tills the soil.

Price.etym: [OE. pris, OF. pris, F. prix, L. pretium; cf. Gr. � I sell � to buy, Skr. pa� to buy, OI. renim I sell. Cf. Appreciate, Depreciate, Interpret, Praise, n. & v., Precious, Prize.]

senses.d: To pay the price of.
q: With thine own blood to price his blood.

senses.d: To set a price on; to value. See Prize.
To ask the price of; as, to price eggs.
