That which pricks, penetrates, or punctures; a sharp and slender thing; a pointed instrument; a goad; a spur, etc.; a point; a skewer.
q: Pins, wooden pricks, nails, sprigs of rosemary.
It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.

senses.d: The act of pricking, or the sensation of being pricked; a sharp, stinging pain; figuratively, remorse.
A mark made by a pointed instrument; a puncture; a point.
A small roll; as, a prick of spun yarn; a prick of tobacco.

Prick.etym: [AS. prica, pricca, pricu; akin to LG. prick, pricke, D. prik, Dan. prik, prikke, Sw. prick. Cf. Prick, v.]

senses.d: To pierce slightly with a sharp-pointed instrument or substance; to make a puncture in, or to make by puncturing; to drive a fine point into; as, to prick one with a pin, needle, etc.; to prick a card; to prick holes in paper.
To fix by the point; to attach or hang by puncturing; as, to prick a knife into a board.
q: The cooks prick it on a prong of iron.

senses.d: To mark or denote by a puncture; to designate by pricking; to choose; to mark; — sometimes with off.
q: Some who are pricked for sheriffs.
Let the soldiers for duty be carefully pricked off.
Those many, then, shall die: their names are pricked.

senses.d: To mark the outline of by puncturing; to trace or form by pricking; to mark by punctured dots; as, to prick a pattern for embroidery; to prick the notes of a musical composition.
To ride or guide with spurs; to spur; to goad; to incite; to urge on; — sometimes with on, or off.
q: Who pricketh his blind horse over the fallows.
The season pricketh every gentle heart.
My duty pricks me on to utter that.

senses.d: To affect with sharp pain; to sting, as with remorse.
q: Now when they heard this, they were pricked in their heart.

senses.d: To make sharp; to erect into a point; to raise, as something pointed; — said especially of the ears of an animal, as a horse or dog; and usually followed by up; — hence, to prick up the ears, to listen sharply; to have the attention and interest strongly engaged.
To render acid or pungent.
To dress; to prink; — usually with up.
To run a middle seam through, as the cloth of a sail.
To drive a nail into (a horse's foot), so as to cause lameness.

Prick.etym: [AS. prician; akin to LG. pricken, D. prikken, Dan. prikke, Sw. pricka. See Prick, n., and cf. Prink, Prig.]

senses.d: To be punctured; to suffer or feel a sharp pain, as by puncture; as, a sore finger pricks.
To spur onward; to ride on horseback.
q: A gentle knight was pricking on the plain.

senses.d: To become sharp or acid; to turn sour, as wine.
To aim at a point or mark.
The act of piercing or puncturing with a sharp point.
The driving of a nail into a horse's foot so as to produce lameness.
A sensation of being pricked.
The mark or trace left by a hare's foot; a prick; also, the act of tracing a hare by its footmarks.
Dressing one's self for show; prinking.
A small European lamprey (Petromyzon branchialis); — called also prid, and sandpiper.

Pride.etym: [Cf. AS. lamprede, LL. lampreda, E. lamprey.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being proud; inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority in talents, beauty, wealth, rank, etc., which manifests itself in lofty airs, distance, reserve, and often in contempt of others.
q: Those that walk in pride he is able to abase.
Pride that dines on vanity sups on contempt.

senses.d: A sense of one's own worth, and abhorrence of what is beneath or unworthy of one; lofty self-respect; noble self-esteem; elevation of character; dignified bearing; proud delight; — in a good sense.
q: Thus to relieve the wretched was his pride.
A people which takes no pride in the noble achievements of remote ancestors will never achieve anything worthy to be remembered with pride by remote descendants.

senses.d: Proud or disdainful behavior or treatment; insolence or arrogance of demeanor; haughty bearing and conduct; insolent exultation; disdain.
q: Let not the foot of pride come against me.
That hardly we escaped the pride of France.

senses.d: That of which one is proud; that which excites boasting or self-gratulation; the occasion or ground of self-esteem, or of arrogant and presumptuous confidence, as beauty, ornament, noble character, children, etc.
q: Lofty trees yclad with summer's pride.
I will cut off the pride of the Philistines.
A bold peasantry, their country's pride.

senses.d: Show; ostentation; glory.
q: Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war.

senses.d: Highest pitch; elevation reached; loftiness; prime; glory; as, to be in the pride of one's life.
q: A falcon, towering in her pride of place.

senses.d: Consciousness of power; fullness of animal spirits; mettle; wantonness; hence, lust; sexual desire; esp., an excitement of sexual appetite in a female beast.

Pride.syn: Self-exaltation; conceit; hauteur; haughtiness; lordliness; loftiness.
Pride.etym: [AS. prȳte; akin to Icel. prȳði honor, ornament, pr��a to adorn, Dan. pryde, Sw. pryda; cf. W. prydus comely. See Proud.]

senses.d: To indulge in pride, or self-esteem; to rate highly; to plume; — used reflexively.
q: Pluming and priding himself in all his services.

senses.d: To be proud; to glory.
The plant privet.
To pry.
A presbyter elder; a minister
One who officiates at the altar, or performs the rites of sacrifice; one who acts as a mediator between men and the divinity or the gods in any form of religion; as, Buddhist priests.
q: Then the priest of Jupiter . . . brought oxen and garlands . . . and would have done sacrifice with the people.
Every priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.

Priest.etym: [OE. prest, preost, AS. preóst, fr. L. presbyter, Gr. � elder, older, n., an elder, compar. of � an old man, the first syllable of which is probably akin to L. pristinus. Cf. Pristine, Presbyter.]

senses.d: To ordain as priest.
The office or character of a priest; the priestly function.
Priests, taken collectively; the order of men set apart for sacred offices; the order of priests.
The one of highest rank; one holding the highest place and authority; a sovereign; a monarch; — originally applied to either sex, but now rarely applied to a female.
q: Go, Michael, of celestial armies prince.
Queen Elizabeth, a prince admirable above her sex.

senses.d: The son of a king or emperor, or the issue of a royal family; as, princes of the blood.

A title belonging to persons of high rank, differing in different countries. In England it belongs to dukes, marquises, and earls, but is given to members of the royal family only. In Italy a prince is inferior to a duke as a member of a particular order of nobility; in Spain he is always one of the royal family.
The chief of any body of men; one at the head of a class or profession; one who is preëminent; as, a merchant prince; a prince of players.

Prince.etym: [F., from L. princeps, -cipis, the first, chief; primus first + capere to take. See Prime, a., and Capacious.]

senses.d: To play the prince.
A female prince; a woman having sovereign power, or the rank of a prince.
q: So excellent a princess as the present queen.

senses.d: The daughter of a sovereign; a female member of a royal family.
The consort of a prince; as, the princess of Wales.

Princess.etym: [F. princesse. See Prince, and cf. Princesse.]

senses.d: A term applied to a lady's long, close-fitting dress made with waist and skirt in one.

Highest in rank, authority, character, importance, or degree; most considerable or important; chief; main; as, the principal officers of a Government; the principal men of a state; the principal productions of a country; the principal arguments in a case.
q: Wisdom is the principal thing.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a prince; princely.

A leader, chief, or head; one who takes the lead; one who acts independently, or who has controlling authority or influence; as, the principal of a faction, a school, a firm, etc.; — distinguished from a subordinate, abettor, auxiliary, or assistant.
The chief actor in a crime, or an abettor who is present at it, — as distinguished from an accessory.
A thing of chief or prime importance; something fundamental or especially conspicuous.
Sovereignty; supreme power; hence, superiority; predominance; high, or the highest, station.
q: Your principalities shall come down, even the crown of your glory.
The prerogative and principality above everything else.

senses.d: A prince; one invested with sovereignty.
The territory or jurisdiction of a prince; or the country which gives title to a prince; as, the principality of Wales.

Principality.etym: [L. principalitas preëminence, excellence: cf. F. principalité, principauté. See Principal.]

senses.d: Beginning; commencement.
q: Doubting sad end of principle unsound.

senses.d: A source, or origin; that from which anything proceeds; fundamental substance or energy; primordial substance; ultimate element, or cause.
q: The soul of man is an active principle.

senses.d: An original faculty or endowment.
q: Nature in your principles hath set .
Those active principles whose direct and ultimate object is the communication either of enjoyment or suffering.

senses.d: A fundamental truth; a comprehensive law or doctrine, from which others are derived, or on which others are founded; a general truth; an elementary proposition; a maxim; an axiom; a postulate.
q: Therefore, leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection.
A good principle, not rightly understood, may prove as hurtful as a bad.

senses.d: A settled rule of action; a governing law of conduct; an opinion or belief which exercises a directing influence on the life and behavior; a rule (usually, a right rule) of conduct consistently directing one's actions; as, a person of no principle.
q: All kinds of dishonesty destroy our pretenses to an honest principle of mind.

senses.d: Any original inherent constituent which characterizes a substance, or gives it its essential properties, and which can usually be separated by analysis; — applied especially to drugs, plant extracts, etc.
q: Cathartine is the bitter, purgative principle of senna.

Principle.etym: [F. principe, L. principium beginning, foundation, fr. princeps, -cipis. See Prince.]

senses.d: To equip with principles; to establish, or fix, in certain principles; to impress with any tenet, or rule of conduct, good or ill.
q: Governors should be well principled.
Let an enthusiast be principled that he or his teacher is inspired.

senses.d: To fix or impress, as a stamp, mark, character, idea, etc., into or upon something.
q: A look will print a thought that never may remove.
Upon his breastplate he beholds a dint, Which in that field young Edward's sword did print.
Perhaps some footsteps printed in the clay.

senses.d: To stamp something in or upon; to make an impression or mark upon by pressure, or as by pressure.
q: Forth on his fiery steed betimes he rode, That scarcely prints the turf on which he trod.

senses.d: To strike off an impression or impressions of, from type, or from stereotype, electrotype, or engraved plates, or the like; in a wider sense, to do the typesetting, presswork, etc., of (a book or other publication); as, to print books, newspapers, pictures; to print an edition of a book.
To stamp or impress with colored figures or patterns; as, to print calico.
To take (a copy, a positive picture, etc.), from a negative, a transparent drawing, or the like, by the action of light upon a sensitized surface.

Print.etym: [Abbrev. fr. imprint. See Imprint, and Press to squeeze.]

senses.d: To use or practice the art of typography; to take impressions of letters, figures, or electrotypes, engraved plates, or the like.
To publish a book or an article.
q: From the moment he prints, he must except to hear no more truth.

senses.d: A mark made by impression; a line, character, figure, or indentation, made by the pressure of one thing on another; as, the print of teeth or nails in flesh; the print of the foot in sand or snow.
q: Where print of human feet was never seen.

senses.d: A stamp or die for molding or impressing an ornamental design upon an object; as, a butter print.
That which receives an impression, as from a stamp or mold; as, a print of butter.
Printed letters; the impression taken from type, as to excellence, form, size, etc.; as, small print; large print; this line is in print.
That which is produced by printing.
A core print. See under Core.
An enterprise.
A place where persons are confined, or restrained of personal liberty; hence, a place or state o� confinement, restraint, or safe custody.
q: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name.
The tyrant Æolus, . . . With power imperial, curbs the struggling winds, And sounding tempests in dark prisons binds.

senses.d: Specifically, a building for the safe custody or confinement of criminals and others committed by lawful authority.

Prison.etym: [F., fr. L. prehensio, prensio, a seizing, arresting, fr. prehendre, prendere, to lay hold of, to seize. See Prehensile, and cf. Prize, n., Misprision.]

senses.d: To imprison; to shut up in, or as in, a prison; to confine; to restrain from liberty.
q: The prisoned eagle dies for rage.
His true respect will prison false desire.

senses.d: To bind (together); to enchain.
q: Sir William Crispyn with the duke was led Together prisoned.

senses.d: One who is confined in a prison.
A person under arrest, or in custody, whether in prison or not; a person held in involuntary restraint; a captive; as, a prisoner at the bar of a court.
q: Prisoner of Hope thou art, — look up and sing.

senses.d: Belonging to, or concerning, an individual person, company, or interest; peculiar to one's self; unconnected with others; personal; one's own; not public; not general; separate; as, a man's private opinion; private property; a private purse; private expenses or interests; a private secretary.
Sequestered from company or observation; appropriated to an individual; secret; secluded; lonely; solitary; as, a private room or apartment; private prayer.
q: Reason . . . then retires Into her private cell when nature rests.

senses.d: Not invested with, or engaged in, public office or employment; as, a private citizen; private life.
q: A private person may arrest a felon.

senses.d: Not publicly known; not open; secret; as, a private negotiation; a private understanding.
Having secret or private knowledge; privy.

Private.etym: [L. privatus apart from the state, peculiar to an individual, private, properly p. p. of privare to bereave, deprive, originally, to separate, fr. privus single, private, perhaps originally, put forward (hence, alone, single) and akin to prae before. See Prior, a., and cf. Deprive, Privy, a.]

senses.d: A secret message; a personal unofficial communication.
Personal interest; particular business.
q: Nor must I be unmindful of my private.

senses.d: Privacy; retirement.
One not invested with a public office.
q: What have kings, that privates have not too?

senses.d: A common soldier; a soldier below the grade of a noncommissioned officer.
The private parts; the genitals.
In a private manner; not openly; without the presence of others.
In a manner affecting an individual; personally; not officially; as, he is not privately benefited.
In a privy manner; privately; secretly.
Of or pertaining to some person exclusively; assigned to private uses; not public; private; as, the privy purse.
Secret; clandestine.
Appropriated to retirement; private; not open to the public.
Admitted to knowledge of a secret transaction; secretly cognizant; privately knowing.
q: His wife also being privy to it.
Myself am one made privy to the plot.

Privy.etym: [F. privé, fr. L. privatus. See Private.]

senses.d: A partaker; a person having an interest in any action or thing; one who has an interest in an estate created by another; a person having an interest derived from a contract or conveyance to which he is not himself a party. The term, in its proper sense, is distinguished from party.
A necessary house or place; a backhouse.
That which is taken from another; something captured; a thing seized by force, stratagem, or superior power.
q: I will depart my pris, or my prey, by deliberation.
His own prize, Whom formerly he had in battle won.

senses.d: Anything captured by a belligerent using the rights of war; esp., property captured at sea in virtue of the rights of war, as a vessel.
q: I'll never wrestle for prize more.
I fought and conquered, yet have lost the prize.

senses.d: That which may be won by chance, as in a lottery.
Anything worth striving for; a valuable possession held or in prospect.
q: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

senses.d: A contest for a reward; competition.
A lever; a pry; also, the hold of a lever.

Prize.etym: [F. prise a seizing, hold, grasp, fr. pris, p. p. of prendre to take, L. prendere, prehendere; in some senses, as 2 (b), either from, or influenced by, F. prix price. See Prison, Prehensile, and cf. Pry, and also Price.]

senses.d: To move with a lever; to force up or open; to pry.
To set or estimate the value of; to appraise; to price; to rate.
q: A goodly price that I was prized at.
I prize it not a straw, but for mine honor.

senses.d: To value highly; to estimate to be of great worth; to esteem.
q: I prized your person, but your crown disdain.

Prize.etym: [F. priser, OF. prisier, preisier, fr. L. pretiare, fr. pretium worth, value, price. See Price, and cf. Praise.]

senses.d: Estimation; valuation.
To move, pass, or go forward or onward; to advance; to continue or renew motion begun; as, to proceed on a journey.
q: If thou proceed in this thy insolence.

senses.d: To pass from one point, topic, or stage, to another; as, to proceed with a story or argument.
To issue or come forth as from a source or origin; to come from; as, light proceeds from the sun.
q: I proceeded forth and came from God.
It proceeds from policy, not love.

senses.d: To go on in an orderly or regulated manner; to begin and carry on a series of acts or measures; to act by method; to prosecute a design.
q: He that proceeds upon other principles in his inquiry.

senses.d: To be transacted; to take place; to occur.
q: He will, after his sour fashion, tell you What hath proceeded worthy note to-day.

senses.d: To have application or effect; to operate.
q: This rule only proceeds and takes place when a person can not of common law condemn another by his sentence.

senses.d: To begin and carry on a legal process.

Proceed.syn: To advance; go on; continue; progress; issue; arise; emanate.
Proceed.etym: [F. procéder. fr. L. procedere, processum, to go before, to proceed; pro forward + cedere to move. See Cede.]

senses.d: The act of one who proceeds, or who prosecutes a design or transaction; progress or movement from one thing to another; a measure or step taken in a course of business; a transaction; as, an illegal proceeding; a cautious or a violent proceeding.
q: The proceedings of the high commission.

senses.d: The course of procedure in the prosecution of an action at law.
The act of proceeding; continued forward movement; procedure; progress; advance.
q: The thoughts of men are widened with the process of the suns.

senses.d: A series of actions, motions, or occurrences; progressive act or transaction; continuous operation; normal or actual course or procedure; regular proceeding; as, the process of vegetation or decomposition; a chemical process; processes of nature.
q: Tell her the process of Antonio's end.

senses.d: A statement of events; a narrative.
Any marked prominence or projecting part, especially of a bone; anapophysis.

The whole course of proceedings in a cause real or personal, civil or criminal, from the beginning to the end of the suit; strictly, the means used for bringing the defendant into court to answer to the action; — a generic term for writs of the class called judicial.
To make known by public announcement; to give wide publicity to; to publish abroad; to promulgate; to declare; as, to proclaim war or peace.
q: To proclaim liberty to the captives.
For the apparel oft proclaims the man.
Throughout the host proclaim A solemn council forthwith to be held.

senses.d: To outlaw by public proclamation.
q: I heard myself proclaimed.

Proclaim.syn: To publish; promulgate; declare; announce. See Announce.
Proclaim.etym: [OE. proclamen, L. proclamare; pro before, forward + clamare to call or cry out: cf. F. proclamer. See Claim.]

senses.d: The act of proclaiming; official or general notice; publication.
q: King Asa made a proclamation throughout all Judah; none was exempted.

senses.d: That which is proclaimed, publicly announced, or officially declared; a published ordinance; as, the proclamation of a king; a Thanksgiving proclamation.
To bring into possession; to cause to accrue to, or to come into possession of; to acquire or provide for one's self or for another; to gain; to get; to obtain by any means, as by purchase or loan.
q: If we procure not to ourselves more woe.

senses.d: To contrive; to bring about; to effect; to cause.
q: By all means possible they procure to have gold and silver among them in reproach.
Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall.

senses.d: To solicit; to entreat.
q: The famous Briton prince and faery knight, . . . Of the fair Alma greatly were procured To make there longer sojourn and abode.

senses.d: To cause to come; to bring; to attract.
q: What unaccustomed cause procures her hither?

senses.d: To obtain for illicit intercourse or prostitution.

Procure.etym: [F. procurer, L. procurare, procuratum, to take care of; pro for + curare to take care, fr. cura care. See Cure, and cf. Proctor, Proxy.]

senses.d: To pimp.
To manage business for another in court.
To bring forward; to lead forth; to offer to view or notice; to exhibit; to show; as, to produce a witness or evidence in court.
q: Produce your cause, saith the Lord.
Your parents did not produce you much into the world.

senses.d: To bring forth, as young, or as a natural product or growth; to give birth to; to bear; to generate; to propagate; to yield; to furnish; as, the earth produces grass; trees produce fruit; the clouds produce rain.
q: This soil produces all sorts of palm trees.
produce prodigious births of body or mind.
The greatest jurist his country had produced.

senses.d: To cause to be or to happen; to originate, as an effect or result; to bring about; as, disease produces pain; vice produces misery.
To give being or form to; to manufacture; to make; as, a manufacturer produces excellent wares.
To yield or furnish; to gain; as, money at interest produces an income; capital produces profit.
To draw out; to extend; to lengthen; to prolong; as, to produce a man's life to threescore.
To extend; — applied to a line, surface, or solid; as, to produce a side of a triangle.

Produce.etym: [L. producere, productum, to bring forward, beget, produce; pro forward, forth + ducere to lead. See Duke.]

senses.d: To yield or furnish appropriate offspring, crops, effects, consequences, or results.
That which is produced, brought forth, or yielded; product; yield; proceeds; result of labor, especially of agricultural labors
agricultural products.
Not sacred or holy; not possessing peculiar sanctity; unconsecrated; hence, relating to matters other than sacred; secular; — opposed to sacred, religious, or inspired; as, a profane place.
q: The profane wreath was suspended before the shrine.

senses.d: Unclean; impure; polluted; unholy.
q: Nothing is profane that serveth to holy things.

senses.d: Treating sacred things with contempt, disrespect, irreverence, or undue familiarity; irreverent; impious.

Profane.syn: Secular; temporal; worldly; unsanctified; unhallowed; unholy; irreligious; irreverent; ungodly; wicked; godless; impious. See Impious.
Profane.etym: [F., fr. L. profanus, properly, before the temple, i.e., without the temple, unholy; pro before + fanum temple. See 1st Fane.]

senses.d: To violate, as anything sacred; to treat with abuse, irreverence, obloquy, or contempt; to desecrate; to pollute; as, to profane the name of God; to profane the Scriptures, or the ordinance of God.
q: The priests in the temple profane the sabbath.

senses.d: To put to a wrong or unworthy use; to make a base employment of; to debase; to abuse; to defile.
q: So idly to profane the precious time.

Profane.etym: [L. profanare: cf. F. profaner. See Profane, a.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being profane; especially, the use of profane language.
To make open declaration of, as of one's knowledge, belief, action, etc.; to avow or acknowledge; to confess publicly; to own or admit freely.
q: The best and wisest of them all professed To know this only, that he nothing knew.

senses.d: To set up a claim to; to make presence to; hence, to put on or present an appearance of.
q: I do profess to be no less than I seem.

senses.d: To present to knowledge of, to proclaim one's self versed in; to make one's self a teacher or practitioner of, to set up as an authority respecting; to declare (one's self to be such); as, he professes surgery; to profess one's self a physician.

Profess.etym: [F. profès, masc., professe, fem., professed (monk or nun), L. professus, p. p. of profiteri to profess; pro before, forward + fateri to confess, own. See Confess.]

senses.d: To take a profession upon one's self by a public declaration; to confess.
To declare friendship.
Openly declared, avowed, acknowledged, or claimed; as, a professed foe; a professed tyrant; a professed Christian.
The act of professing or claiming; open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment; as, professions of friendship; a profession of faith.
q: A solemn vow, promise, and profession.

senses.d: That which one professed; a declaration; an avowal; a claim; as, his professions are insincere.
q: The Indians quickly perceive the coincidence or the contradiction between professions and conduct.

senses.d: That of which one professed knowledge; the occupation, if not mechanical, agricultural, or the like, to which one devotes one's self; the business which one professes to understand, and to follow for subsistence; calling; vocation; employment; as, the profession of arms; the profession of a clergyman, lawyer, or physician; the profession of lecturer on chemistry.
q: Hi tried five or six professions in turn.

senses.d: The collective body of persons engaged in a calling; as, the profession distrust him.
The act of entering, or becoming a member of, a religious order.

Profession.etym: [F., fr. L. professio. See Profess, v.]

senses.d: Acquisition beyond expenditure; excess of value received for producing, keeping, or selling, over cost; hence, pecuniary gain in any transaction or occupation; emolument; as, a profit on the sale of goods.
q: Let no man anticipate uncertain profits.

senses.d: Accession of good; valuable results; useful consequences; benefit; avail; gain; as, an office of profit,
q: This I speak for your own profit.
If you dare do yourself a profit and a right.

Profit.syn: Benefit; avail; service; improvement; advancement; gain; emolument.
Profit.etym: [F., fr. L. profectus advance, progress, profit, fr. profectum. See Proficient.]

senses.d: To be of service to; to be good to; to help on; to benefit; to advantage; to avail; to aid; as, truth profits all men.
q: The word preached did not profit them.
It is a great means of profiting yourself, to copy diligently excellent pieces and beautiful designs.

senses.d: To gain advantage; to make improvement; to improve; to gain; to advance.
q: I profit not by thy talk.

senses.d: To be of use or advantage; to do or bring good.
q: Riches profit not in the day of wrath.

senses.d: Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; useful; helpful; advantageous; beneficial; as, a profitable trade; profitable business; a profitable study or profession.
q: What was so profitable to the empire became fatal to the emperor.

senses.d: Gain; advantage; profit.
q: That thy profiting may appear to all.

senses.d: Descending far below the surface; opening or reaching to a great depth; deep.

Intellectually deep; entering far into subjects; reaching to the bottom of a matter, or of a branch of learning; thorough; as, a profound investigation or treatise; a profound scholar; profound wisdom.
Characterized by intensity; deeply felt; pervading; overmastering; far-reaching; strongly impressed; as, a profound sleep.
q: Of the profound corruption of this class there can be no doubt.

senses.d: Bending low, exhibiting or expressing deep humility; lowly; submissive; as, a profound bow.
q: What humble gestures! What profound reverence!

Profound.etym: [F. profond, L. profundus; pro before, forward + fundus the bottom. See Found to establish, Bottom lowest part.]

senses.d: The deep; the sea; the ocean.
q: God in the fathomless profound Hath all this choice commanders drowned.

senses.d: An abyss.
To cause to sink deeply; to cause to dive or penetrate far down.
To dive deeply; to penetrate.
An ancestor in the direct line; a forefather.
q: And reverence thee their great progenitor.

Progenitor.etym: [OF. progeniteur, L. progenitor, fr. progignere, progenitum, to bring forth, to beget; pro forth + gignere to beget. See Gender kind.]

senses.d: One who prognosticates; a foreknower or foreteller of a future course or event by present signs.
To extend in space or length; as, to prolong a line.
To lengthen in time; to extend the duration of; to draw out; to continue; as, to prolong one's days.
q: Prolong awhile the traitor's life.
The unhappy queen with talk prolonged the night.

senses.d: To put off to a distant time; to postpone.

Prolong.etym: [F. prolonger, L. prolongare; pro before, forth + longus long. See Long, a., and cf. Prolongate, Purloin. ]

senses.d: A rope with a hook and a toggle, sometimes used to drag a gun carriage or to lash it to the limber, and for various other purposes.

In general, a declaration, written or verbal, made by one person to another, which binds the person who makes it to do, or to forbear to do, a specified act; a declaration which gives to the person to whom it is made a right to expect or to claim the performance or forbearance of a specified act.
q: For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise: but God gave it to Abraham by promise.

senses.d: An engagement by one person to another, either in words or in writing, but properly not under seal, for the performance or nonperformance of some particular thing. The word promise is used to denote the mere engagement of a person, without regard to the consideration for it, or the corresponding duty of the party to whom it is made.
That which causes hope, expectation, or assurance; especially, that which affords expectation of future distinction; as, a youth of great promise.
q: My native country was full of youthful promise.

senses.d: Bestowal, fulfillment, or grant of what is promised.
q: He . . . commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father.

Promise.etym: [F. promesse, L. promissum, fr. promittere, promissum, to put forth, foretell, promise; pro forward, for + mittere to send. See Mission. ]

senses.d: To engage to do, give, make, or to refrain from doing, giving, or making, or the like; to covenant; to engage; as, to promise a visit; to promise a cessation of hostilities; to promise the payment of money.
To afford reason to expect; to cause hope or assurance of; as, the clouds promise rain.
To make declaration of or give assurance of, as some benefit to be conferred; to pledge or engage to bestow; as, the proprietors promised large tracts of land; the city promised a reward.
q: I dare promise myself you will attest the truth of all I have advanced.

senses.d: To give assurance by a promise, or binding declaration.
To afford hopes or expectation; to give ground to expect good; rarely, to give reason to expect evil.
q: Will not the ladies be afeard of the lion? I fear it, I promise you.

senses.d: Making a promise or promises; affording hope or assurance; as, promising person; a promising day.

To contribute to the growth, enlargement, or prosperity of (any process or thing that is in course); to forward; to further; to encourage; to advance; to excite; as, to promote learning; to promote disorder; to promote a business venture.
To exalt in station, rank, or honor; to elevate; to raise; to prefer; to advance; as, to promote an officer.
q: I will promote thee unto very great honor.
Exalt her, and she shall promote thee.

Promote.syn: To forward; advance; further; patronize; help; exalt; prefer; elevate; dignify.
Promote.etym: [L. promotus, p. p. of promovere to move forward, to promote; pro forward + movere to move. See Move.]

senses.d: To urge on or incite another, as to strife; also, to inform against a person.
The act of promoting, advancing, or encouraging; the act of exalting in rank or honor; also, the condition of being advanced, encouraged, or exalted in honor; preferment.
q: Promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south.

senses.d: To utter articulately; to speak out or distinctly; to utter, as words or syllables; to speak with the proper sound and accent as, adults rarely learn to pronounce a foreign language correctly.
To utter officially or solemnly; to deliver, as a decree or sentence; as, to pronounce sentence of death.
q: Sternly he pronounced The rigid interdiction.

senses.d: To speak or utter rhetorically; to deliver; to recite; as, to pronounce an oration.
q: Speak the speech, I pray you, as I pronounced it to you.

senses.d: To declare or affirm; as, he pronounced the book to be a libel; he pronounced the act to be a fraud.
q: The God who hallowed thee and blessed, Pronouncing thee all good.

Pronounce.syn: To deliver; utter; speak. See Deliver.
Pronounce.etym: [F. prononcer, L. pronunciare; pro before, forth + nunciare, nuntiare, to announce. See Announce.]

senses.d: To give a pronunciation; to articulate; as, to pronounce faultlessly.
To make declaration; to utter on opinion; to speak with confidence.
Pronouncement; declaration; pronunciation.
Strongly marked; unequivocal; decided.
q: views became every day more pronounced.

senses.d: Pertaining to, or indicating, pronunciation; as, a pronouncing dictionary.
Any effort, process, or operation designed to establish or discover a fact or truth; an act of testing; a test; a trial.
q: For whatsoever mother wit or art Could work, he put in proof.
You shall have many proofs to show your skill.
Formerly, a very rude mode of ascertaining the strength of spirits was practiced, called the proof.

senses.d: That degree of evidence which convinces the mind of any truth or fact, and produces belief; a test by facts or arguments that induce, or tend to induce, certainty of the judgment; conclusive evidence; demonstration.
q: I'll have some proof.
It is no proof of a man's understanding to be able to confirm whatever he pleases.

senses.d: The quality or state of having been proved or tried; firmness or hardness that resists impression, or does not yield to force; impenetrability of physical bodies.
Firmness of mind; stability not to be shaken.
A trial impression, as from type, taken for correction or examination; — called also proof sheet.
A process for testing the accuracy of an operation performed. Cf. Prove, v. t., 5.
Armor of excellent or tried quality, and deemed impenetrable; properly, armor of proof.

Proof.syn: Testimony; evidence; reason; argument; trial; demonstration. See Testimony.
Proof.etym: [OF. prove, proeve, F. preuve, fr. L. proba, fr. probare to prove. See Prove.]

senses.d: Used in proving or testing; as, a proof load, or proof charge.
Firm or successful in resisting; as, proof against harm; waterproof; bombproof.
q: I . . . have found thee Proof against all temptation.
This was a good, stout proof article of faith.

senses.d: Being of a certain standard as to strength; — said of alcoholic liquors.
A shell, used as a die. See Props.
To support, or prevent from falling, by placing something under or against; as, to prop up a fence or an old building; (Fig.) to sustain; to maintain; as, to prop a declining state.
q: Till the bright mountains prop the incumbent sky.
For being not propp'd by ancestry.
I prop myself upon those few supports that are left me.

Prop.etym: [Akin to LG. & D. proppen to cram, stuff, thrust into, stop, G. pfropfen, Dan. proppe, Sw. proppa; of uncertain origin, cf. G. pfropfen to graft, fr. L. propago set, layer of a plant, slip, shoot. Cf. 3d. Prop, Propagate.]

senses.d: That which sustains an incumbent weight; that on which anything rests or leans for support; a support; a stay; as, a prop for a building.

Prop.etym: [Akin to LG., D., & Dan. prop stopple, stopper, cork, Sw. propp, G. pfropf. See Prop, v.]

senses.d: Belonging to one; one's own; individual.
q: Now learn the difference, at your proper cost, Betwixt true valor and an empty boast.

senses.d: Belonging to the natural or essential constitution; peculiar; not common; particular; as, every animal has his proper instincts and appetites.
q: Those high and peculiar attributes . . . which constitute our proper humanity.

senses.d: Befitting one's nature, qualities, etc.; suitable in all respect; appropriate; right; fit; decent; as, water is the proper element for fish; a proper dress.
q: The proper study of mankind is man.
In Athens all was pleasure, mirth, and play, All proper to the spring, and sprightly May.

senses.d: Becoming in appearance; well formed; handsome.
q: Moses . . . was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child.

senses.d: Pertaining to one of a species, but not common to the whole; not appellative; — opposed to common; as, a proper name; Dublin is the proper name of a city.
Rightly so called; strictly considered; as, Greece proper; the garden proper.
Represented in its natural color; — said of any object used as a charge.

Proper.etym: [OE. propre, F. propre, fr. L. proprius. Cf. Appropriate.]

senses.d: Properly; hence, to a great degree; very; as, proper good.
A declaration of something to come; a foretelling; a prediction; esp., an inspired foretelling.
q: He hearkens after prophecies and dreams.
Prophecy came not in old time by the will of man.

senses.d: A book of prophecies; a history; as, the prophecy of Ahijah.
Public interpretation of Scripture; preaching; exhortation or instruction.

Prophecy.etym: [OE. prophecie, OF. profecie, F. prophétie, L. prophetia, fr. Gr. �, fr. � to be an interpreter of the gods, to prophesy, fr. � prophet. See Prophet.]

senses.d: To foretell; to predict; to prognosticate.
q: He doth not prophesy good concerning me.
Then I perceive that will be verified Henry the Fifth did sometime prophesy.

senses.d: To foreshow; to herald; to prefigure.
q: Methought thy very gait did prophesy A royal nobleness; I must embrace thee.

senses.d: To utter predictions; to make declaration of events to come.
To give instruction in religious matters; to interpret or explain Scripture or religious subjects; to preach; to exhort; to expound.
One who prophesies, or foretells events; a predicter; a foreteller.
One inspired or instructed by God to speak in his name, or announce future events, as, Moses, Elijah, etc.
An interpreter; a spokesman.
A mantis.

Prophet.etym: [F. prophète, L. propheta, fr. Gr. �, literally, one who speaks for another, especially, one who speaks for a god an interprets his will to man, fr. � to say beforehand; � for, before + � to say or speak. See Fame. ]

senses.d: A female prophet.
The act of appeasing the wrath and conciliating the favor of an offended person; the act of making propitious.
That which propitiates; atonement or atoning sacrifice; specifically, the influence or effects of the death of Christ in appeasing the divine justice, and conciliating the divine favor.
q: He is the propitiation for our sins.

senses.d: The relation or adaptation of one portion to another, or to the whole, as respect magnitude, quantity, or degree; comparative relation; ratio; as, the proportion of the parts of a building, or of the body.
q: The image of Christ, made after his own proportion.
Formed in the best proportions of her sex.
Documents are authentic and facts are true precisely in proportion to the support which they afford to his theory.

senses.d: Harmonic relation between parts, or between different things of the same kind; symmetrical arrangement or adjustment; symmetry; as, to be out of proportion.
The portion one receives when a whole is distributed by a rule or principle; equal or proper share; lot.
q: Let the women . . . do the same things in their proportions and capacities.

senses.d: A part considered comparatively; a share.

The equality or similarity of ratios, especially of geometrical ratios; or a relation among quantities such that the quotient of the first divided by the second is equal to that of the third divided by the fourth; — called also geometrical proportion, in distinction from arithmetical proportion, or that in which the difference of the first and second is equal to the difference of the third and fourth.
The rule of three, in arithmetic, in which the three given terms, together with the one sought, are proportional.

Proportion.etym: [F., fr. L. proportio; pro before + portio part or share. See Portion.]

senses.d: To adjust in a suitable proportion, as one thing or one part to another; as, to proportion the size of a building to its height; to proportion our expenditures to our income.
q: In the loss of an object we do not proportion our grief to the real value . . . but to the value our fancies set upon it.

senses.d: To form with symmetry or suitableness, as the parts of the body.
q: Nature had proportioned her without any fault.

senses.d: To divide into equal or just shares; to apportion.

A new convert especially a convert to some religion or religious sect, or to some particular opinion, system, or party; thus, a Gentile converted to Judaism, or a pagan converted to Christianity, is a proselyte.
q: Ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte.
Fresh confidence the speculatist takes From every harebrained proselyte he makes.

Proselyte.etym: [OE. proselite, OF. proselite, F. proselytus, Gr. �, adj., that has come, n., a new comer, especially, one who has come over from heathenism to the Jewish religion; � toward, to + (prob.) the root of � to come.]

senses.d: To convert to some religion, opinion, or system; to bring over.
That which is embraced by eye in vision; the region which the eye overlooks at one time; view; scene; outlook.
q: His eye discovers unaware The goodly prospect of some foreign land.

senses.d: Especially, a picturesque or widely extended view; a landscape; hence, a sketch of a landscape.
q: I went to Putney . . . to take prospects in crayon.

senses.d: A position affording a fine view; a lookout.
q: Him God beholding from his prospect high.

senses.d: Relative position of the front of a building or other structure; face; relative aspect.
q: And their prospect was toward the south.

senses.d: The act of looking forward; foresight; anticipation; as, a prospect of the future state.
q: Is he a prudent man as to his temporal estate, that lays designs only for a day, without any prospect to, or provision for, the remaining part of life ?

senses.d: That which is hoped for; ground for hope or expectation; expectation; probable result; as, the prospect of success.
q: These swell their prospectsd exalt their pride, When offers are disdain'd, and love deny'd.

Prospect.etym: [L. prospectus, fr. prospicere, prospectum, to look forward; pro before, forward + specere, spicere, look, to see: cf. OF. prospect. See Spy, v., and cf. Prospectus.]

senses.d: To look over; to explore or examine for something; as, to prospect a district for gold.
To make a search; to seek; to explore, as for mines or the like; as, to prospect for gold.
To favor; to render successful.
q: All things concur toprosper our design.

Prosper.etym: [F. prospérer v. i., or L. prosperare, v. i., or L. prosperare, v. t., fr. prosper or prosperus. See Prosperous.]

senses.d: To be successful; to succeed; to be fortunate or prosperous; to thrive; to make gain.
q: They, in their earthly Canaan placed, Long time shall dwell and prosper.

senses.d: To grow; to increase.
q: Black cherry trees prosper even to considerable timber.

senses.d: The state of being prosperous; advance or gain in anything good or desirable; successful progress in any business or enterprise; attainment of the object desired; good fortune; success; as, commercial prosperity; national prosperity.
q: Now prosperity begins to mellow.
Prosperities can only be enjoyed by them who fear not at all to lose them.

Prosperity.syn: Prosperousness; thrift; weal; welfare; well being; happiness.

senses.d: Tending to prosperity; favoring; favorable; helpful.
q: A happy passage and a prosperous wind.

senses.d: Being prospered; advancing in the pursuit of anything desirable; making gain, or increase; thriving; successful; as, a prosperous voyage; a prosperous undertaking; a prosperous man or nation.
q: By moderation either state to bear Prosperous or adverse.

Prosperous.syn: Fortunate; successful; flourishing; thriving; favorable; auspicious; lucky. See Fortunate.
Prosperous.etym: [L. prosperus or prosper, originally, answering to hope; pro according to + the root of sperare to hope. See Despair.]

senses.d: To offer, as a woman, to a lewd use; to give up to lewdness for hire.
To devote to base or unworthy purposes; to give up to low or indiscriminate use; as, to prostitute talents; to prostitute official powers.

Prostitute.etym: [L. prostitutus, p. p. of prostituere to prostitute; pro before, forth + statuere to put, place. See Statute.]

senses.d: Openly given up to lewdness; devoted to base or infamous purposes.
q: Made bold by want, and prostitute for bread.

senses.d: A woman giver to indiscriminate lewdness; a strumpet; a harlot.
A base hireling; a mercenary; one who offers himself to infamous employments for hire.
q: No hireling she, no prostitute to praise.

senses.d: The act of protecting, or the state of being protected; preservation from loss, injury, or annoyance; defense; shelter; as, the weak need protection.
q: To your protection I commend me, gods.

senses.d: That which protects or preserves from injury; a defense; a shield; a refuge.
q: Let them rise up . . . and be your protection.

senses.d: A writing that protects or secures from molestation or arrest; a pass; a safe-conduct; a passport.
q: He . . . gave them protections under his hand.

senses.d: A theory, or a policy, of protecting the producers in a country from foreign competition in the home market by the imposition of such discriminating duties on goods of foreign production as will restrict or prevent their importation; — opposed to free trade.

Protection.syn: Preservation; defense; guard; shelter; refuge; security; safety.

senses.d: To affirm in a public or formal manner; to bear witness; to declare solemnly; to avow.
q: He protest that his measures are pacific.
The lady doth protest too much, methinks.

senses.d: To make a solemn declaration (often a written one) expressive of opposition; — with against; as, he protest against your votes.
q: The conscience has power . . . to protest againts the exorbitancies of the passions.

Protest.syn: To affirm; asseverate; assert; aver; attest; testify; declare; profess. See Affirm.
Protest.etym: [F. protester, L. protestari, pro before + testari to be a witness, testis a witness. See Testify.]

senses.d: To make a solemn declaration or affirmation of; to proclaim; to display; as, to protest one's loyalty.
q: I will protest your cowardice.

senses.d: To call as a witness in affirming or denying, or to prove an affirmation; to appeal to.
q: Fiercely opposed My journey strange, with clamorous uproar Protesting fate supreme.

senses.d: A solemn declaration of opinion, commonly a formal objection against some act; especially, a formal and solemn declaration, in writing, of dissent from the proceedings of a legislative body; as, the protest of lords in Parliament.

A solemn declaration in writing, in due form, made by a notary public, usually under his notarial seal, on behalf of the holder of a bill or note, protesting against all parties liable for any loss or damage by the nonacceptance or nonpayment of the bill, or by the nonpayment of the note, as the case may be.

Protest.etym: [Cf. F. protêt, It. protesto. See Protest, v.]

senses.d: Feeling or manifesting pride, in a good or bad sense
q: Nor much expect A foe so proud will first the weaker seek.
O death, made proud with pure and princely beauty !
And shades impervious to the proud world's glare.

senses.d: Having a feeling of high self-respect or self-esteem; exulting (in); elated; — often with of; as, proud of one's country.
q: Are we proud men proud of being proud ?

senses.d: Giving reason or occasion for pride or self-gratulation; worthy of admiration; grand; splendid; magnificent; admirable; ostentatious.
q: Till tower, and dome, and bridge-way proud Are mantled with a golden cloud.

senses.d: Excited by sexual desire; — applied particularly to the females of some animals.

Proud.etym: [OE. proud, prout, prud, prut, AS. prūt; akin to Icel. prūðr stately, handsome, Dan. prud handsome. Cf. Pride.]

senses.d: In a proud manner; with lofty airs or mien; haughtily; arrogantly; boastfully.
q: Proudly he marches on, and void of fear.

senses.d: To try or to ascertain by an experiment, or by a test or standard; to test; as, to prove the strength of gunpowder or of ordnance; to prove the contents of a vessel by a standard measure.
q: Thou hast proved mine heart.

senses.d: To evince, establish, or ascertain, as truth, reality, or fact, by argument, testimony, or other evidence.
q: They have inferred much from slender premises, and conjectured when they could not prove.

senses.d: To ascertain or establish the genuineness or validity of; to verify; as, to prove a will.
To gain experience of the good or evil of; to know by trial; to experience; to suffer.
q: Where she, captived long, great woes did prove.

senses.d: To test, evince, ascertain, or verify, as the correctness of any operation or result; thus, in subtraction, if the difference between two numbers, added to the lesser number, makes a sum equal to the greater, the correctness of the subtraction is proved.
To take a trial impression of; to take a proof of; as, to prove a page.

Prove.syn: To try; verify; justify; confirm; establish; evince; manifest; show; demonstrate.
Prove.etym: [OE. prover, F. prouver, fr. L. probare to try, approve, prove, fr. probus good, proper. Cf. Probable, Proof, Probe.]

senses.d: To make trial; to essay.
To be found by experience, trial, or result; to turn out to be; as, a medicine proves salutary; the report proves false.
q: So life a winter's morn may prove.

senses.d: To succeed; to turn out as expected.
Dry food for domestic animals, as hay, straw, corn, oats, or a mixture of ground grain; feed.
q: Good provender laboring horses would have.

senses.d: Food or provisions.

Provender.etym: [OE. provende, F. provende, provisions, provender, fr. LL. praebenda (prae and pro being confused), a daily allowance of provisions, a prebend. See Prebend.]

senses.d: An old and common saying; a phrase which is often repeated; especially, a sentence which briefly and forcibly expresses some practical truth, or the result of experience and observation; a maxim; a saw; an adage.
A striking or paradoxical assertion; an obscure saying; an enigma; a parable.
q: His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb.

senses.d: A familiar illustration; a subject of contemptuous reference.
q: Thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a by word, among all nations.

senses.d: A drama exemplifying a proverb.

Proverb.etym: [OE. proverbe, F. proverbe, from L. proverbium; pro before, for + verbum a word. See Verb.]

senses.d: To name in, or as, a proverb.
q: Am I not sung and proverbed for a fool ?

senses.d: To provide with a proverb.
q: I am proverbed with a grandsire phrase.

senses.d: To write or utter proverbs.
To look out for in advance; to procure beforehand; to get, collect, or make ready for future use; to prepare.
To supply; to afford; to contribute.
q: Bring me berries, or such cooling fruit As the kind, hospitable woods provide.

senses.d: To furnish; to supply; — formerly followed by of, now by with.
To establish as a previous condition; to stipulate; as, the contract provides that the work be well done.
To foresee.
To appoint to an ecclesiastical benefice before it is vacant. See Provisor.

Provide.etym: [L. providere, provisum; pro before + videre to see. See Vision, and cf. Prudent, Purvey.]

senses.d: To procure supplies or means in advance; to take measures beforehand in view of an expected or a possible future need, especially a danger or an evil; — followed by against or for; as, to provide against the inclemency of the weather; to provide for the education of a child.
q: Government is a contrivance of human wisdom to provide for human wants.

senses.d: To stipulate previously; to condition; as, the agreement provides for an early completion of the work.
On condition; by stipulation; with the understanding; if; — usually followed by that; as, provided that nothing in this act shall prejudice the rights of any person whatever.
q: Provided the deductions are logical, they seem almost indifferent to their truth.

senses.d: The act of providing or preparing for future use or application; a making ready; preparation.
q: Providence for war is the best prevention of it.

senses.d: Foresight; care; especially, the foresight and care which God manifests for his creatures; hence, God himself, regarded as exercising a constant wise prescience.
q: The world was all before them, where to choose Their place of rest, and Providence their guide.

senses.d: A manifestation of the care and superintendence which God exercises over his creatures; an event ordained by divine direction.
q: He that hath a numerous family, and many to provide for, needs a greater providence of God.

senses.d: Prudence in the management of one's concerns; economy; frugality.
q: It is a high point of providence in a prince to cast an eye rather upon actions than persons.

Providence.etym: [L. providentia: cf. F. providence. See Provident, and cf. Prudence.]

senses.d: A country or region, more or less remote from the city of Rome, brought under the Roman government; a conquered country beyond the limits of Italy.
A country or region dependent on a distant authority; a portion of an empire or state, esp. one remote from the capital.
A region of country; a tract; a district.
q: Over many a tract of heaven they marched, and many a province wide.
Other provinces of the intellectual world.

senses.d: A region under the supervision or direction of any special person; the district or division of a country, especially an ecclesiastical division, over which one has jurisdiction; as, the province of Canterbury, or that in which the archbishop of Canterbury exercises ecclesiastical authority.
The proper or appropriate business or duty of a person or body; office; charge; jurisdiction; sphere.
q: The woman'sprovince is to be careful in her economy, and chaste in her affection.

senses.d: Specif.: Any political division of the Dominion of Canada, having a governor, a local legislature, and representation in the Dominion parliament. Hence, colloquially, The Provinces, the Dominion of Canada.

Province.etym: [F., fr. L. provincia; prob. fr. pro before, for + the root of vincere to conquer. See Victor.]

senses.d: The act of providing, or making previous preparation.
That which is provided or prepared; that which is brought together or arranged in advance; measures taken beforehand; preparation.
q: Making provision for the relief of strangers.

senses.d: Especially, a stock of food; any kind of eatables collected or stored; — often in the plural.
q: And of provisions laid in large, For man and beast.

senses.d: That which is stipulated in advance; a condition; a previous agreement; a proviso; as, the provisions of a contract; the statute has many provisions.
A canonical term for regular induction into a benefice, comprehending nomination, collation, and installation.
A nomination by the pope to a benefice before it became vacant, depriving the patron of his right of presentation.

Provision.etym: [L. provisio: cf. F. provision. See Provide.]

senses.d: To supply with food; to victual; as, to provision a garrison.
q: They were provisioned for a journey.

senses.d: The act of provoking, or causing vexation or, anger.
That which provokes, or excites anger; the cause of resentment; as, to give provocation.
Incitement; stimulus; as, provocation to mirth.
Such prior insult or injury as may be supposed, under the circumstances, to create hot blood, and to excuse an assault made in retort or redress.
An appeal to a court.

To call forth; to call into being or action; esp., to incense to action, a faculty or passion, as love, hate, or ambition; hence, commonly, to incite, as a person, to action by a challenge, by taunts, or by defiance; to exasperate; to irritate; to offend intolerably; to cause to retaliate.
q: Obey his voice, provoke him not.
Ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath.
Such acts Of contumacy will provoke the Highest To make death in us live.
Can honor's voice provoke the silent dust?
To the poet the meaning is what he pleases to make it, what it provokes in his own soul.

Provoke.syn: To irritate; arouse; stir up; awake; excite; incite; anger. See Irritate.
Provoke.etym: [F. provoquer, L. provocare to call forth; pro forth + vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice, cry, call. See Voice.]

senses.d: To cause provocation or anger.
To appeal.
Having the power or quality of exciting resentment; tending to awaken passion or vexation; as, provoking words or treatment.
The quality or state of being prudent; wisdom in the way of caution and provision; discretion; carefulness; hence, also, economy; frugality.
q: Prudence is principally in reference to actions to be done, and due means, order, seasons, and method of doing or not doing.
Prudence supposes the value of the end to be assumed, and refers only to the adaptation of the means. It is the relation of right means for given ends.

Prudence.syn: Wisdom; forecast; providence; considerateness; judiciousness; discretion; caution; circumspection; judgment. See Wisdom.
Prudence.etym: [F., fr. L. prudentia, contr. from providentia. See Prudent, and cf. Providence.]

senses.d: Sagacious in adapting means to ends; circumspect in action, or in determining any line of conduct; practically wise; judicious; careful; discreet; sensible; — opposed to rash; as, a prudent man; dictated or directed by prudence or wise forethought; evincing prudence; as, prudent behavior.
q: Moses established a grave and prudent law.

senses.d: Frugal; economical; not extravagant; as, a prudent woman; prudent expenditure of money.

Prudent.syn: Cautious; wary; circumspect; considerate; discreet; judicious; provident; economical; frugal.
Prudent.etym: [L. prudens, -entis, contr. from providens: cf. F. prudent. See Provident.]

senses.d: In a prudent manner.
To lop or cut off the superfluous parts, branches, or shoots of; to clear of useless material; to shape or smooth by trimming; to trim: as, to prune trees; to prune an essay.
q: Taking into consideration how they are to be pruned and reformed.
Our delightful task To prune these growing plants, and tend these flowers.

senses.d: To cut off or cut out, as useless parts.
q: Horace will our superfluous branches prune.

senses.d: To preen; to prepare; to dress.
q: His royal bird Prunes the immortal wing and cloys his beak.

Prune.etym: [OE. proine, probably fr. F. provigner to lay down vine stocks for propagation; hence, probably, the meaning, to cut away superfluous shoots. See Provine.]

senses.d: To dress; to prink; -used humorously or in contempt.
A plum; esp., a dried plum, used in cookery; as, French or Turkish prunes; California prunes.

Prune.etym: [F. prune, from L. prunum a plum. See Plum.]

senses.d: The act of trimming, or removing what is superfluous.
That which is cast off by bird in pruning her feathers; leavings.
A lever; also, leverage.

Pry.etym: [Corrupted fr. prize a lever. See Prize, n.]

senses.d: To raise or move, or attempt to raise or move, with a pry or lever; to prize.
To peep narrowly; to gaze; to inspect closely; to attempt to discover something by a scrutinizing curiosity; — often implying reproach.
q: Watch thou and wake when others be asleep, To pry into the secrets of the state.

senses.d: Curious inspection; impertinent peeping.
A sacred song; a poetical composition for use in the praise or worship of God.
q: Humus devout and holy psalms Singing everlastingly.

senses.d: Especially, one of the hymns by David and others, collected into one book of the Old Testament, or a modern metrical version of such a hymn for public worship.

Psalm.etym: [OE. psalm, salm, AS. sealm, L. psalmus, psalma, fr. Gr. �, �, fr. � to pull, twitch, to play upon a stringed instrument, to sing to the harp: cf. OF. psalme, salme, F. psaume.]

senses.d: To extol in psalms; to sing; as, psalming his praises.
A writer or composer of sacred songs; — a title particularly applied to David and the other authors of the Scriptural psalms.
A clerk, precentor, singer, or leader of music, in the church.

Psalmist.etym: [L. psalmista, Gr. �: cf. F. psalmiste. See Psalm.]

senses.d: A stringed instrument of music used by the Hebrews, the form of which is not known.
q: Praise the Lord with harp; sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings.

Psaltery.etym: [OE. sautrie, OF. psalterie, F. psaltérion, L. psalterium psaltery, psalter, from Gr. �, fr. �. See Psalm, Psalter.]

senses.d: A farmer of the taxes and public revenues; hence, a collector of toll or tribute. The inferior officers of this class were often oppressive in their exactions, and were regarded with great detestation.
q: As Jesus at meat . . . many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.
How like a fawning publican he looks!

senses.d: The keeper of an inn or public house; one licensed to retail beer, spirits, or wine.

Publican.etym: [L. publicanus: cf. F. publicain. See Public.]

senses.d: To make public; to make known to mankind, or to people in general; to divulge, as a private transaction; to promulgate or proclaim, as a law or an edict.
q: Published was the bounty of her name.
The unwearied sun, from day to day, Does his Creator's power display, And publishes to every land The work of an almighty hand.

senses.d: To make known by posting, or by reading in a church; as, to publish banns of marriage.
To send forth, as a book, newspaper, musical piece, or other printed work, either for sale or for general distribution; to print, and issue from the press.
To utter, or put into circulation; as, to publish counterfeit paper.

Publish.syn: To announce; proclaim; advertise; declare; promulgate; disclose; divulge; reveal. See Announce.
Publish.etym: [F. publier, L. publicare, publicatum. See Public, and -ish.]

senses.d: A sudden and single emission of breath from the mouth; hence, any sudden or short blast of wind; a slight gust; a whiff.
Anything light and filled with air.
An exaggerated or empty expression of praise, especially one in a public journal.

Puff.etym: [Akin to G. & Sw. puff a blow, Dan. puf, D. pof; of imitative origin. Cf. Buffet.]

senses.d: To blow in puffs, or with short and sudden whiffs.
To blow, as an expression of scorn; — with at.
q: It is really to defy Heaven to puff at damnation.

senses.d: To breathe quick and hard, or with puffs, as after violent exertion.
q: The ass comes back again, puffing and blowing, from the chase.

senses.d: To swell with air; to be dilated or inflated.
To breathe in a swelling, inflated, or pompous manner; hence, to assume importance.
q: Then came brave Glory puffing by.

Puff.etym: [Akin to G. puffen to pop, buffet, puff, D. poffen to pop, puffen to blow, Sw. puffa to push, to cuff, Dan. puffe to pop, thump. See Puff, n.]

senses.d: To drive with a puff, or with puffs.
q: The clearing north will puff the clouds away.

senses.d: To repel with words; to blow at contemptuously.
q: I puff the prostitute away.

senses.d: To cause to swell or dilate; to inflate; to ruffle with puffs; — often with up; as, a bladder puffed with air.
q: The sea puffed up with winds.

senses.d: To inflate with pride, flattery, self-esteem, or the like; — often with up.
q: Puffed up with military success.

senses.d: To praise with exaggeration; to flatter; to call public attention to by praises; to praise unduly.
Puffed up; vain.
To draw, or attempt to draw, toward one; to draw forcibly.
q: Ne'er pull your hat upon your brows.
He put forth his hand . . . and pulled her in.

senses.d: To draw apart; to tear; to rend.
q: He hath turned aside my ways, and pulled me in pieces; he hath made me desolate.

senses.d: To gather with the hand, or by drawing toward one; to pluck; as, to pull fruit; to pull flax; to pull a finch.
To move or operate by the motion of drawing towards one; as, to pull a bell; to pull an oar.
To hold back, and so prevent from winning; as, the favorite was pulled.
To take or make, as a proof or impression; — hand presses being worked by pulling a lever.
To strike the ball in a particular manner. See Pull, n., 8.
q: Never pull a straight fast ball to leg.

Pull.etym: [AS. pullian; cf. LG. pulen, and Gael. peall, piol, spiol.]

senses.d: To exert one's self in an act or motion of drawing or hauling; to tug; as, to pull at a rope.
The act of pulling or drawing with force; an effort to move something by drawing toward one.
q: I awakened with a violent pull upon the ring which was fastened at the top of my box.

senses.d: A contest; a struggle; as, a wrestling pull.
A pluck; loss or violence suffered.
q: Two pulls at once; His lady banished, and a limb lopped off.

senses.d: A knob, handle, or lever, etc., by which anything is pulled; as, a drawer pull; a bell pull.
The act of rowing; as, a pull on the river.
The act of drinking; as, to take a pull at the beer, or the mug.
Something in one's favor in a comparison or a contest; an advantage; means of influencing; as, in weights the favorite had the pull.
A kind of stroke by which a leg ball is sent to the off side, or an off ball to the side.
q: The pull is not a legitimate stroke, but bad cricket.

senses.d: Plucked; pilled; moulting.
An elevated place, or inclosed stage, in a church, in which the clergyman stands while preaching.
q: I stand like a clerk in my pulpit.

senses.d: The whole body of the clergy; preachers as a class; also, preaching.
q: I say the pulpit (in the sober use Of its legitimate, peculiar powers) Must stand acknowledged, while the world shall stand, The most important and effectual guard, Support, and ornament of virtue's cause.

senses.d: A desk, or platform, for an orator or public speaker.

Pulpit.etym: [L. pulpitum: cf. OF. pulpite, F. pulpitre.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the pulpit, or preaching; as, a pulpit orator; pulpit eloquence.
Leguminous plants, or their seeds, as beans, pease, etc.
q: If all the world Should, in a pet of temperance, feed on pulse.

Pulse.etym: [OE. puls, L. puls, pultis, a thick pap or pottage made of meal, pulse, etc. See Poultice, and cf. Pousse.]

senses.d: The beating or throbbing of the heart or blood vessels, especially of the arteries.
Any measured or regular beat; any short, quick motion, regularly repeated, as of a medium in the transmission of light, sound, etc.; oscillation; vibration; pulsation; impulse; beat; movement.
q: The measured pulse of racing oars.
When the ear receives any simple sound, it is struck by a single pulse of the air, which makes the eardrum and the other membranous parts vibrate according to the nature and species of the stroke.

Pulse.etym: [OE. pous, OF. pous, F. pouls, fr. L. pulsus (sc. venarum), the beating of the pulse, the pulse, from pellere, pulsum, to beat, strike; cf. Gr. � to swing, shake, � to shake. Cf. Appeal, Compel, Impel, Push.]

senses.d: To beat, as the arteries; to move in pulses or beats; to pulsate; to throb.
To drive by a pulsation; to cause to pulsate.

To impose a penalty upon; to afflict with pain, loss, or suffering for a crime or fault, either with or without a view to the offender's amendment; to cause to suffer in retribution; to chasten; as, to punish traitors with death; a father punishes his child for willful disobedience.
q: A greater power Now ruled him, punished in the shape he sinned.

senses.d: To inflict a penalty for (an offense) upon the offender; to repay, as a fault, crime, etc., with pain or loss; as, to punish murder or treason with death.
To injure, as by beating; to pommel.

Punish.syn: To chastise; castigate; scourge; whip; lash; correct; discipline. See Chasten.
Punish.etym: [OE. punischen, F. punir, from L. punire, punitum, akin to poena punishment, penalty. See Pain, and -ish.]

senses.d: To deal with roughly or harshly; — chiefly used with regard to a contest; as, our troops punished the enemy.
The act of punishing.
Any pain, suffering, or loss inflicted on a person because of a crime or offense.
q: I never gave them condign punishment.
The rewards and punishments of another life.

senses.d: A penalty inflicted by a court of justice on a convicted offender as a just retribution, and incidentally for the purposes of reformation and prevention.
Severe, rough, or disastrous treatment.
To utter a low, murmuring, continued sound, as a cat does when pleased.

Pur.etym: [Of imitative origin; cf. Prov. G. purren.]

senses.d: To signify or express by purring.
The low, murmuring sound made by a cat to express contentment or pleasure.
To pursue and obtain; to acquire by seeking; to gain, obtain, or acquire.
q: That loves the thing he can not purchase.
Your accent is Something finer than you could purchase in so removed a dwelling.
His faults . . . hereditary Rather than purchased.

senses.d: To obtain by paying money or its equivalent; to buy for a price; as, to purchase land, or a house.
q: The field which Abraham purchased of the sons of Heth.

senses.d: To obtain by any outlay, as of labor, danger, or sacrifice, etc.; as, to purchase favor with flattery.
q: One poor retiring minute . . . Would purchase thee a thousand thousand friends.
A world who would not purchase with a bruise?

senses.d: To expiate by a fine or forfeit.
q: Not tears nor prayers shall purchase out abuses.

senses.d: To acquire by any means except descent or inheritance.
To apply to (anything) a device for obtaining a mechanical advantage; to get a purchase upon, or apply a purchase to; as, to purchase a cannon.

Purchase.etym: [OE. purchasen, porchacen, OF. porchacier, purchacier, to pursue, to seek eagerly, F. pourchasser; OF. pour, por, pur, for (L. pro) + chacier to pursue, to chase. See Chase.]

senses.d: To put forth effort to obtain anything; to strive; to exert one's self.
q: Duke John of Brabant purchased greatly that the Earl of Flanders should have his daughter in marriage.

senses.d: To acquire wealth or property.
q: Sure our lawyers Would not purchase half so fast.

senses.d: The act of seeking, getting, or obtaining anything.
q: I'll . . . get meat to have thee, Or lose my life in the purchase.

senses.d: The act of seeking and acquiring property.
The acquisition of title to, or properly in, anything for a price; buying for money or its equivalent.
q: It is foolish to lay out money in the purchase of repentance.

senses.d: That which is obtained, got, or acquired, in any manner, honestly or dishonestly; property; possession; acquisition.
q: We met with little purchase upon this coast, except two small vessels of Golconda.
A beauty-waning and distressed widow . . . Made prize and purchase of his lustful eye.

senses.d: That which is obtained for a price in money or its equivalent.

Any mechanical hold, or advantage, applied to the raising or removing of heavy bodies, as by a lever, a tackle, capstan, and the like; also, the apparatus, tackle, or device by which the advantage is gained.
q: A politician, to do great things, looks for a power — what our workmen call a purchase.

senses.d: Acquisition of lands or tenements by other means than descent or inheritance, namely, by one's own act or agreement.

Purchase.etym: [OE. purchds, F. pourchas eager pursuit. See Purchase, v. t.]

senses.d: Separate from all heterogeneous or extraneous matter; free from mixture or combination; clean; mere; simple; unmixed; as, pure water; pure clay; pure air; pure compassion.
q: The pure fetters on his shins great.
A guinea is pure gold if it has in it no alloy.

senses.d: Free from moral defilement or quilt; hence, innocent; guileless; chaste; — applied to persons.
q: Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience.

senses.d: Free from that which harms, vitiates, weakens, or pollutes; genuine; real; perfect; — applied to things and actions.
q: Such was the origin of a friendship as warm and pure as any that ancient or modern history records.

senses.d: Ritually clean; fitted for holy services.
q: Thou shalt set them in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the Lord.

senses.d: Of a single, simple sound or tone; — said of some vowels and the unaspirated consonants.

Pure.syn: Unmixed; clear; simple; real; true; genuine; unadulterated; uncorrupted; unsullied; untarnished; unstained; stainless; clean; fair; unspotted; spotless; incorrupt; chaste; unpolluted; undefiled; immaculate; innocent; guiltless; guileless; holy.
Pure.etym: [OE. pur, F. pur, fr. L. purus; akin to putus pure, clear, putare to clean, trim, prune, set in order, settle, reckon, consider, think, Skr. p� to clean, and perh. E. fire. Cf. Putative.]

senses.d: In a pure manner (in any sense of the adjective).
Nicely; prettily.
The state of being pure (in any sense of the adjective).
To cleanse, clear, or purify by separating and carrying off whatever is impure, heterogeneous, foreign, or superfluous.
To operate on as, or by means of, a cathartic medicine, or in a similar manner.
To clarify; to defecate, as liquors.
To clear of sediment, as a boiler, or of air, as a steam pipe, by driving off or permitting escape.
To clear from guilt, or from moral or ceremonial defilement; as, to purge one of guilt or crime.
q: When that he hath purged you from sin.
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean.

senses.d: To clear from accusation, or the charge of a crime or misdemeanor, as by oath or in ordeal.
To remove in cleansing; to deterge; to wash away; — often followed by away.
q: Purge away our sins, for thy name's sake.
We 'll join our cares to purge away Our country's crimes.

Purge.etym: [F. purger, L. purgare; purus pure + agere to make, to do. See Pure, and Agent.]

senses.d: To become pure, as by clarification.
To have or produce frequent evacuations from the intestines, as by means of a cathartic.
The act of purging.
q: The preparative for the purge of paganism of the kingdom of Northumberland.

senses.d: That which purges; especially, a medicine that evacuates the intestines; a cathartic.

Purge.etym: [Cf. F. purge. See Purge, v. t.]

senses.d: That purges; cleansing.
The act of cleansing; excessive evacuations; especially, diarrhea.
The act of purifying; the act or operation of separating and removing from anything that which is impure or noxious, or heterogeneous or foreign to it; as, the purification of liquors, or of metals.
The act or operation of cleansing ceremonially, by removing any pollution or defilement.
q: When the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished.

senses.d: A cleansing from guilt or the pollution of sin; the extinction of sinful desires, appetites, and inclinations.
One who, or that which, purifies or cleanses; a cleanser; a refiner.
To make pure or clear from material defilement, admixture, or imperfection; to free from extraneous or noxious matter; as, to purify liquors or metals; to purify the blood; to purify the air.
Hence, in figurative uses: (a) To free from guilt or moral defilement; as, to purify the heart.
q: And fit them so Purified to receive him pure.

senses.d: To free from ceremonial or legal defilement.
q: And Moses took the blood, and put it upon the horns of the altar, . . . and purified the altar.
Purify both yourselves and your captives.

senses.d: To free from improprieties or barbarisms; as, to purify a language.

Purify.etym: [F. purifier, L. purificare; purus pure + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Pure, and -fy.]

senses.d: To grow or become pure or clear.
A Jewish festival, called also the Feast of Lots, instituted to commemorate the deliverance of the Jews from the machinations of Haman.
The condition of being pure.
freedom from foreign admixture or deleterious matter; as, the purity of water, of wine, of drugs, of metals.
Cleanness; freedom from foulness or dirt.
Freedom from guilt or the defilement of sin; innocence; chastity; as, purity of heart or of life.
Freedom from any sinister or improper motives or views.
Freedom from foreign idioms, or from barbarous or improper words or phrases; as, purity of style.

Purity.etym: [OE. purete, purte, OF. purté, F. pureté, from L. puritas, fr. purus pure. See Pure.]

senses.d: To take or carry away for one's self; hence, to steal; to take by theft; to filch.
q: Had from his wakeful custody purloined The guarded gold.
when did the muse from Fletcher scenes purloin ?

Purloin.etym: [OF. purloignier, porloignier, to retard, delay; pur, por, pour, for (L. pro) + loin far, far off (L. longe). See Prolong, and cf. Eloign.]

senses.d: To practice theft; to steal.
A color formed by, or resembling that formed by, a combination of the primary colors red and blue.
q: Arraying with reflected purple and gold The clouds that on his western throne attend.

senses.d: Cloth dyed a purple color, or a garment of such color; especially, a purple robe, worn as an emblem of rank or authority; specifically, the purple rode or mantle worn by Roman emperors as the emblem of imperial dignity; as, to put on the imperial purple.
q: Thou shalt make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen, and purple, and scarlet.

senses.d: Hence: Imperial sovereignty; royal rank, dignity, or favor; loosely and colloquially, any exalted station; great wealth.
A cardinalate. See Cardinal.
Any species of large butterflies, usually marked with purple or blue, of the genus Basilarchia (formerly Limenitis) as, the banded purple (B. arthemis). See Illust. under Ursula.
Any shell of the genus Purpura.
A disease of wheat. Same as Earcockle.

Purple.etym: [OE. purpre, pourpre, OF. purpre, porpre, pourpre, F. pourpre, L. purpura purple fish, purple dye, fr. Gr. � the purple fish, a shell from the purple dye was obtained, purple dye; cf. � dark (said of the sea), purple, � to grow dark (said of the sea), to be troubled; perh. akin to L. furere to rage,

senses.d: Exhibiting or possessing the color called purple, much esteemed for its richness and beauty; of a deep red, or red and blue color; as, a purple robe.
Imperial; regal; — so called from the color having been an emblem of imperial authority.
q: Hide in the dust thy purple pride.

senses.d: Blood-red; bloody.
q: May such purple tears be alway shed.
